2027-05-02.title: Sixth Sunday of Easter
readings: The gift of the Holy Spirit had been poured out even on the Gentiles
The Lord has revealed to the nations his saving power (or: Alleluia)
No one has greater love than this, to lay down one's life for one's friends
2027-05-02.alt: Year B. Gloria and Creed. The memorial of St Athanasius (2 May) is not kept, because a Sunday of Easter takes precedence. Where the Ascension is celebrated on the Seventh Sunday of Easter, as in India this year (Sunday 9 May), the Lectionary allows the second reading and Gospel of the Seventh Sunday (1 John 4:11–16; John 17:11b–19) to be read today; the readings of the Sixth Sunday are given here. Regina Caeli at noon until Pentecost. Liturgical colour: white.
2027-05-02.verse: This is my commandment, that you love one another as I have loved you.
theo: The first reading takes us to Caesarea, the Roman port city on the coast of Judea, and to the house of a Roman army officer. Cornelius is a centurion, “a devout man who feared God with all his household,” who gave alms and prayed constantly. An angel has told him to send for Peter; Peter, meanwhile, has seen a strange vision on a rooftop in Joppa and has heard a voice: “What God has made clean, you must not call profane.” Now Peter enters the house of a Gentile, something a devout Jew of the time would not normally do. Cornelius falls at his feet to worship him, “But Peter made him get up, saying, ‘Stand up; I am only a mortal.’” Then Peter speaks words that open a new chapter in the history of the Church: “I truly understand that God shows no partiality, but in every nation anyone who fears him and does what is right is acceptable to him.” And before Peter has even finished, God himself settles the question: “the Holy Spirit fell upon all who heard the word.” The Jewish believers who came with Peter are astounded “that the gift of the Holy Spirit had been poured out even on the Gentiles,” for they hear them “speaking in tongues and extolling God.” It is a Pentecost in a Gentile home. Peter can only draw the conclusion: “Can anyone withhold the water for baptizing these people who have received the Holy Spirit just as we have?” And he orders them to be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ.

The Psalm sings what Caesarea shows: “O sing to the Lord a new song, for he has done marvelous things.” “The Lord has made known his victory; he has revealed his vindication in the sight of the nations.” The God of Israel “has remembered his steadfast love and faithfulness to the house of Israel,” and now “all the ends of the earth have seen the victory of our God.” The faithfulness of God to his own people does not shut the door to the nations; it is the door through which they come in.

The second reading gives us the shortest and perhaps the deepest definition of God in the whole Bible: “God is love.” St John does not say that God has love, or that God sometimes loves, but that love is what God is. That is why “everyone who loves is born of God and knows God,” and “whoever does not love does not know God.” Then John tells us what kind of love he means, so that we do not confuse it with a feeling: “In this is love, not that we loved God but that he loved us and sent his Son to be the atoning sacrifice for our sins.” Love begins with God, not with us. It is first received, then given. Our love for one another is not the starting point of religion but its fruit.

The Gospel continues the Last Supper discourse, just after the image of the vine heard last Sunday. Jesus now speaks of the source of the vine's life: “As the Father has loved me, so I have loved you; abide in my love.” There is a chain of love: from the Father to the Son, from the Son to the disciples, and from the disciples to one another. “This is my commandment, that you love one another as I have loved you.” The measure is not “as you love yourself” but “as I have loved you,” and within hours he will show what that means: “No one has greater love than this, to lay down one's life for one's friends.” Then comes one of the most moving sentences Jesus ever spoke: “I do not call you servants any longer, because the servant does not know what the master is doing; but I have called you friends.” God's own Son calls us his friends, and he shares with us all that he has heard from the Father. And it is his choice before it is ours: “You did not choose me but I chose you. And I appointed you to go and bear fruit, fruit that will last.” At Caesarea the friendship of Jesus reached people whom many thought could never be his friends. Today, as the Ascension and Pentecost draw near, the same Spirit reminds the Church that no one is outside the reach of that love.
conn: Caesarea.

Caesarea Maritima, the port built by Herod the Great on the Mediterranean coast and the seat of the Roman governor of Judea. Pilate lived there; an inscription bearing his name was found in its theatre in 1961.
Cornelius.

A centurion, commander of about a hundred soldiers, of “the Italian Cohort” (Acts 10:1). Luke calls him one who “feared God”: a Gentile who worshipped the God of Israel and prayed, without becoming a Jew.
“No partiality.”

The Greek word behind “shows no partiality” (prosōpolēmptēs) means, literally, one who receives faces, who judges by appearance. The Old Testament already says that God “is not partial” (Deuteronomy 10:17).
The Gentile Pentecost.
The Spirit falls on Cornelius's household before Baptism, so that no one can deny that God has accepted them. Peter will appeal to this event at the council of Jerusalem (Acts 15:7–9).
The reading's omissions.

The Lectionary skips Acts 10:27–33 (Peter's arrival and Cornelius's account) and 10:36–43 (Peter's summary of the life, death and resurrection of Jesus), so that the reading moves straight from Peter's principle to the gift of the Spirit.
Psalm 98.
A hymn to God the King and his victory. Its call for a “new song” was heard by the early Church as the song of the Resurrection.
“God is love.”
1 John 4:8 and again 4:16. The Greek word is agapē, self-giving love. Pope Benedict XVI began his first encyclical, Deus Caritas Est (2005), with this verse.
“Atoning sacrifice.”
Greek hilasmos (1 John 2:2; 4:10): the offering that takes away sin and restores communion. Love is shown above all in the Cross.
Friends.

In the ancient world the “friend of the king” was a trusted counsellor who knew the king's mind. In the Old Testament Abraham is called the friend of God (Isaiah 41:8), and the Lord spoke to Moses “as one speaks to a friend” (Exodus 33:11). Jesus gives this title to all his disciples.
The Seventh Sunday option.

Because India keeps the Ascension on Sunday 9 May, the readings of the Seventh Sunday of Easter will not be heard this year; the Lectionary therefore permits its second reading and Gospel to be used today. Parishes follow the local Ordo.
altar: “No one has greater love than this, to lay down one's life for one's friends.” At every Mass that love is made present: the one sacrifice of the Cross is offered sacramentally on the altar, and the Lord who calls us friends gives us his Body and Blood as the food of friendship.
The Eucharist is the meal of friends to whom the Master has told everything. In it we receive the love with which the Father loves the Son, so that we may love one another as he has loved us.
outline: Opening
Ask: who are your real friends? How do you know?
Point 1 · God shows no partiality
Peter in the house of Cornelius.
Point 2 · God is love
Love begins with God and is first received.
Point 3 · As I have loved you
The new measure: the Cross.
Point 4 · I have called you friends
Chosen and sent to bear fruit that lasts.
Closing image
A crowded Gentile household in Caesarea, everyone praising God, and Peter calling for water.
Take-home line
“I have called you friends.”
live: Cross a line of partiality
This week, greet, welcome or eat with someone from a different community, caste, language or background, as Peter entered the house of Cornelius.
Receive before you give
Begin each day with one minute of thanks: Lord, you loved me first. Let your love be the source of mine today.
Love as he loved
Choose one person who is hard to love and do one concrete thing for them that costs you time or pride.
Live as a friend
Talk to Jesus this week as to a friend: tell him honestly about your day each night, and listen.
fathers: St Gregory the Great (in substance)

All the commands of the Lord are about love, and yet he speaks of love as one commandment. Why? Because as many branches spring from one root, so many virtues are born from the one root of charity; a branch of good work has no greenness unless it stays in the root of love.
St Augustine (in substance)
Let us love God, for he first loved us. We could not love him unless he had first loved us; our love for him is his gift, poured into our hearts by the Holy Spirit.
St Thomas Aquinas (in substance)
Charity is a kind of friendship of the human person with God, founded on God sharing his own happiness with us. This is why Jesus can say: I have called you friends.
St John Chrysostom (in substance)

Peter did not say, God accepts people of every nation without faith; he said, the one who fears him and does what is right is acceptable, that is, worthy to be called to faith. God looks not at a person's race but at the heart.
magis: Catechism 221
St John goes further when he affirms that God is love: God's very being is love, and he has destined us to share in that exchange of love.
Catechism 1823–1825
Jesus makes charity the new commandment: by loving his own to the end he shows the Father's love; Christ died out of love for us while we were still enemies.
Catechism 1828

The moral life animated by charity gives the Christian the spiritual liberty of the children of God; he no longer stands before God as a slave in servile fear but as a child, responding to the love of him who first loved us.
Lumen Gentium 9
At all times and in every race God has given welcome to whoever fears him and does what is right (Acts 10:35); yet he willed to make people holy and save them not as individuals but as one people.
Deus Caritas Est 1 (Benedict XVI, 2005)
“God is love, and those who abide in love abide in God, and God abides in them”: these words express the heart of the Christian faith; being Christian begins with an encounter with a Person.
saints: St Athanasius (not kept this year)
Bishop of Alexandria (about 296 to 373), Doctor of the Church, who defended the true divinity of Christ against the Arians and was exiled five times. His memorial gives way to the Sunday.
This week

3 May: Sts Philip and James, Apostles (feast). 4–5 May: Easter weekdays. 6 May: in India an Easter weekday (where the Ascension is kept on Thursday, it is celebrated that day). 7 May: First Friday. 9 May: in India, the Ascension of the Lord.
2027-05-02.prayer: Father, you are love, and you loved us first: you sent your Son as the atoning sacrifice for our sins, and in him you show no partiality, but welcome everyone who fears you and does what is right. Lord Jesus, you call us no longer servants but friends; keep us in your love as you abide in the Father's love, and teach us to love one another as you have loved us, even to laying down our lives. Pour out your Holy Spirit on us, as on the household of Cornelius, so that we may sing a new song and bear fruit that will last. With the Blessed Virgin Mary, whom we honour this month, we ask this in your name, who live and reign for ever and ever. Alleluia. Amen.

2027-05-06.title: Thursday of the Sixth Week of Easter
readings: Paul stayed with Aquila and Priscilla and worked with them, and every sabbath he argued in the synagogue
The Lord has revealed to the nations his saving power (or: Alleluia)
You will have pain, but your pain will turn into joy
2027-05-06.alt: Easter weekday. The paschal candle burns beside the ambo; the Alleluia is sung before the Gospel; the Regina Caeli (Queen of Heaven) replaces the Angelus until Pentecost. Liturgical colour: white. In India the Solemnity of the Ascension of the Lord is transferred to Sunday 9 May, so today the Easter weekday is celebrated with these readings. Where the Ascension is kept on this Thursday, the fortieth day after Easter (for example in the Vatican and a number of other countries), today is the Solemnity of the Ascension, a holy day of obligation there.
2027-05-06.verse: Very truly, I tell you, you will weep and mourn, but the world will rejoice; you will have pain, but your pain will turn into joy.
theo: Paul has left Athens, where only a handful of people believed, and has come to Corinth. It was a very different city: a busy Roman colony on the narrow neck of land between two seas, with a harbour on each side, full of sailors, traders, slaves, soldiers and pilgrims to its temples. There Paul finds a Jewish couple, Aquila and Priscilla, “who had recently come from Italy … because Claudius had ordered all Jews to leave Rome.” The Roman historian Suetonius also mentions that expulsion, around the year 49. Paul goes to see them, “and, because he was of the same trade, he stayed with them.” They were tentmakers, workers in leather and cloth. The great apostle of the nations earns his bread with a needle and a knife in a workshop, and on the sabbath he goes to the synagogue “and would try to convince Jews and Greeks.” When Silas and Timothy arrive from Macedonia, perhaps bringing a gift from the Philippians, Paul is able to give himself entirely to “proclaiming the word, testifying to the Jews that the Messiah was Jesus.”

Not everyone welcomes the message. Some in the synagogue oppose Paul, and he makes a solemn gesture: he shakes out his clothes and declares that he is now going to the Gentiles. But notice where he goes: next door, to the house of Titius Justus, “a worshiper of God,” whose house stands right beside the synagogue. Paul does not walk away from his people in anger; he stays close. And the very next line tells us that “Crispus, the official of the synagogue, became a believer in the Lord, together with all his household,” and that “many of the Corinthians who heard Paul became believers and were baptized.” Years later Paul will remember that he baptized Crispus with his own hands (1 Corinthians 1:14). The reading is not a story of Jews against Christians: it is a story of one Jewish community in which some believed and some did not, and of a Jewish apostle, working beside Jewish friends, who opened the door of the Messiah to everyone. The Psalm sings the meaning of it: “All the ends of the earth have seen the victory of our God.”

The Gospel takes us back to the Last Supper. Jesus says something the disciples cannot understand: “A little while, and you will no longer see me, and again a little while, and you will see me.” They whisper among themselves: “What does he mean by this ‘a little while’? We do not know what he is talking about.” Jesus does not explain the timetable. He tells them what the waiting will feel like: “you will weep and mourn, but the world will rejoice; you will have pain, but your pain will turn into joy.” He does not say that the pain will be replaced by joy, as if it were thrown away; he says it will turn into joy, as the cross itself became the sign of victory. The first “little while” was the three days of the Passion. But the Fathers heard a second meaning too: the whole time of the Church, between the Ascension and the Lord's return, is also “a little while.” Today, in Rome and in many places, the Church celebrates the Ascension, the day the disciples stopped seeing Jesus with their eyes. In India we shall celebrate it on Sunday. Either way, we are the people of the little while: we do not yet see him, and we are learning, in work and witness like Paul's, to let our pains be turned into joy.
conn: Corinth.

A Roman colony and the capital of the province of Achaia, on the isthmus between the Gulf of Corinth and the Saronic Gulf, with the ports of Lechaeum and Cenchreae. Paul stayed there about eighteen months (Acts 18:11) and later wrote at least two letters to its church.
Aquila and Priscilla.

A Jewish married couple, Aquila from Pontus on the Black Sea. Paul calls them “Prisca and Aquila, who work with me in Christ Jesus” (Romans 16:3). They are named six times in the New Testament, and Priscilla is usually named first.
The edict of Claudius.

The emperor Claudius (41–54) expelled Jews from Rome because of disturbances, which Suetonius links to someone called “Chrestus,” probably a garbled form of Christus. The date is usually given as about AD 49.
Tentmakers.
The Greek skēnopoioi means makers of tents, probably working in leather. Paul supported himself by his trade so as not to be a burden to his churches (1 Thessalonians 2:9; Acts 20:34).
Shaking out his clothes.

A prophetic gesture: I am not responsible for your refusal. Jesus told the Twelve to shake the dust from their feet where they were not received (Luke 9:5); Paul did so at Antioch in Pisidia (Acts 13:51).
Titius Justus and Crispus.
A God-fearing Gentile and the official of the synagogue, the man who arranged its services. Paul names Crispus among the few he baptized himself (1 Corinthians 1:14).
“A little while.”
The Greek mikron occurs seven times in John 16:16–19. The repetition shows how puzzled the disciples were, and how gently Jesus stays with their question.
Ascension Thursday and India.

Acts 1:3 speaks of forty days of appearances, so the Ascension falls on the fortieth day, a Thursday. Many bishops' conferences, including those of India, transfer it to the following Sunday so that the whole people can celebrate it.
altar: Paul's needle and Christ's altar belong together: at every Mass the priest offers bread, “fruit of the earth and work of human hands.” Our work, our tents and tools and kitchens, is carried to the altar and joined to the sacrifice of Christ.

In the “little while” of the Church we do not see the Lord with our eyes, yet he is not absent. Under the signs of bread and wine he is truly present, Body and Blood, soul and divinity, until he comes again.
outline: Opening
Hold up a needle and thread. Ask: can a needle preach the Gospel?
Point 1 · Because he was of the same trade
Paul the worker beside Aquila and Priscilla.
Point 2 · Next door to the synagogue
Rejection, perseverance, and Crispus who believed.
Point 3 · A little while
Pain that turns into joy.
Closing image
A tent-maker's workshop in Corinth at dusk, the work laid down, and three friends praying together over bread.
Take-home line
“Your pain will turn into joy.”
live: Work as witness
Do your work today, at home, office, field or school, as carefully as if Christ were your customer. Offer it to him at the start.
Stay next door
Think of someone who rejected your faith or your kindness. Do not cut them off; stay near, pray for them, keep the door open.
Name the little while
Write down one sorrow you are carrying now. Pray over it: Lord, turn this pain into joy, in your time.
fathers: St Augustine (in substance)
This “little while” is the whole space of the present age. It seems long to us while it lasts; when it is over, we shall see how short it was. Let us wait for the joy that no one can take from us.
St John Chrysostom (in substance)
Paul was not ashamed to sit in a workshop and stitch skins, and from that workshop he spoke to the world. The needle did not lessen the apostle; it showed his greatness.
St Benedict (Rule, ch. 48, in substance)

Idleness is the enemy of the soul. Let the brothers be busy at fixed times with the work of their hands, and at other times with sacred reading; then they are truly monks, when they live by the labour of their hands, like our fathers and the apostles.
magis: Catechism 2427
Human work proceeds directly from persons created in the image of God; by work we share in the work of creation, and work united to Christ can be redemptive.
Laborem Exercens 6 (St John Paul II, 1981)
Work is for the human person, not the person for work; Jesus the carpenter shows the dignity of every kind of labour.
Catechism 1820
Christian hope unfolds from the beginning of Jesus' preaching; it sustains us in the time of trial and opens us to the joy of heaven.
Nostra Aetate 4 (Vatican II, 1965)
The Church remembers the spiritual bond that ties the people of the New Covenant to Abraham's stock; what happened in the Passion cannot be charged against all Jews, then or now.
Catechism 659–664
The Ascension: the risen Christ enters into divine glory and is seated at the right hand of the Father, from where he will come again.
saints: St Dominic Savio

A pupil of St John Bosco in Turin, who died in 1857 aged fourteen and was canonized in 1954. His resolution at his First Communion was “death rather than sin.” The Salesian family keeps his feast on 6 May; he is a patron of choirboys and of expectant mothers.
This week
7 May: First Friday; the novena to the Holy Spirit may begin. 9 May: THE ASCENSION OF THE LORD (in India); World Communications Day. 10 May: St John of Avila (optional). 11 May: Easter weekday.
2027-05-06.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, risen from the dead, you said to your friends: a little while, and you will no longer see me, and again a little while, and you will see me. We live in that little while. When we weep and mourn, stay near us; when the world laughs at our faith, keep us steady; and turn our pain into joy, as you turned the cross into the tree of life. Bless the work of our hands, as you blessed Paul and Aquila and Priscilla in their workshop. Let our labour be a witness, our homes be open, and our hearts be patient until we see you face to face. You live and reign with the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, for ever and ever. Alleluia. Amen.

2027-05-09.title: The Ascension of the Lord
readings: As they were watching, he was lifted up, and a cloud took him out of their sight
God mounts his throne to shouts of joy: a blare of trumpets for the Lord (or: Alleluia)
God seated him at his right hand in the heavenly places (or: Ephesians 4:1–13, shorter form 4:1–7, 11–13)
The Lord Jesus was taken up into heaven and sat down at the right hand of God
2027-05-09.alt: Solemnity, Year B. In India the Ascension is transferred from Thursday 6 May to this Sunday, and so the Seventh Sunday of Easter is not celebrated this year; where the Ascension was kept on Thursday, today is the Seventh Sunday of Easter (Acts 1:15–17, 20–26; 1 John 4:11–16; John 17:11b–19). Gloria and Creed; Preface of the Ascension; the proper form of the Communicantes in the Roman Canon. World Communications Day. The novena to the Holy Spirit continues until Pentecost. Regina Caeli at noon. Liturgical colour: white.
2027-05-09.verse: They said, “Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking up toward heaven? This Jesus, who has been taken up from you into heaven, will come in the same way as you saw him go into heaven.”
theo: St Luke wrote two books, and today's first reading is the hinge between them. “In the first book, Theophilus, I wrote about all that Jesus did and taught from the beginning until the day when he was taken up to heaven.” The Gospel of Luke ends with the Ascension; the Acts of the Apostles begins with it. The Ascension is not an epilogue to the story of Jesus; it is the beginning of the story of the Church. Luke tells us that after his suffering Jesus “presented himself alive to them by many convincing proofs, appearing to them during forty days and speaking about the kingdom of God.” Forty is the number of preparation: the flood, Moses on the mountain, Israel in the desert, Elijah's journey, Jesus' fast. These forty days prepare the apostles for a new way of being with their Lord. And their last question shows how much they still have to learn: “Lord, is this the time when you will restore the kingdom to Israel?” Jesus does not scold them. He redirects them: “It is not for you to know the times or periods … But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you; and you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem, in all Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth.” That one verse is the table of contents of the whole Book of Acts.

Then the moment itself: “as they were watching, he was lifted up, and a cloud took him out of their sight.” The cloud in the Bible is not weather; it is the sign of God's presence. The cloud led Israel through the desert, filled the tabernacle and the Temple, and overshadowed Jesus at the Transfiguration. Daniel saw “one like a human being coming with the clouds of heaven” to receive an everlasting kingdom (Daniel 7:13–14). So Jesus does not go up into the sky as a rocket goes into space; he enters the glory of God, and he takes our human nature, his risen body with its wounds, with him. And immediately two men in white, like the two at the empty tomb, ask the disciples a question that is also for us: “Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking up toward heaven?” The Ascension is not an invitation to stand and stare. The same Jesus “will come in the same way,” and until then there is work to do.

The Psalm is the song of a King's enthronement: “God has gone up with a shout, the Lord with the sound of a trumpet. Sing praises to God, sing praises; sing praises to our King, sing praises.” The Church has sung it on this feast from the earliest centuries. In the second reading Paul prays that the Ephesians may have “the eyes of your heart enlightened” to see what God has done: he “raised him from the dead and seated him at his right hand in the heavenly places, far above all rule and authority and power and dominion.” To sit at the right hand means to share the Father's power and glory. And Paul adds the astonishing consequence: God “has made him the head over all things for the church, which is his body, the fullness of him who fills all in all.” The Head has gone into heaven, but the Body is still here, joined to him. Where the Head has gone, the Body is called to follow. (The alternative reading, Ephesians 4, makes the same point another way: “When he ascended on high … he gave gifts to his people,” apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors and teachers, to build up the Body.)

Mark's Gospel, in its closing verses, gives the Ascension in a few strong lines. Jesus sends the eleven: “Go into all the world and proclaim the good news to the whole creation.” Belief and baptism will bring salvation; signs will accompany those who believe. Then: “the Lord Jesus, after he had spoken to them, was taken up into heaven and sat down at the right hand of God.” And at once, without a pause: “And they went out and proclaimed the good news everywhere, while the Lord worked with them and confirmed the message by the signs that accompanied it.” That is the key to the whole feast. Jesus sits at the right hand of God, and at the same moment he works with his disciples on earth. He is not further away; he is closer, no longer limited to one place, present to every place where the Gospel is proclaimed. These verses (Mark 16:9–20) are missing from some ancient manuscripts, but the Church received them as inspired Scripture, and Trent confirmed the canon with them.

Today is also World Communications Day, kept on the Sunday before Pentecost since 1967, at the wish of the Second Vatican Council. It is fitting. The Lord who ascends gives his Church a message for “the whole creation” and the ends of the earth. In our age the ends of the earth are reached by phone screens and radio, by newspapers and the internet. Every Christian with a mobile phone is in some way an evangelist, for good or ill. And between the Ascension and Pentecost, the Church does what the apostles did: they returned to Jerusalem and devoted themselves to prayer “together with certain women, including Mary the mother of Jesus” (Acts 1:14). We are in those nine days. Let us look up to where Christ has gone, and then look around at the world he sends us to, and pray with his Mother: Come, Holy Spirit.
conn: Theophilus.
The name means “friend of God.” Luke dedicates both his books to him (Luke 1:3; Acts 1:1); he may have been a patron, or the name may stand for every reader who loves God.
Forty days.
Only Luke gives the number. It echoes Moses on Sinai (Exodus 24:18), Elijah's journey to Horeb (1 Kings 19:8) and Jesus' fast in the desert (Luke 4:2): a time of preparation before a new beginning.
The place.
Luke places the Ascension near Bethany (Luke 24:50), on the Mount of Olives (Acts 1:12), the mountain from which, according to Zechariah 14:4, the Lord would come in the last days.
The cloud.

The sign of God's glorious presence: the pillar of cloud (Exodus 13:21), the cloud on the tabernacle (Exodus 40:34), the cloud of the Transfiguration (Mark 9:7), and the clouds of the Son of Man (Daniel 7:13).
Two men in white.
They recall the two men in dazzling clothes at the empty tomb (Luke 24:4) and Moses and Elijah at the Transfiguration (Luke 9:30). Their question turns the apostles from gazing to witnessing.
“Restore the kingdom to Israel.”
The hope of Israel's renewal was real and good (Luke 1:32–33; 24:21). Jesus does not deny it, but reveals a wider kingdom, reaching the ends of the earth through the Spirit.
The right hand of God.

A royal image from Psalm 110:1, the Old Testament verse most quoted in the New. To sit at the right hand is to share the King's authority. The Creed says: “he ascended into heaven and is seated at the right hand of the Father.”
The ending of Mark.

Mark 16:9–20, the “longer ending,” is absent from the oldest Greek manuscripts but was widely known from the second century (St Irenaeus quotes it). The Church accepts it as part of the inspired, canonical Scripture.
Psalm 47.
An enthronement psalm. Verse 5, “God has gone up with a shout,” has been sung on the Ascension since ancient times, and often gives the feast's Alleluia verse.
World Communications Day.

Called for by the Second Vatican Council's decree Inter Mirifica (1963) and first kept in 1967; it is a worldwide day asked for by the Council itself. The Pope's message is usually published on 24 January, the feast of St Francis de Sales, patron of writers and journalists.
In India.

The Latin bishops of India keep the Ascension on the Sunday after the fortieth day, so that the whole people of God can take part, as they do with the Epiphany and Corpus Christi (please verify with your diocesan Ordo).
altar: The Preface of the Ascension prays that Christ ascended “not to distance himself from our lowly state but that we, his members, might be confident of following where he, our Head and Founder, has gone before.” Every Mass is a door opened between earth and heaven, where the ascended Lord comes down to us under the signs of bread and wine.

The Letter to the Hebrews says that Christ “entered into heaven itself, now to appear in the presence of God on our behalf” (Hebrews 9:24). The sacrifice of Calvary, offered once for all, is presented by our High Priest for ever before the Father, and the same sacrifice is made present on our altars.

St Leo the Great taught (in substance) that what was visible in our Redeemer has passed over into the sacraments. The disciples could no longer touch him; we can receive him. The ascended Lord is not absent: in the Eucharist he is truly, really and substantially present, Body and Blood, soul and divinity.
outline: Opening
Picture a crowd at an airport watching a plane disappear into the clouds. Ask: what do people do after the plane is gone?
Point 1 · Why do you stand looking up?
From gazing to witnessing.
Point 2 · Seated at the right hand
Our human nature in the glory of God.
Point 3 · Head over all things for the church
The Head in heaven, the Body on earth.
Point 4 · Go into all the world
The Lord who works with us.
Closing image
The apostles walking down the Mount of Olives back to the city, and Mary waiting for them in the upper room.
Take-home line
“The Lord worked with them.”
live: Lift up your heart
Each morning this week pray Colossians 3:1: seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God. Then decide one thing you will do today for heaven's sake.
Come down the mountain
Choose one concrete act of witness: invite someone to Mass, speak of your faith at work, or visit a sick person in the parish.
Use your phone as a disciple
On World Communications Day, review what you post and forward. Share one message of hope or one Gospel verse, and refuse to forward one rumour or harsh word.
Pray the nine days
Continue the novena to the Holy Spirit with your family until Pentecost, perhaps with a decade of the Rosary each evening, as the apostles prayed with Mary.
fathers: St Augustine (Sermon on the Ascension, in substance)

Today our Lord Jesus Christ ascended into heaven; let our hearts ascend with him. He is there, yet he is with us here; we are here, yet we are with him there. He is in heaven, and still he says to the persecutor: why do you persecute me? because he is the Head and we are his Body.
St Leo the Great (in substance)

The Ascension of Christ is our own elevation; where the glory of the Head has gone before, the hope of the body is also called. Today we are not only confirmed as possessors of paradise, but in Christ we have entered the heights of heaven.
St Leo the Great (in substance)
What was visible in our Redeemer has passed over into the sacraments; and faith, made more excellent and firmer, now follows the teaching of the Spirit and not bodily sight.
St Gregory the Great (Homily on Mark 16, in substance)

The signs at the beginning were needed for the faith to grow, as we water a young plant until it takes root. Now the Church does spiritually what the apostles did bodily: she casts out the demon of sin, speaks the new language of praise, and lays hands of kindness on the sick.
St John Chrysostom (in substance)

Today our nature, which once was thought unworthy of the earth, has been lifted above the heavens and seated on the royal throne. The angels who once guarded paradise against us now see our nature at the right hand of God.
magis: Catechism 659
Christ's body was glorified at the moment of his Resurrection; the Ascension marks the definitive entrance of Jesus' humanity into God's heavenly domain.
Catechism 661–662

Only the one who came from the Father can return to him: Christ opens the way for us, and as High Priest he intercedes constantly for us as the mediator who assures us of the outpouring of the Holy Spirit.
Catechism 663–664
Being seated at the Father's right hand signifies the inauguration of the Messiah's kingdom, the fulfilment of Daniel's vision: a kingdom that will have no end.
Catechism 849
The missionary mandate: “Go therefore and make disciples of all nations.” Sent by God to the nations, the Church strives to preach the Gospel to all.
Catechism 1003
United with Christ by Baptism, believers already truly share in the heavenly life of the risen Christ, though this life remains hidden with Christ in God.
Inter Mirifica 18 (Vatican II, 1963)
An annual day should be held in every diocese to teach the faithful their duties in the use of the means of social communication, to pray for this cause and to support the Church's work in it.
Catechism 2494
The information provided by the media is at the service of the common good; society has a right to information based on truth, freedom, justice and solidarity.
Evangelii Gaudium 120 (Pope Francis, 2013)
Every baptized person is a missionary disciple; we no longer say that we are disciples and missionaries, but that we are always missionary disciples.
saints: Seventh Sunday of Easter (not kept in India this year)

Where the Ascension is kept on Thursday, today the Church reads of the choice of Matthias and of Jesus' prayer for his disciples, “Holy Father, protect them in your name.” In India these readings are not used this year; the feast of St Matthias comes on Friday 14 May.
This week

10 May: St John of Avila (optional). 12 May: Sts Nereus and Achilleus; St Pancras (optional). 13 May: Our Lady of Fatima (optional). 14 May: ST MATTHIAS, APOSTLE (feast). 15 May: last weekday of Easter; Vigil of Pentecost in the evening. 16 May: PENTECOST SUNDAY.
2027-05-09.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, King of glory, today you ascended above all the heavens and took your seat at the right hand of the Father. You did not leave us orphans: you took our human nature into the glory of God, and you remain with us, working with your Church and confirming her word. Lift up our hearts to where you are, so that we seek the things that are above; and send us down the mountain into the world, to proclaim the good news to the whole creation. Be the Head of your Body, the Church; give us the eyes of the heart to see the hope to which you have called us; and make all who speak and write and broadcast in our time servants of truth and peace. With Mary your Mother and the apostles we wait for the Holy Spirit whom you promised. Come again in glory, Lord Jesus, as you went into heaven. You live and reign with the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, for ever and ever. Alleluia. Amen.

2027-05-16.title: Pentecost Sunday
readings: All of them were filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak in other languages
Lord, send forth your Spirit, and renew the face of the earth (or: Alleluia)
In the one Spirit we were all baptized into one body
Come, Holy Spirit (the Sequence is obligatory today and is sung before the Alleluia)
As the Father has sent me, so I send you. Receive the Holy Spirit
2027-05-16.alt: Solemnity, Mass during the Day, Year B. Gloria, Sequence and Creed. In place of the second reading Galatians 5:16–25 may be read, and in place of the Gospel John 15:26–27; 16:12–15. Today the fifty days of Easter come to their close: at the dismissal the double Alleluia is sung for the last time, and after Evening Prayer the paschal candle is moved to the baptistery, where it will be lit at baptisms and beside the coffin at funerals. From tomorrow the Angelus replaces the Regina Caeli, and Ordinary Time resumes. Liturgical colour: red.
2027-05-16.verse: All of them were filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak in other languages, as the Spirit gave them ability.
theo: “When the day of Pentecost had come, they were all together in one place.” Pentecost was not a new feast invented by the Church. It was one of the three great pilgrim feasts of Israel, Shavuot, the Feast of Weeks, kept fifty days after Passover (the Greek word pentēkostē means “fiftieth”). It began as a harvest festival, when the first loaves of the new wheat were offered to God (Leviticus 23:16); in the time of Jesus many also linked it with the gift of the Law at Sinai, which came about fifty days after the Exodus. That is why Jerusalem is full of “devout Jews from every nation under heaven.” And now, fifty days after the Passover of Jesus' death and resurrection, God gives the first harvest of the new creation and a new law, written not on stone but on hearts. The signs recall Sinai, where “the Lord had descended upon it in fire” with thunder and a trumpet blast: “suddenly from heaven there came a sound like the rush of a violent wind, and it filled the entire house where they were sitting. Divided tongues, as of fire, appeared among them, and a tongue rested on each of them.” Wind and breath are one word in Hebrew (ruach) and in Greek (pneuma); John the Baptist had promised one who would baptise “with the Holy Spirit and fire.” Then the gift is named: “All of them were filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak in other languages, as the Spirit gave them ability.”

The crowd that gathers is astonished: “Are not all these who are speaking Galileans? And how is it that we hear, each of us, in our own native language?” Luke lists the nations, from Parthians and Medes in the east to visitors from Rome in the west, Jews and proselytes, Cretans and Arabs. The Fathers of the Church saw here the reversal of Babel. At Babel people tried to build “a tower with its top in the heavens” and “make a name for ourselves,” and they ended unable to understand one another, scattered over the earth (Genesis 11). At Pentecost God comes down as a gift, and the scattered are gathered: not by forcing everyone into one language, but by making the one Gospel heard in every language. The Church is born speaking many tongues. Here, in a land of many languages, we can feel the meaning of this: the same Good News is proclaimed today in Malayalam and Tamil, Hindi and Konkani, Telugu and Kannada and English, and it is one faith. What they all hear is the same: “in our own languages we hear them speaking about God's deeds of power.” The Psalm sings the Spirit's work on all creation: “When you send forth your spirit, they are created; and you renew the face of the ground.” The Lectionary refrain prays it as a petition: Lord, send forth your Spirit, and renew the face of the earth.

St Paul, writing to a quarrelsome community in Corinth, shows us the Spirit's work inside the Church. First, faith itself is his gift: “no one can say ‘Jesus is Lord’ except by the Holy Spirit.” Every act of faith, every prayer, even the simplest “Jesus,” is already the Spirit at work in us. Then he speaks of variety in unity: “there are varieties of gifts, but the same Spirit; and there are varieties of services, but the same Lord; and there are varieties of activities, but it is the same God who activates all of them in everyone.” Spirit, Lord, God: Paul names the whole Trinity in one breath. And the purpose of every gift is clear: “To each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good.” Gifts are not medals for display but tools for building up others. Finally the image of the body: “For in the one Spirit we were all baptized into one body,” and “we were all made to drink of one Spirit.” Baptism plunged us into the Spirit; Confirmation sealed us with him; the Eucharist makes us one body. If the second reading from Galatians is chosen, Paul lists “the fruit of the Spirit”: “love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, generosity, faithfulness, gentleness, and self-control.” These are the signs that the Spirit lives in us.

The Gospel takes us back to the evening of Easter Day. The disciples are behind locked doors “for fear of the Jews,” which in John's Gospel means the Temple authorities who had handed Jesus over, not the Jewish people as such; the disciples themselves were Jews. Jesus comes and stands among them: “Peace be with you.” He shows them his hands and his side, the wounds that are now the proof of his love and his victory. Then he sends them: “As the Father has sent me, so I send you.” And “he breathed on them and said to them, ‘Receive the Holy Spirit.’” The verb John uses for “breathed” is the same word the Greek Bible uses in Genesis, when the Lord God “breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and the man became a living being.” The risen Christ breathes a new creation into his disciples. And the first work of that new creation is forgiveness: “If you forgive the sins of any, they are forgiven them; if you retain the sins of any, they are retained.” The Church has always heard in these words the institution of the sacrament of Penance: the Holy Spirit is given for the forgiveness of sins. If the alternative Gospel is read, Jesus promises “the Advocate … the Spirit of truth,” who “will guide you into all the truth.”

Luke tells us who was in the upper room when the Spirit came: the apostles, “together with certain women, including Mary the mother of Jesus” (Acts 1:14). The one who conceived the Son of God by the power of the Holy Spirit was there when the same Spirit came upon the Church. Mary prayed with the apostles for the gift she had already received in fullness; she is the Mother of the Church at its birth, and tomorrow the Church will honour her with that title. Today the Church prays the ancient Sequence, Veni, Sancte Spiritus, with its tender names for the Spirit: Father of the poor, giver of gifts, light of hearts, best of comforters, sweet guest of the soul, rest in labour, coolness in the heat, comfort in tears. It asks him to wash what is stained, water what is dry, heal what is wounded, bend what is rigid, warm what is cold, and guide what has gone astray. That is the prayer for every Christian today. The Easter season ends not with an ending but with a sending. The candle that stood by the ambo for fifty days goes to the font, because the fire of Easter now burns in the baptised, sent out into the world with the Spirit's peace.
conn: Pentecost (pentēkostē).

Greek for “fiftieth.” In Israel, Shavuot, the Feast of Weeks (Exodus 34:22; Leviticus 23:15–21; Deuteronomy 16:9–12), seven weeks after Passover. A pilgrim feast, which is why Jerusalem was crowded with Jews from many lands.
Wind and fire.
Hebrew ruach and Greek pneuma mean wind, breath and spirit. Fire recalls the burning bush (Exodus 3:2), the pillar of fire, and Sinai wrapped in smoke and fire (Exodus 19:18).
Babel reversed.

Genesis 11:1–9: proud builders end in confusion and scattering. Acts 2: a gift from above brings understanding and gathering. Many Fathers, among them St Cyril of Jerusalem and St Augustine, made this connection.
The list of nations.

Fifteen peoples, from Persia (Parthians, Medes, Elamites) to Rome, and from Crete to Arabia. Luke paints the whole known world gathered in Jerusalem, a preview of the Gospel's journey “to the ends of the earth” (Acts 1:8).
“Jesus is Lord.”

Perhaps the earliest Christian creed. Kyrios, Lord, was the word the Greek Bible used for the divine name of God. To call Jesus Lord is to confess his divinity, which no one can do except by the Spirit (1 Corinthians 12:3).
Charisms.

Paul's word charismata means gifts of grace. He lists many: wisdom, knowledge, faith, healing, miracles, prophecy, discernment, tongues and their interpretation (1 Corinthians 12:8–10). All are “for the common good.”
“For fear of the Jews.”

In John's Gospel “the Jews” often means the religious authorities in Jerusalem who opposed Jesus. The Church teaches that the Jewish people as a whole, then or now, cannot be blamed for his death (Nostra Aetate 4; Catechism 597–598).
He breathed on them.
The Greek emphysaō appears in Genesis 2:7 (God breathes life into Adam), Ezekiel 37:9 (breath enters the dry bones) and Wisdom 15:11. In John 20:22 the risen Jesus does what only the Creator does.
Forgive and retain.
The Council of Trent taught that in John 20:22–23 Christ gave the apostles and their successors the power to forgive and retain sins in the sacrament of Penance (Catechism 976, 1441–1442, 1461).
The Sequence.

Veni, Sancte Spiritus, a medieval Latin poem usually attributed to Stephen Langton, Archbishop of Canterbury (died 1228), sometimes called the Golden Sequence. It is one of only two sequences that are obligatory in the Roman Rite (with Victimae paschali laudes at Easter).
Red.
The colour of fire and of the martyrs, whose courage was the Spirit's gift. Pentecost is the only Sunday of the Easter season in red.
altar: At every Mass, just before the consecration, the priest extends his hands over the bread and wine and asks the Father to send the Holy Spirit upon them, so that they may become the Body and Blood of our Lord Jesus Christ. This calling down of the Spirit is called the epiclesis. Without Pentecost there would be no Eucharist.

After the consecration the Church prays a second time for the Spirit, now upon us: that, “filled with his Holy Spirit,” we “may become one body, one spirit in Christ” (Eucharistic Prayer III). Paul's words come true at the altar: “we were all made to drink of one Spirit.”
outline: Opening
Light a candle and switch on a fan beside it. Ask: what happens to a flame when the wind blows? Some flames go out; this one, by God's power, spreads.
Point 1 · Wind and fire
The Feast of Weeks fulfilled: a new harvest, a new law written on hearts.
Point 2 · Each in their own language
Babel reversed; one Gospel in every tongue.
Point 3 · Varieties of gifts, the same Spirit
Faith itself is his gift; every gift is for the common good.
Point 4 · Receive the Holy Spirit
The breath of new creation, peace and the forgiveness of sins.
Point 5 · With Mary in the upper room
The Mother of the Church at its birth.
Closing image
The paschal candle carried from the ambo to the font: the Easter fire now burns in the baptised.
Take-home line
“Lord, send forth your Spirit, and renew the face of the earth.”
live: Pray the Sequence
Pray the Veni, Sancte Spiritus slowly today and each day this week, stopping at the line you most need: heal what is wounded, warm what is cold, guide what has gone astray.
Name your gift
Ask yourself, and perhaps a friend: what gift has the Spirit given me for the common good? Then use it this week in your parish or neighbourhood.
Receive mercy
The first gift of the risen Lord's breath is forgiveness. If it has been long since your last confession, go this week.
Speak someone's language
Pentecost is about being understood. Take time to listen to someone who feels unheard, perhaps someone of another language, generation or background, and speak to them in a way they can understand.
Renew your Confirmation
Recall the day you were confirmed and the words: Be sealed with the Gift of the Holy Spirit. Thank God for it, and ask for a fresh outpouring.
fathers: St Irenaeus of Lyons (in substance)
Where the Church is, there is the Spirit of God; and where the Spirit of God is, there is the Church and every kind of grace.
St Augustine (in substance)
What the soul is to the human body, the Holy Spirit is to the Body of Christ, which is the Church. If you want to live by the Spirit of Christ, stay in the Body of Christ.
St Cyril of Jerusalem (in substance)

The Spirit is like rain. One and the same rain falls from heaven, yet it becomes white in the lily, red in the rose, purple in the violet. So the one Spirit gives wisdom to one, prophecy to another, and to each as he wills.
St Basil the Great (in substance)
Through the Holy Spirit comes our return to paradise, our ascent to the kingdom of heaven, our adoption as children of God, our boldness to call God Father, our share in the grace of Christ.
St Leo the Great (in substance)
At Pentecost the Holy Spirit did not begin to work in the saints for the first time; he came with a new fullness, overflowing the measure of earlier gifts.
magis: Catechism 731–732
On the day of Pentecost the Passover of Christ is fulfilled in the outpouring of the Holy Spirit; the Holy Trinity is fully revealed, and the Church is made known to the world.
Catechism 767–768
The Church was made manifest at Pentecost; the Spirit equips her with hierarchical and charismatic gifts.
Catechism 1287–1288
Confirmation perpetuates the grace of Pentecost in the Church.
Catechism 1830–1832
The seven gifts of the Holy Spirit and the fruits of the Spirit.
Catechism 976, 1441–1442
Christ gave the apostles the power to forgive sins: “Receive the Holy Spirit.”
Lumen Gentium 4
The Spirit was sent on the day of Pentecost to sanctify the Church continually; he dwells in the Church and in the hearts of the faithful as in a temple.
Dominum et Vivificantem 25 (St John Paul II, 1986)
Pentecost is the definitive manifestation of what was accomplished in the Upper Room on Easter Sunday; the era of the Church began with the coming of the Spirit.
saints: The Blessed Virgin Mary in the upper room

The apostles devoted themselves to prayer “together with certain women, including Mary the mother of Jesus” (Acts 1:14). Tradition honours her as Queen of the Apostles. Tomorrow, the Monday after Pentecost, the Church celebrates her as Mother of the Church.
This week

17 May: The Blessed Virgin Mary, Mother of the Church (memorial); Ordinary Time resumes (Week 7, Year I). 18 May: St John I, pope and martyr (optional). 20 May: St Bernardine of Siena (optional). 21 May: St Christopher Magallanes and companions (optional). 22 May: St Rita of Cascia (optional). 23 May: The Most Holy Trinity.
2027-05-16.prayer: O God, who by the mystery of today's great feast sanctify your whole Church in every people and nation, pour out, we pray, the gifts of the Holy Spirit across the face of the earth and, with the divine grace that was at work when the Gospel was first proclaimed, fill now once more the hearts of believers. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, who lives and reigns with you in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, for ever and ever. Amen. Let us also pray: Come, Holy Spirit, fill the hearts of your faithful and kindle in them the fire of your love. Breath of the risen Christ, give us his peace and the joy of forgiveness. Tongue of fire, give us words to speak of God's deeds of power in every language we know. Giver of gifts, make each of us useful for the common good, and make us one body in Christ. With Mary, who waited with the apostles, we pray: send forth your Spirit, and renew the face of the earth. Amen.

2027-05-23.title: The Most Holy Trinity
readings: The Lord is God in heaven above and on the earth beneath; there is no other
Blessed the people the Lord has chosen to be his own
You have received a spirit of adoption. When we cry, “Abba! Father!”
Baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit
2027-05-23.alt: Solemnity, Year B. Gloria and Creed. The Sunday after Pentecost is kept as the Solemnity of the Most Holy Trinity, and it takes the place of the Eighth Sunday in Ordinary Time this year. The Angelus is prayed at noon. Liturgical colour: white.
2027-05-23.verse: Go therefore and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.
theo: Last Sunday the Easter season ended with the outpouring of the Holy Spirit. Today the Church pauses and looks at the whole mystery that Easter and Pentecost have revealed: the one God who is Father, Son and Holy Spirit. This is not a puzzle invented by theologians. It is the name into which every one of us was baptised, and the Church calls it “the central mystery of Christian faith and life” (CCC 234). The first reading prepares the ground. Moses, at the end of the desert years, asks Israel to look back over all history: “ask now about former ages, long before your own, ever since the day that God created human beings on the earth; ask from one end of heaven to the other: has anything so great as this ever happened or has its like ever been heard of?” Has any people heard the voice of God speaking out of the fire and lived? Has any god gone to take a nation for himself “by a mighty hand and an outstretched arm”? Israel's God is not a distant idea but the God who speaks and acts, who chooses and rescues. And from that history comes the confession that stands at the root of our faith: “So acknowledge today and take to heart that the Lord is God in heaven above and on the earth beneath; there is no other.” Christians do not believe in three gods. The Trinity is the one God of Israel, revealed in his innermost life.

The Psalm sings of this God who creates by his word and his breath: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were made, and all their host by the breath of his mouth.” The Fathers of the Church loved this verse, for in it they heard, quietly hidden in the Old Testament, the Word and the Spirit of the Father at work in creation. The Lord is the God whose “word is upright,” who “loves righteousness and justice,” whose “steadfast love” fills the earth; and his eye is “on those who fear him, on those who hope in his steadfast love.” So the people can say: “Our soul waits for the Lord; he is our help and shield.” The refrain gathers it up: blessed the people the Lord has chosen to be his own.

St Paul, in the Letter to the Romans, shows that the Trinity is not only a truth to be believed but a life into which we are drawn. “For all who are led by the Spirit of God are children of God. For you did not receive a spirit of slavery to fall back into fear, but you have received a spirit of adoption.” The Holy Spirit, given to us in Baptism, does not make us servants of a distant master; he makes us sons and daughters, so that we dare to say what Jesus said in Gethsemane: “Abba! Father!” It is “that very Spirit bearing witness with our spirit that we are children of God, and if children, then heirs, heirs of God and joint heirs with Christ.” Here is the Trinity at prayer within us: the Spirit, in us, crying to the Father, with the voice of the Son. We are not outside the mystery looking in. We have been taken inside it.

The Gospel is the last scene of Matthew. The eleven disciples go to the mountain in Galilee where Jesus had told them to go. “When they saw him, they worshiped him; but some doubted.” Even at the end, faith and hesitation stand side by side, and Jesus does not wait for perfect disciples. He comes near and says: “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me. Go therefore and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.” Notice the singular: in the name, not the names. One God, one name, three Persons. Then comes the promise that closes the whole Gospel: “And remember, I am with you always, to the end of the age.” Matthew's Gospel began with Emmanuel, God with us (1:23); it ends with the same promise. The Trinity is not a God who keeps himself far away. The Father sent the Son; the Son sends us; the Spirit makes us children; and the risen Lord remains with us every day. As St Gregory of Nazianzus put it (in substance), no sooner do I think of the One than I am surrounded by the splendour of the Three; no sooner do I distinguish the Three than I am carried back to the One.
conn: Deuteronomy 4.

Part of Moses' first great speech on the plains of Moab, before Israel enters the land. It looks back on the Exodus and on Sinai (called Horeb in Deuteronomy) to call Israel to faithfulness. Two chapters later comes the Shema: “Hear, O Israel: The Lord is our God, the Lord alone” (Deuteronomy 6:4), which Jesus himself called the first commandment (Mark 12:29).
The voice out of the fire.

At Horeb the people heard the voice of God from the midst of the fire on the mountain and lived (Deuteronomy 4:12, 33; 5:24). God speaks, but he is not seen; Israel was to make no image of him (4:15–16).
Psalm 33:6.

“By the word of the Lord … and by the breath of his mouth.” The Hebrew word for breath is ruach, also the word for Spirit. Many Fathers, among them St Irenaeus, saw here the Word and the Spirit as the “two hands” of the Father in creation.
“Abba.”

An Aramaic word for “father,” used by Jesus in Gethsemane (Mark 14:36). Paul keeps the Aramaic word in Greek letters here and in Galatians 4:6, a sign that the first Christians treasured the very word Jesus used.
Adoption.
In Roman law an adopted son received the full name, rights and inheritance of his new father. Paul uses the image to say that in Christ we truly share the Son's relationship with the Father.
“Some doubted.”
The Greek word (edistasan) appears in Matthew only here and in 14:31, when Peter sinks in the waves and Jesus says, “You of little faith, why did you doubt?” It means hesitation more than unbelief.
“In the name.”

The command to baptise “in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” is the oldest Trinitarian formula of the Church; it is also given in the Didache (chapter 7), a Christian writing of the late first or early second century.
Nicaea and Constantinople.

The Creed we profess today was formulated at the Councils of Nicaea (325) and Constantinople (381), which confessed the Son “consubstantial with the Father” and the Holy Spirit as “the Lord, the giver of life … who with the Father and the Son is adored and glorified.”
Trinity Sunday.
A feast of the Holy Trinity was kept in many places in the Middle Ages; Pope John XXII extended it to the whole Latin Church in 1334, on the Sunday after Pentecost.
An Indian voice.

Brahmabandhab Upadhyay (1861–1907), a Bengali Catholic, wrote a Sanskrit hymn to the Trinity, “Vande Saccidanandam,” using the Indian words for being, consciousness and bliss. He did not claim that the Hindu idea and the Christian mystery are the same; he tried to praise the Trinity in words his people could feel.
altar: Every Mass is the prayer of the Trinity. We begin “in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit”; the Eucharistic Prayer is addressed to the Father, through the Son, in the Holy Spirit, who is called down upon the gifts to make them the Body and Blood of Christ; and it ends: “Through him, and with him, and in him, O God, almighty Father, in the unity of the Holy Spirit, all glory and honour is yours.”

In Holy Communion the promise of today's Gospel takes flesh: “I am with you always.” The Son, really present, comes to dwell in us; and where the Son is, the Father and the Spirit are, for the three Persons are never separated. Each Communion draws us deeper into the life of the Trinity.
outline: Opening
Make the sign of the cross slowly with everyone. Ask: how many times have I done this without thinking of what I am saying?
Point 1 · Has anything so great ever happened?
The God of Israel speaks, chooses and rescues.
Point 2 · There is no other
One God: the Trinity is not three gods but the one God revealed in his inner life.
Point 3 · Abba! Father!
The Spirit makes us children and prays in us.
Point 4 · In the name
Baptised into the Trinity, sent to all nations, never alone.
Closing image
A child running into the arms of a father, while the mother laughs nearby: love given, love received, love shared.
Take-home line
“I am with you always, to the end of the age.”
live: Make the sign of the cross with meaning
Each time you sign yourself this week, pause for a breath on each name: Father, Son, Holy Spirit.
Pray Abba
Spend five minutes each day simply saying, slowly and from the heart, “Abba, Father,” and let the Spirit pray in you.
Remember your Baptism
Find out the date of your Baptism and mark it in your calendar; on that day, thank God, renew your baptismal promises, and visit the font if you can.
Make disciples
Share your faith this week with one person who is searching: a word, an invitation to Mass, a book, a prayer together.
fathers: St Gregory of Nazianzus (in substance)

Above all, guard this great deposit of faith, for which I live and fight: the profession of faith in the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. I give you one Godhead and power, found in the Three, and containing the Three in a distinct way (Oration 40, quoted in CCC 256).
St Augustine (in substance)

If you see love, you see the Trinity. For love means one who loves, the one who is loved, and love itself. Look into your own heart: there you will find an image, faint but true, of the God who is love (On the Trinity, Book 8).
St Athanasius (in substance)

The Father does all things through the Word in the Holy Spirit; in this way the unity of the Holy Trinity is preserved, and one God is preached in the Church, who is over all, and through all, and in all (Letters to Serapion).
St Hilary of Poitiers (in substance)

Keep, I pray you, this faith of mine undefiled, and grant me to the end of my life the voice of my conscience, so that I may always hold fast to what I professed when I was baptised in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit (On the Trinity, Book 12).
magis: Catechism 234
The mystery of the Most Holy Trinity is the central mystery of Christian faith and life, the mystery of God in himself, the source of all the other mysteries of faith.
Catechism 253–255

The Trinity is One: not three gods but one God in three Persons, the “consubstantial Trinity.” The divine Persons are really distinct from one another by their relations of origin, and they are relative to one another.
Catechism 257–260

The whole divine economy is the common work of the three Persons. The ultimate end of that economy is that we be drawn into the perfect unity of the Blessed Trinity; even now we are called to be a dwelling for the Trinity.
Catechism 849–850

The mission of the Church comes from the eternal love of the Holy Trinity: she is sent to make disciples of all nations so that all may share the communion of the Father and the Son in their Spirit of love.
Lumen Gentium 4
The universal Church is “a people made one with the unity of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit” (quoting St Cyprian).
Dominum et Vivificantem 10 (St John Paul II, 1986)
In his intimate life God “is love,” and the Holy Spirit is personal love, the Person-Love and the Person-Gift of the Father and the Son.
saints: St Elizabeth of the Trinity (1880–1906)

A Carmelite nun of Dijon in France, who died at twenty-six and was canonised by Pope Francis in 2016. Her prayer, “O my God, Trinity whom I adore,” is quoted by the Catechism (CCC 260). She wanted her whole life to be a “praise of glory” to the Trinity dwelling in her soul.
This week

24 May: Monday of the Eighth Week; Mary Help of Christians (Salesian communities); World Day of Prayer for the Church in China. 25 May: St Bede, St Gregory VII, St Mary Magdalene de' Pazzi (optional). 26 May: St Philip Neri (memorial). 27 May: St Augustine of Canterbury (optional); where it is kept on Thursday, the Solemnity of the Body and Blood of Christ; in India it is kept on Sunday 30 May. 29 May: St Paul VI (optional). 30 May: Corpus Christi (India). 31 May: the Visitation of the Blessed Virgin Mary (feast).
2027-05-23.prayer: God our Father, you sent into the world the Word of truth and the Spirit of sanctification, and so made known to us your wonderful mystery. Lord Jesus Christ, eternal Son, you have made us children of your Father and you remain with us always, to the end of the age. Holy Spirit, Lord and giver of life, you cry in our hearts “Abba! Father!” and bear witness that we are children of God. Most Holy Trinity, one God, we adore you, we praise you, we thank you. Keep us faithful to the faith of our Baptism, make our families and our parish an image of your communion of love, and send us to make disciples of all nations. With the Blessed Virgin Mary, daughter of the Father, mother of the Son and temple of the Holy Spirit, and with all the saints, we give you glory, now and for ever. Amen.

2027-05-30.title: The Most Holy Body and Blood of Christ (Corpus Christi)
readings: See the blood of the covenant that the Lord has made with you
I will lift up the cup of salvation and call on the name of the Lord (or: Alleluia)
How much more will the blood of Christ … purify our conscience from dead works to worship the living God!
Praise, O Zion, praise your Saviour (shorter form from Ecce panis angelorum, Behold the bread of angels)
This is my body. This is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many
2027-05-30.alt: Solemnity. Year B. In India the Latin Church keeps Corpus Christi on this Sunday, and so the Ninth Sunday in Ordinary Time is not celebrated; where the solemnity is kept on Thursday (as at the Vatican and in many countries), it was celebrated on 27 May. Gloria and Creed. The Sequence Lauda Sion may be sung before the Gospel Acclamation, in full or in the shorter form. Where possible, a procession with the Blessed Sacrament follows the Mass, ending with Benediction. Liturgical colour: white.
2027-05-30.verse: While they were eating, he took a loaf of bread, and after blessing it he broke it, gave it to them, and said, “Take; this is my body.” Then he took a cup, and after giving thanks he gave it to them, and all of them drank from it.
theo: On this Sunday the Church kneels before the gift that Jesus left on the night before he died: his own Body and Blood. In Holy Week we remembered the Last Supper in the shadow of the Passion. Today, in the light of Easter and Pentecost, we celebrate the same gift with open joy, carry it through our streets and adore it. The readings of Year B have one thread running through all of them: blood and covenant. The first reading takes us to the foot of Mount Sinai. Moses has come down and “told the people all the words of the LORD and all the ordinances; and all the people answered with one voice, and said, ‘All the words that the LORD has spoken we will do.’” Then he builds an altar with twelve pillars, one for each tribe. Young men offer sacrifices, and Moses does something that seems strange to us: he takes half of the blood and dashes it against the altar, which stands for God, and after reading the book of the covenant aloud and hearing the people promise again, he dashes the other half on the people, saying: “See the blood of the covenant that the LORD has made with you in accordance with all these words.” For the people of the Bible, blood is life. The same life now touches both the altar and the people: God and Israel are bound together like blood relatives, one family. That is what a covenant means. The Psalm is the song of one who has been rescued and asks how to give thanks: “What shall I return to the LORD for all his bounty to me? I will lift up the cup of salvation and call on the name of the LORD.” Christians have always heard in it the voice of the Church at every Mass.

The Letter to the Hebrews explains what Moses' ceremony was pointing to. The high priest of the old covenant entered the Holy of Holies once a year with the blood of animals. “But when Christ came as a high priest of the good things that have come, then through the greater and perfect tent (not made with hands, that is, not of this creation), he entered once for all into the Holy Place, not with the blood of goats and calves, but with his own blood, thus obtaining eternal redemption.” The author reasons from the lesser to the greater: if the blood of animals could make people outwardly clean for worship, “how much more will the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without blemish to God, purify our conscience from dead works to worship the living God!” Notice that the whole Trinity is at work: Christ offers himself, through the eternal Spirit, to God the Father. And the result is a new covenant: “For this reason he is the mediator of a new covenant, so that those who are called may receive the promised eternal inheritance.” Moses sprinkled blood on the outside of the people. Christ's blood reaches the conscience, the inner heart, and makes us able to worship the living God.

The Gospel brings us into the upper room. Jesus sends two disciples into the city: “a man carrying a jar of water will meet you; follow him,” and he will show them “a large room upstairs, furnished and ready.” The Lord himself prepares the place of the meal. That evening, while they are eating the Passover, “he took a loaf of bread, and after blessing it he broke it, gave it to them, and said, ‘Take; this is my body.’ Then he took a cup, and after giving thanks he gave it to them, and all of them drank from it. He said to them, ‘This is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many.’” The disciples, good Jews who knew Exodus 24, could not miss the echo: the blood of the covenant. What Moses sprinkled from a basin, Jesus gives to drink, and it is his own blood. He does not say: this is a sign of my body; he says: this is my body. The Church has always taken him at his word. By the power of the Holy Spirit and the words of Christ spoken by the priest, the whole substance of the bread becomes the Body of Christ and the whole substance of the wine becomes his Blood, while the appearances of bread and wine remain; the Church calls this change transubstantiation (Council of Trent; Catechism 1376). Christ is present in the Eucharist truly, really and substantially, Body and Blood, soul and divinity. And because the Eucharist makes present the one sacrifice of the cross, the Mass is not only a meal but the sacrifice of the new covenant. The Gospel ends simply: “When they had sung the hymn, they went out to the Mount of Olives.” The hymn was probably the Hallel psalms, which include today's Psalm 116. From the table Jesus goes out to give his body and pour out his blood. Today we too go out from the altar in procession, carrying him through our towns and villages, so that the whole world may see the One who gave his life for many.
conn: “The blood of the covenant.”

The phrase in Exodus 24:8 is repeated by Jesus in Mark 14:24 and recalled at every Mass. In the Bible a covenant is not a contract but a family bond; blood shared by the altar and the people makes them kin. Jesus seals the new covenant with his own blood.
Twelve pillars.
Moses sets up twelve pillars for the twelve tribes (Exodus 24:4). At the Last Supper Jesus sits with the Twelve, the foundation of the renewed Israel, the Church.
“A man carrying a jar of water.”
Carrying water was usually women's work, so a man with a jar would be easy to recognise. The Lord himself prepares everything for the meal, as he still prepares the altar for us.
The Passover.

The Last Supper took place in the setting of the Passover, the memorial of Israel's liberation from Egypt, when the blood of the lamb saved the firstborn (Exodus 12). Jesus is the true Paschal Lamb (1 Corinthians 5:7).
“This is my body.”

Jesus does not say “this represents” but “this is.” The Church teaches that the whole substance of bread and wine is changed into the substance of the Body and Blood of Christ (transubstantiation), while the appearances remain (Catechism 1376).
“Poured out for many.”

An echo of the Servant in Isaiah 53:12, who “poured out himself to death” and “bore the sin of many.” In Hebrew idiom “many” means the great multitude, without limit; Christ died for all (Catechism 605).
“The greater and perfect tent.”
Hebrews compares the earthly tabernacle, where the high priest entered once a year, with heaven itself, where Christ has entered once for all with his own blood (Hebrews 9:24).
“The hymn.”
At the end of the Passover meal Jews sang the second part of the Hallel, Psalms 115–118; Psalm 116, today's Psalm, belongs to it. Jesus sang the Psalms on his way to the Passion.
Corpus Christi.

The feast arose in the thirteenth century in Liège, through the visions of St Juliana of Cornillon, and was extended to the whole Church by Pope Urban IV in 1264. St Thomas Aquinas composed its Office and the Sequence Lauda Sion.
altar: What Moses dashed from a basin and Jesus gave in the upper room is given to us today at this altar. The bread and wine we bring become, by the power of the Holy Spirit and the words of Christ, his true Body and Blood. We do not receive a symbol but the living Lord, Body and Blood, soul and divinity.

The Mass is the sacrifice of the new covenant: the one offering of Christ on the cross made present, not repeated. That is why we adore the Blessed Sacrament after Mass, in the tabernacle and in the monstrance, and carry him in procession: the same Lord who was offered for us remains with us.
outline: Opening
Ask: if you saw Jesus carried through your street today, what would you do? Kneel, look away, or follow?
Point 1 · The blood of the covenant
At Sinai blood touches altar and people: God makes Israel his family.
Point 2 · How much more the blood of Christ
Christ enters heaven with his own blood and purifies our conscience.
Point 3 · This is my body
In the upper room Jesus gives himself, truly present, the sacrifice of the new covenant.
Point 4 · They went out
From the altar to the street: adoration, procession, mission.
Closing image
A small white Host in a golden monstrance, carried slowly down a village road, and people kneeling on both sides.
Take-home line
“Take; this is my body.”
live: Make a visit
This week, spend ten minutes before the Blessed Sacrament in your parish church, or in an adoration chapel, simply looking at him and letting him look at you.
Prepare for Communion
Before Mass next Sunday, prepare with a short examination of conscience, keep the Eucharistic fast, and go to confession if you are in serious sin.
Join the procession
If your parish holds a Eucharistic procession, walk in it with your family; if not, kneel in silence at the moment of Benediction.
Give thanks after Communion
Do not rush out after Mass. Stay two minutes after receiving Holy Communion to thank him, using the words of the Psalm: What shall I return to the Lord?
fathers: St Cyril of Jerusalem (in substance)

Do not regard the bread and wine as bare elements, for they are the Body and Blood of Christ according to the Lord's own declaration. Even if the senses suggest otherwise, let faith make you sure. Judge not by taste but by faith.
St Ambrose (in substance)

The word of Christ, which could make out of nothing what did not exist, can it not change things that exist into what they were not? It is no less to give new natures to things than to change their natures.
St Thomas Aquinas (in substance)

In the hymn Adoro te devote he prays: sight, touch and taste are deceived in you, but hearing alone is trusted; I believe whatever the Son of God has said, for nothing is truer than this word of Truth.
magis: Catechism 1374
Christ is present in the Eucharist truly, really and substantially, Body and Blood, soul and divinity.
Catechism 1376
The Council of Trent: by consecration the whole substance of bread and wine is changed into the Body and Blood of Christ; this change is called transubstantiation.
Catechism 1365–1367
The Eucharist is the memorial of Christ's Passover and a true sacrifice: the one sacrifice of the cross made present.
Catechism 1378–1379
Worship of the Eucharist: adoration of the Blessed Sacrament inside and outside Mass, and processions.
Lumen Gentium 11; St John Paul II, Ecclesia de Eucharistia 1
The Eucharist is the source and summit of the whole Christian life; the Church draws her life from the Eucharist.
saints: Corpus Christi in history

St Juliana of Cornillon (d. 1258), a nun near Liège, longed for a feast of the Blessed Sacrament; the bishop of Liège first kept it in 1246. Pope Urban IV extended it to the whole Church in 1264 (bull Transiturus), and St Thomas Aquinas wrote its Office. In India the solemnity is kept on the Sunday after Trinity.
This week

31 May: the Visitation of the Blessed Virgin Mary (feast), close of the Marian month. 1 Jun: St Justin, martyr. 3 Jun: Sts Charles Lwanga and companions, martyrs. 4 Jun: the Most Sacred Heart of Jesus (solemnity). 5 Jun: the Immaculate Heart of the Blessed Virgin Mary.
2027-05-30.prayer: O God, who in this wonderful Sacrament have left us a memorial of your Passion, grant us, we pray, so to revere the sacred mysteries of your Body and Blood that we may always experience in ourselves the fruits of your redemption. Who live and reign with God the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, for ever and ever. Amen. Let us also pray: Lord Jesus, true God and true man, hidden under the appearance of bread and wine, we adore you. You sealed the new covenant with your own blood; purify our conscience to worship the living God. What shall we return to you for all your goodness? We will lift up the cup of salvation and call on your name. Walk with us through our streets today, bless our homes, and make us one body in you. Amen.

2027-05-01.title: Saturday of the Fifth Week of Easter
readings: Come over to Macedonia and help us
Make a joyful noise to the Lord, all the earth (or: Alleluia)
If the world hates you, be aware that it hated me before it hated you
2027-05-01.alt: Saturday of the Fifth Week of Easter (Year I). Optional memorial of St Joseph the Worker: the weekday readings are given here; the proper readings of the memorial, Genesis 1:26–2:3 or Colossians 3:14–15, 17, 23–24, with Psalm 90 and Matthew 13:54–58, may be used instead.
