In India 1 May is also May Day, Labour Day. Today the month of May, dedicated to the Blessed Virgin Mary, begins. Liturgical colour: white.
2027-05-01.verse: If the world hates you, be aware that it hated me before it hated you.
theo: Paul sets out on his second missionary journey, and the first thing Luke tells us is about a young man. In Lystra, the town where Paul had once been stoned and left for dead, there is a disciple named Timothy, “the son of a Jewish woman who was a believer; but his father was a Greek.” The believers speak well of him, and Paul wants him as a companion. Then the little band travels from town to town, handing on the decisions of the apostles and elders in Jerusalem, “so the churches were strengthened in the faith and increased in numbers daily.” What follows is strange. The missionaries try to preach in the province of Asia, and the Holy Spirit forbids them. They try to go north into Bithynia, and “the Spirit of Jesus did not allow them.” Two doors close, one after the other. They end up at Troas, on the coast, with nowhere obvious to go. And there, in the night, Paul sees a man of Macedonia standing and pleading: “Come over to Macedonia and help us.” At once they cross the sea. Notice the small change in the text: from this verse Luke begins to write “we.” The writer has joined the journey. The Gospel is about to enter Europe, and it enters through closed doors, a dream in the night, and a plea for help.

The Gospel moves from the joy of the mission to its cost. At the Last Supper Jesus warns his friends: “If the world hates you, be aware that it hated me before it hated you.” In John's Gospel “the world” here does not mean the earth God made and loves (John 3:16), but human life organised without God and against him. The disciple who belongs to Christ will not always be welcome in it. “Remember the word that I said to you, ‘Servants are not greater than their master.’ If they persecuted me, they will persecute you; if they kept my word, they will keep yours also.” Paul would learn this soon enough in Macedonia: beatings in Philippi, riots in Thessalonica. And yet the plea “help us” was real. The same world that resists the Gospel is crying out for it. Today, on the first of May, the Church also honours St Joseph the Worker. Pope Pius XII gave this memorial to the Church in 1955, so that the workers' day would also be a day of the carpenter of Nazareth. The people of Nazareth once asked of Jesus, “Is not this the carpenter's son?” Joseph's hidden work, with the Blessed Virgin Mary beside him, made a home where the Son of God grew up. On this day we pray for all who work, for all who cannot find work, and for all whose work is unjust or unsafe; and we begin the month of May with the Mother of Jesus.
outline: Opening
Ask: when a door closes in your life, do you see a wall or a signpost?
Point 1 · The Spirit closes two doors
Asia and Bithynia forbidden; the way to Macedonia opened.
Point 2 · Come over and help us
The cry of a world that needs the Gospel.
Point 3 · Hated before you
Disciples share the lot of their Master.
Point 4 · The carpenter's son
St Joseph the Worker and the dignity of work.
Take-home line
“Come over to Macedonia and help us.”
live: Read the closed door (Acts 16:6–7)
Think of one plan of yours that failed recently. Ask the Holy Spirit in prayer: Lord, where are you leading me instead?
Honour work today (Colossians 3:23)
Do your work today, at home or outside, as done for the Lord, and thank one worker whom people usually ignore: a cleaner, a driver, a cook, a watchman.
2027-05-01.prayer: Lord Jesus, risen from the dead, you sent your apostles across the sea in answer to the cry “Come over and help us.” When our plans fail and doors close, give us the humility to follow your Spirit. When the world resists your word, keep us faithful, for you were hated before us. Through the prayers of St Joseph, the carpenter of Nazareth, bless all who work and all who look for work, and give us a share in the Easter joy of your Mother, whose month begins today. Amen.
altar: At the offertory the priest calls the bread “fruit of the earth and work of human hands” and the wine “fruit of the vine and work of human hands.” On this day of St Joseph the Worker, our work is carried to the altar with them, and the Lord changes that bread and wine into his own Body and Blood. Nothing we do in honest labour is lost if it is offered with him.

2027-05-03.title: Saints Philip and James, Apostles
readings: Then he appeared to James, then to all the apostles
Their voice goes out through all the earth (or: Alleluia)
Have I been with you all this time, Philip, and you still do not know me?
2027-05-03.alt: Feast. Gloria; no Creed. Proper readings of the feast replace the Monday of the Sixth Week of Easter. Psalm verses in NRSV numbering (Lectionary Ps 19:2–3, 4–5). The two apostles are kept together because their relics were placed together in the Basilica of the Holy Apostles in Rome in the sixth century. Liturgical colour: red.
2027-05-03.verse: Jesus said to him, “Have I been with you all this time, Philip, and you still do not know me? Whoever has seen me has seen the Father. How can you say, ‘Show us the Father’?”
theo: Today the Church keeps the feast of two of the Twelve whom the Gospels mention only briefly: Philip, and James the son of Alphaeus, often called James the Less to distinguish him from James the brother of John. The first reading was chosen because of one line in it. St Paul is reminding the Corinthians of the Gospel he handed on to them, the core of the faith that he “in turn had received”: “that Christ died for our sins in accordance with the scriptures, and that he was buried, and that he was raised on the third day in accordance with the scriptures, and that he appeared to Cephas, then to the twelve.” Then come the other witnesses: more than five hundred at once, “most of whom are still alive”; “then he appeared to James, then to all the apostles. Last of all, as to one untimely born, he appeared also to me.” This is one of the oldest texts in the whole New Testament. Paul wrote it around the year 54, but he is quoting a summary of the faith he had received years earlier, very soon after the Resurrection. The apostles' faith is not a pious idea that grew slowly; it is the testimony of people who saw the risen Lord. The James to whom the Lord appeared is, in Paul's letters, “James the Lord's brother” (Galatians 1:19), the leader of the Church in Jerusalem. The Latin tradition has long identified him with the apostle James the son of Alphaeus, whom we honour today. Scholars discuss whether these are one man or two, and the Church has not settled the question; what is sure is that the liturgy wants us to see in today's James a witness of the Resurrection.

The Psalm gives the reason the apostles still speak to us: “There is no speech, nor are there words; their voice is not heard; yet their voice goes out through all the earth, and their words to the end of the world.” The psalmist was speaking of the sun, the moon and the stars, which praise God without words. St Paul applies the verse to the preachers of the Gospel (Romans 10:18). Two quiet men from Galilee, of whom we know very little, have a voice that has reached the ends of the earth, as far as India.

The Gospel gives us Philip at the Last Supper. Philip came from Bethsaida, the town of Andrew and Peter, on the shore of the Lake of Galilee. He was among the very first to be called: Jesus “found Philip and said to him, ‘Follow me’” (John 1:43). At once Philip found his friend Nathanael and told him, “We have found him about whom Moses in the law and also the prophets wrote.” When Nathanael scoffed, Philip did not argue; he said, “Come and see.” At the feeding of the five thousand, Jesus tested Philip: “Where are we to buy bread for these people to eat?” And Philip, practical as ever, did the arithmetic: “Six months' wages would not buy enough bread.” Later, some Greeks came to Philip, perhaps because of his Greek name: “Sir, we wish to see Jesus.” Now, at the supper, Jesus has said, “I am the way, and the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me. If you know me, you will know my Father also.” And Philip, honest and a little puzzled, speaks for every seeker: “Lord, show us the Father, and we will be satisfied.” The answer of Jesus is gentle and astonishing: “Have I been with you all this time, Philip, and you still do not know me? Whoever has seen me has seen the Father.” Philip has been looking past Jesus for God, when God was looking at him through the face of Jesus. The Son is not a messenger who points to a distant Father; he is in the Father and the Father is in him.

Then Jesus makes a promise to all who believe: “the one who believes in me will also do the works that I do and, in fact, will do greater works than these, because I am going to the Father.” Greater works, because after the Ascension the Gospel will spread through the whole world by the apostles, by Philip and James and all the rest. And “I will do whatever you ask in my name.” Tradition says that Philip preached in Asia Minor and died at Hierapolis in Phrygia; in 2011 archaeologists working there reported finding a tomb they believe to be his. James, according to the Jewish historian Josephus, was stoned in Jerusalem around the year 62 on the orders of the high priest; the Christian writer Hegesippus, quoted by Eusebius, tells of his prayer for his killers. The letter of James, which tradition ascribes to the Lord's brother, gives us a James who is utterly practical: “be doers of the word, and not merely hearers.” Philip who brought others to Jesus, James who lived what he believed: two faces of the one apostolic faith that has come down to us.
conn: Philip.

A Greek name meaning “lover of horses.” From Bethsaida (John 1:44). He appears in John 1:43–46; 6:5–7; 12:20–22; 14:8–9. He is not the same person as Philip the deacon and evangelist of Acts 6:5; 8:5–40; 21:8, though early writers sometimes confused the two.
James son of Alphaeus.

Named in all four lists of the Twelve (Matthew 10:3; Mark 3:18; Luke 6:15; Acts 1:13). “The Less” (Mark 15:40, “James the younger”) may refer to his age or his stature, and distinguishes him from James son of Zebedee.
James “the Lord's brother.”

Leader of the Church of Jerusalem (Acts 12:17; 15:13; 21:18; Galatians 1:19; 2:9). In the Semitic usage of the Bible “brother” can mean a close relative such as a cousin (CCC 500). The Latin tradition, following St Jerome, identifies him with the son of Alphaeus; many Eastern traditions distinguish them.
A very early creed.

1 Corinthians 15:3–5 uses the technical words “handed on” and “received,” the language of passing down a tradition. Paul probably received it in Damascus or Jerusalem within a few years of the Resurrection.
“Untimely born.”
Greek ektrōma, a child born too early or abnormally. Paul uses it of himself, the persecutor called last of all.
Psalm 19.
A hymn in two parts: the glory of God in the heavens (verses 1–6) and in the law (verses 7–14). Romans 10:18 applies verse 4 to the apostles' preaching.
The date of the feast.

The relics of the two apostles were placed in the Basilica of the Holy Apostles (Santi Apostoli) in Rome, dedicated about 570 on 1 May. The feast was kept on 1 May, moved to 11 May in 1955 when St Joseph the Worker was given 1 May, and to 3 May in the 1969 calendar.
The letter of James.
Tradition ascribes it to James the Lord's brother. It is the source of the Church's teaching on the anointing of the sick (James 5:14–15).
Hierapolis.
A city in Phrygia, today Pamukkale in Turkey. Early writers (Polycrates of Ephesus, about 190, quoted by Eusebius) place Philip's grave there.
altar: “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father.” At Mass we do not see the face of Jesus as Philip did, but he is no less present: the risen Lord who appeared to James and the apostles gives himself to us under the signs of bread and wine, truly his Body and Blood.

The apostles handed on what they had received. St Paul uses the same words for the Eucharist: “For I received from the Lord what I also handed on to you” (1 Corinthians 11:23). The Mass we celebrate today is the apostolic tradition, received from Philip, James and the Twelve.
outline: Opening
Ask: if someone asked you, “Show me God,” what would you show them?
Point 1 · What I in turn had received
The oldest creed and the witness of James.
Point 2 · Their voice goes out through all the earth
Quiet apostles, a worldwide voice.
Point 3 · Show us the Father
Philip's honest question.
Point 4 · Whoever has seen me
Jesus, the face of the Father.
Closing image
Philip at the supper table, looking at Jesus as if for the first time.
Take-home line
“Whoever has seen me has seen the Father.”
live: Come and see
Like Philip with Nathanael, invite one person this week to come with you to Mass, adoration or a prayer group, without arguing, simply: come and see.
Learn the creed by heart
Read 1 Corinthians 15:3–5 slowly today and pray the Apostles' Creed with attention, thanking God for those who handed on the faith to you.
Look at Jesus
Spend ten minutes with a Gospel scene this week, asking: Lord, show me the Father in your face.
Be a doer of the word
In the spirit of St James, choose one practical act of mercy this week: visit a sick person, help someone in need, keep your word.
fathers: St Augustine (in substance)

Philip wanted to see the Father, as if the Father were greater than the one he saw. But the Son is equal to the Father. Seeing the Son in his humanity, Philip was being led to see in faith the one who is God with the Father.
St Cyril of Alexandria (in substance)

Jesus does not say: whoever has seen me has seen someone like the Father, but: has seen the Father. The Son is the perfect image of the one who begot him, as the brightness of a light shows the light itself.
St Jerome (in substance)
James, called the brother of the Lord, was so holy that the people longed to touch the hem of his garment; he governed the Church of Jerusalem for many years and ended his life as a martyr.
St John Chrysostom (in substance)
See how Philip says: show us the Father, and we will be satisfied. He seeks nothing more. So it is with us: when we have found God, nothing else is needed.
magis: Catechism 516
Christ's whole earthly life, his words and deeds, his silences and sufferings, is revelation of the Father: “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father.”
Catechism 639–642
The Resurrection is a real event with historically verified manifestations; 1 Corinthians 15:3–8 is among the earliest testimonies; the apostles are witnesses of the Resurrection.
Catechism 857
The Church is apostolic: built on the foundation of the apostles, keeping and handing on their teaching, and taught and guided by their successors.
Catechism 2614
When Jesus openly entrusts to his disciples the mystery of prayer to the Father, he reveals to them what their prayer and ours must be: to ask in his name.
Dei Verbum 4
Jesus perfected revelation: to see him is to see the Father (John 14:9); by his presence, words, works, death and resurrection he completed and confirmed it.
Benedict XVI, General Audiences (28 June and 6 September 2006)
On James the Less: faith must become concrete in works of love. On Philip: the apostle invites us, as he invited Nathanael, to come and see, to meet Jesus personally.
saints: St Philip, Apostle
Of Bethsaida in Galilee, one of the first called; he brought Nathanael to Jesus and the Greeks to Jesus. Tradition says he preached in Asia Minor and died at Hierapolis in Phrygia.
St James, Apostle

Son of Alphaeus, called James the Less; in the Latin tradition identified with James the brother of the Lord, bishop of Jerusalem, witness of the Resurrection and martyr there around 62. His relics are venerated with Philip's in the Basilica of the Holy Apostles, Rome.
This week
4–5 May: Easter weekdays. 6 May: in India an Easter weekday (Ascension where kept on Thursday). 7 May: First Friday. 8 May: Easter weekday. 9 May: in India, the Ascension of the Lord.
2027-05-03.prayer: God our Father, you gladden us each year with the feast of the Apostles Philip and James. Through their prayers, grant us a share in the passion and resurrection of your only-begotten Son, so that we may come to see you for ever. Lord Jesus, way, truth and life, you said to Philip, whoever has seen me has seen the Father: open our eyes to see the Father in your face, and make us, like James, doers of the word and not hearers only. As Philip brought others to you, let us say to our friends, come and see; and through the faith handed on to us by the apostles, keep us witnesses of your Resurrection until you come again. Amen.

2027-05-04.title: Tuesday of the Sixth Week of Easter
readings: Believe on the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved, you and your household
Your right hand delivers me, O Lord (or: Alleluia)
It is to your advantage that I go away, for if I do not go away, the Advocate will not come to you
2027-05-04.alt: Easter weekday of the sixth week (Year I). The Alleluia is sung before the Gospel, the paschal candle burns beside the ambo, and the Regina Caeli takes the place of the Angelus until Pentecost. The Church is now turning towards the Ascension and the coming of the Holy Spirit. Liturgical colour: white.
2027-05-04.verse: Nevertheless I tell you the truth: it is to your advantage that I go away, for if I do not go away, the Advocate will not come to you; but if I go, I will send him to you.
theo: Paul and Silas have barely arrived in Philippi, the first city of Macedonia where the Gospel is preached, when trouble begins. They have driven a spirit of fortune-telling out of a slave girl, and her owners, who made money from her, drag them before the magistrates. The crowd joins in; the magistrates have them stripped and beaten with rods, and they are thrown into the innermost cell with their feet fastened in the stocks. Then comes one of the most beautiful sentences in the Acts of the Apostles: “About midnight Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God, and the prisoners were listening to them.” Bleeding, chained, in the dark, they sing. Suddenly an earthquake shakes the foundations, the doors fly open and everyone's chains are unfastened. The jailer wakes, sees the open doors, and draws his sword to kill himself, for a Roman jailer who lost his prisoners could pay with his life. “But Paul shouted in a loud voice, ‘Do not harm yourself, for we are all here.’” The prisoners have not fled. The jailer falls trembling before them and asks the question of every human heart: “Sirs, what must I do to be saved?” The answer is simple: “Believe on the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved, you and your household.” That same night the jailer washes their wounds, and he and his family are baptized. He brings them into his house, sets food before them, and “he and his entire household rejoiced that he had become a believer in God.” The night that began with beatings ends with Baptism and a meal of joy.

The Psalm is the song of Paul and Silas at midnight: “I give you thanks, O Lord, with my whole heart.” “On the day I called, you answered me, you increased my strength of soul.” And even in the middle of trouble: “you stretch out your hand, and your right hand delivers me.” In the Gospel Jesus prepares the disciples for his going away. They are full of sorrow; they cannot imagine life without him. But he tells them something surprising: “it is to your advantage that I go away, for if I do not go away, the Advocate will not come to you; but if I go, I will send him to you.” The Ascension is not a loss but the condition of a greater gift. While Jesus walked in Galilee he could be in only one place at a time; through the Holy Spirit he will be present in every disciple, in every prison cell and every home. And the Spirit will “prove the world wrong about sin and righteousness and judgment”: he will show that the real sin is refusing to believe in Jesus, that the one condemned on the cross was the righteous one now gone to the Father, and that the ruler of this world, not Jesus, has been judged. The same Spirit sang in Paul and Silas at midnight, shook the prison, and turned a jailer into a brother. In these days before the Ascension, the Church learns to trust that the Lord who goes away is not leaving us alone.
outline: Opening
Ask: what would you do at midnight in prison, after a beating?
Point 1 · Singing at midnight
Praise in the dark, and the prisoners listening.
Point 2 · What must I do to be saved?
The jailer's question and the Gospel's answer.
Point 3 · Better that I go
The Ascension makes room for the Advocate.
Take-home line
“If I go, I will send him to you.”
live: Sing in the night (Acts 16:25)
When something goes wrong today, pause and say or sing one line of praise before you say anything else.
Answer the jailer's question (Acts 16:31)
Think of one person who is near despair. Pray for them by name today, and send them a word of hope.
2027-05-04.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, you went away to the Father so that the Advocate might come to us. As Paul and Silas sang to you at midnight, teach us to praise you in our darkest hours. Stretch out your right hand and deliver all who are imprisoned, in body or in spirit. Send us your Holy Spirit, to convince the world of the truth and to make us messengers of salvation to everyone who asks, what must I do to be saved? Amen.
altar: After his Baptism the jailer of Philippi “set food before them” and the whole household rejoiced. The first Christians often joined Baptism and a meal of joy. At the altar the risen Lord himself sets food before the baptized: his own Body and Blood, the meal of those who have been saved.

2027-05-05.title: Wednesday of the Sixth Week of Easter
readings: What therefore you worship as unknown, this I proclaim to you
Heaven and earth are full of your glory (or: Alleluia)
When the Spirit of truth comes, he will guide you into all the truth
2027-05-05.alt: Easter weekday of the sixth week (Year I). The Alleluia is sung before the Gospel, the paschal candle burns beside the ambo, and the Regina Caeli takes the place of the Angelus until Pentecost. The Church is now turning towards the Ascension and the coming of the Holy Spirit. Liturgical colour: white. Tomorrow, in India, is an Easter weekday; the Ascension is kept on Sunday 9 May.
2027-05-05.verse: When the Spirit of truth comes, he will guide you into all the truth; for he will not speak on his own, but will speak whatever he hears, and he will declare to you the things that are to come.
theo: Paul has been hurried out of Thessalonica and Beroea and brought, almost alone, to Athens, the most famous city of learning in the ancient world. Walking its streets, he sees temples, statues and altars everywhere. He is invited to speak at the Areopagus, the hill and council where the city's philosophers and judges met. His speech is a model of how to speak of Christ to people of another culture. He does not begin with insults; he begins with respect: “Athenians, I see how extremely religious you are in every way.” He has noticed an altar “To an unknown god,” and he builds on it: “What therefore you worship as unknown, this I proclaim to you.” Then he speaks of the Creator who “made the world and everything in it,” who does not live in shrines made by hands, who gives to all “life and breath and all things,” and who made all nations from one ancestor, “so that they would search for God and perhaps grope for him and find him, though indeed he is not far from each one of us.” He even quotes their own poets: “In him we live and move and have our being,” and “For we too are his offspring.” Only at the end does he name what is new: God has fixed a day of judgment “by a man whom he has appointed, and of this he has given assurance to all by raising him from the dead.”

At the word “resurrection” the meeting breaks up. “When they heard of the resurrection of the dead, some scoffed; but others said, ‘We will hear you again about this.’” It looks like a failure, and Paul soon leaves for Corinth. Yet Luke adds: “some of them joined him and became believers, including Dionysius the Areopagite and a woman named Damaris, and others with them.” Seeds are sown even where the harvest is small. The Psalm calls the whole creation to praise, “kings of the earth and all peoples,” “young men and women alike, old and young together,” for the Lord's “glory is above earth and heaven.” In the Gospel Jesus explains why the Church's understanding of him can grow without changing: “I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now. When the Spirit of truth comes, he will guide you into all the truth.” The Spirit does not bring a new Gospel; “he will take what is mine and declare it to you.” He leads the Church deeper into the one truth that is Christ. That is what Paul did at Athens: he found in the Greeks' own searching a door for the truth of Christ. The Second Vatican Council teaches that the Church rejects nothing that is true and holy in other religions, while she proclaims without ceasing Christ, “the way, and the truth, and the life” (Nostra Aetate 2). In a land of many temples and many seekers like India, Paul at the Areopagus is a teacher for us: respectful, clear, and unashamed of the Resurrection.
outline: Opening
Ask: how do you speak about Jesus to a friend of another faith?
Point 1 · To an unknown god
Paul begins with respect and with the Creator.
Point 2 · Not far from each one of us
In him we live and move and have our being.
Point 3 · Some scoffed, some believed
Dionysius, Damaris and the hidden harvest.
Point 4 · Into all the truth
The Spirit leads the Church deeper into Christ.
Take-home line
“He will guide you into all the truth.”
live: Look for the unknown altar (Acts 17:23)
Notice today one good thing in a friend or colleague of another faith: their prayerfulness, honesty or generosity. Thank God for it.
Ask the Spirit of truth (John 16:13)
Before reading the Bible or the Catechism today, pray: Come, Spirit of truth, guide me into the truth of Jesus.
2027-05-05.prayer: God our Creator, in you we live and move and have our being, and you are not far from each one of us. You let the peoples of the earth search for you and grope for you; reveal to them your Son, whom you raised from the dead. Give us the respect, clarity and courage of St Paul at Athens. Send us the Spirit of truth, who takes what belongs to Jesus and declares it to us, so that we may be led into all the truth and praise you with all creation. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.
altar: The Athenians worshipped an unknown god. At the altar the God who is “not far from each one of us” comes closer still: in the Eucharist the risen Christ is truly present, so that we who live and move and have our being in God may also receive God into ourselves.

2027-05-07.title: Friday of the Sixth Week of Easter
readings: Do not be afraid, but speak and do not be silent; for I am with you
God is king of all the earth (or: Alleluia)
No one will take your joy from you
2027-05-07.alt: Easter weekday. The paschal candle burns beside the ambo; the Alleluia is sung before the Gospel; the Regina Caeli (Queen of Heaven) replaces the Angelus until Pentecost. Liturgical colour: white. First Friday of the month: in many parishes the Holy Hour, confessions and the devotion to the Sacred Heart of Jesus. From today until the Saturday before Pentecost, nine days in all, the Church may pray the novena to the Holy Spirit, as the apostles prayed with Mary in the upper room.
2027-05-07.verse: So you have pain now; but I will see you again, and your hearts will rejoice, and no one will take your joy from you.
theo: Paul has been in Corinth for some time. He has been opposed, he has moved next door to the synagogue, and he has seen the synagogue official believe. Yet he is afraid. Writing to the Corinthians later, he admits it: “And I came to you in weakness and in fear and in much trembling” (1 Corinthians 2:3). He knew what usually came next in a city: riots, beatings, flight by night. So the Lord speaks to him in a vision: “Do not be afraid, but speak and do not be silent; for I am with you, and no one will lay a hand on you to harm you, for there are many in this city who are my people.” The Lord does not promise that there will be no trouble. He promises his presence, and he gives Paul a new way of looking at the noisy port city: many in this city are already mine, though they do not know it yet. So Paul stays “a year and six months, teaching the word of God among them,” the longest stay of his journeys so far.

Then the trouble comes. When Gallio becomes proconsul of Achaia, some leaders of the Jewish community bring Paul before the tribunal, accusing him of persuading people to worship God against the law. Gallio, the brother of the philosopher Seneca, will not even hear Paul's defence: this is “a matter of questions about words and names and your own law, see to it yourselves.” An inscription found at Delphi dates Gallio's year in Corinth to about 51 or 52, and so this scene is one of the fixed points by which we date Paul's life. A Roman judge's indifference becomes, for a time, the protection of the Gospel. Paul stays on, then sails for Syria with Priscilla and Aquila, cutting his hair at Cenchreae because of a vow, a sign that he still lived as a devout Jew. Luke's phrase “the Jews” here means the group in that synagogue who opposed Paul, not the Jewish people; the official Crispus had believed, and Sosthenes, perhaps the same “brother Sosthenes” who later writes with Paul (1 Corinthians 1:1), suffers in the uproar.

The Gospel gives the image of a woman in labour: “she has pain, because her hour has come. But when her child is born, she no longer remembers the anguish because of the joy of having brought a human being into the world.” Jesus uses the word “hour,” the word he uses for his own Passion. His cross is a birth. On this First Friday the Church looks at the pierced Heart of Jesus. From his opened side came blood and water (John 19:34), and the Fathers saw there the birth of the Church, as Eve was formed from the side of the sleeping Adam. The pain of Good Friday was a labour, and its child is a new people. That is why the joy Jesus promises is a joy that “no one will take from you”: it is not a mood that comes and goes, but the life of the Risen One born in us. And the Psalm, an ancient song for the Lord's enthronement, already rings with Ascension joy: “Clap your hands, all you peoples; shout to God with loud songs of joy.”
conn: The night vision.
Like Jacob at Bethel (Genesis 28:15) and Jeremiah at his call (Jeremiah 1:8), Paul hears “I am with you.” Luke tells of several visions given to Paul at turning points (Acts 16:9; 23:11; 27:23–24).
“Many in this city are my people.”
Corinth was famous for its wealth and its loose living. The Lord sees not a hopeless city but a people still to be gathered.
Gallio.
Lucius Junius Gallio Annaeanus, brother of Seneca. An inscription at Delphi, a letter of the emperor Claudius, places his proconsulship in about AD 51–52.
The tribunal.
The Greek bēma, a raised speaking platform. Its remains can still be seen in the forum of ancient Corinth.
Sosthenes.
Successor of Crispus as official of the synagogue. A Sosthenes is named with Paul at the start of 1 Corinthians; many think he is the same man, later a believer.
The vow at Cenchreae.
Probably a vow like the Nazirite vow (Numbers 6), ended by cutting the hair. Cenchreae, Corinth's eastern port, later had a church with “our sister Phoebe” as its deacon (Romans 16:1).
Psalm 47.
A psalm of God's kingship. Christian liturgy has long sung it on the Ascension: “God has gone up with a shout, the Lord with the sound of a trumpet” (Psalm 47:5).
The woman in labour.
A prophetic image of the birth of the messianic age (Isaiah 26:17; 66:7–9). In John, Jesus' “hour” is the hour of his Passion and glorification (John 12:23; 13:1).
First Friday.

St Margaret Mary Alacoque (1647–1690) reported that the Lord asked for Communion of reparation on the first Friday of nine consecutive months. The devotion spread throughout the Church, and in India and Kerala it remains strong.
altar: The Heart of Jesus, opened on the cross, is not only a memory. At every Mass the same sacrifice is made present on the altar, and the Lord who was pierced gives us his Body and Blood, the fruit of his labour of love.
First Friday Communion is a way of answering love with love. We receive the Heart that was pierced for us and offer our own hearts, with their sins and sorrows, to be healed and set on fire.
outline: Opening
Ask a mother in the congregation, in your mind: do you remember the pain, or the face of your child?
Point 1 · Do not be afraid, but speak
The Lord's word to a fearful apostle.
Point 2 · Words and names and your own law
A judge who would not judge, and a door kept open.
Point 3 · Her hour has come
The labour of the cross and the birth of joy.
Closing image
A newborn laid on its mother's breast, and above, a crucifix with the side opened.
Take-home line
“No one will take your joy from you.”
live: Speak one word
Is there a truth of faith you have kept silent about at home or at work out of fear? Say it gently today.
Keep the First Friday
Go to confession or spend a quiet half hour before the Blessed Sacrament this weekend, and consecrate your family to the Sacred Heart.
Begin the novena
Pray each day until Pentecost: Come, Holy Spirit, fill the hearts of your faithful and kindle in them the fire of your love.
fathers: St John Chrysostom (in substance)
The Lord did not take away the danger from Paul; he took away the fear. He did not say: no one will attack you, but: no one will harm you, for I am with you. That is the courage of the saints.
St John Chrysostom (Catecheses, in substance)

From his side came water and blood, the signs of Baptism and the Eucharist. From these the Church is born. As God formed Eve from the side of Adam while he slept, so Christ gave us the Church from his side as he slept on the cross.
St Augustine (in substance)
The joy that no one takes away is Christ himself. Every other joy can be lost; this one is kept in heaven, where he is, and so it is safe.
magis: Catechism 478
Jesus knew and loved us each and all during his life, his agony and his Passion; his Sacred Heart, pierced by our sins and for our salvation, is the chief sign of that love.
Haurietis Aquas (Pius XII, 1956)
The devotion to the Sacred Heart is the worship of the love of God for us shown in the Heart of Jesus.
Dilexit Nos 1–2 (Pope Francis, 2024)
“He loved us”: the Heart of Christ is the centre where we learn to love and are healed of an empty, heartless life.
Catechism 2472
The duty of Christians to take part in the life of the Church impels them to act as witnesses of the Gospel by word and deed.
Dignitatis Humanae 2 (Vatican II, 1965)
The human person has a right to religious freedom; no one may be forced to act against conscience in religious matters.
saints: St Rose Venerini
An Italian woman of Viterbo (1656–1728) who opened some of the first public schools for girls in Italy and founded the Venerini Sisters. She died on 7 May 1728 and was canonized in 2006.
This week
9 May: THE ASCENSION OF THE LORD (in India); World Communications Day. 10 May: St John of Avila (optional). 11 May: Easter weekday.
2027-05-07.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, you said to Paul in the night: do not be afraid, but speak, for I am with you. Speak that word to us. When we are silent from fear, give us courage; when we are opposed, give us patience; when we are protected, give us thanks. On this First Friday we come to your pierced Heart. From your opened side the Church was born; from your labour of love comes our joy. Take our hearts, heal them, and make them like yours. Send us your Holy Spirit, for whom we begin to wait with Mary your Mother, and give us the joy that no one can take from us. You live and reign for ever and ever. Alleluia. Amen.

2027-05-08.title: Saturday of the Sixth Week of Easter
readings: Apollos showed by the scriptures that the Messiah is Jesus
God is king of all the earth (or: Alleluia)
The Father himself loves you, because you have loved me and have believed
2027-05-08.alt: Easter weekday. The paschal candle burns beside the ambo; the Alleluia is sung before the Gospel; the Regina Caeli (Queen of Heaven) replaces the Angelus until Pentecost. Liturgical colour: white. Saturday, a day traditionally dedicated to the Blessed Virgin Mary. In India the Ascension is celebrated tomorrow; this evening's Mass is the Vigil Mass of the Ascension. Second day of the novena to the Holy Spirit.
2027-05-08.verse: For the Father himself loves you, because you have loved me and have believed that I came from God.
theo: Today's short reading opens Paul's third great journey. After a visit to Antioch, his home church, “he departed and went from place to place through the region of Galatia and Phrygia, strengthening all the disciples.” Luke gives only one line to hundreds of kilometres on foot, but the purpose is clear: a missionary does not only found churches; he goes back to strengthen them. Then the scene moves to Ephesus, where Priscilla and Aquila have settled, and a new figure appears: Apollos, a Jew from Alexandria in Egypt, the great city of books and scholars. Luke paints him warmly: “an eloquent man, well-versed in the scriptures,” instructed in the Way of the Lord, speaking “with burning enthusiasm” and teaching “accurately the things concerning Jesus, though he knew only the baptism of John.” He had a gift, a fire, and a gap.

What happens next is a quiet model of Christian correction. “When Priscilla and Aquila heard him, they took him aside and explained the Way of God to him more accurately.” They do not interrupt him in the synagogue or denounce him to the apostles. They take him aside, probably into their home and workshop, and teach him. A tentmaking couple instruct a brilliant preacher, and he is humble enough to learn. Notice too that Luke again names Priscilla first: a woman and her husband together hand on the faith. Then the believers write a letter of recommendation, Apollos crosses to Achaia, and there “he greatly helped those who through grace had become believers.” Paul will later sum up the partnership: “I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth” (1 Corinthians 3:6). No one owns the Gospel; each hands on what was received.

In the Gospel Jesus, at the Last Supper, speaks of a new way of praying: “if you ask anything of the Father in my name, he will give it to you … Ask and you will receive, so that your joy may be complete.” To ask in his name is not to add a formula at the end of a prayer; it is to pray as one who belongs to him, wanting what he wants. And then the most tender sentence: “the Father himself loves you, because you have loved me and have believed that I came from God.” We do not need Jesus to persuade an unwilling Father; the Father already loves us. Jesus sums up his whole life in one line: “I came from the Father and have come into the world; again, I am leaving the world and am going to the Father.” That is the movement the Church celebrates tomorrow in India, the Ascension. On this Saturday, a day dedicated to Our Lady, we remember that the apostles waited for the Spirit with Mary, the mother of Jesus (Acts 1:14). She, who asked so simply at Cana, teaches us to ask in his name.
conn: Galatia and Phrygia.
Regions of central Asia Minor (modern Turkey) where Paul had founded churches on his earlier journeys (Acts 16:6). The Letter to the Galatians was written to churches in this area.
Ephesus.
A great port city on the west coast of Asia Minor, with the famous temple of Artemis. Paul will soon stay there more than two years (Acts 19:10).
Apollos.

An Alexandrian Jew; Alexandria had a large Jewish community and was the city where the Greek translation of the Scriptures, the Septuagint, was made. Apollos later became so popular in Corinth that some said “I belong to Apollos” (1 Corinthians 1:12).
“The Way.”
One of the earliest names for the Christian faith in Acts (9:2; 19:9; 24:14): not only a doctrine but a way of life following Jesus.
The baptism of John.
A baptism of repentance in preparation for the Messiah. Apollos knew Jesus, but not yet the full gift of Christian Baptism in the Holy Spirit (see Acts 19:1–7, read on Monday).
Letters of recommendation.
Early Christian communities welcomed travelling teachers with such letters (2 Corinthians 3:1; Romans 16:1). They were a sign of communion between churches.
“In my name.”
In the Bible a name stands for the person. To ask in Jesus' name is to come before the Father as members of his Son, through him and with him.
Saturday and Mary.

From early times Saturday has been dedicated to the Blessed Virgin Mary; at Fatima (1917, and to Lucia in 1925) Our Lady also asked for the Communion of reparation on the first Saturday of five consecutive months, in honour of her Immaculate Heart.
altar: At every Mass the Church prays “through Christ our Lord”: every prayer is offered to the Father in the name of the Son. Above all in the Eucharistic Prayer, “through him, and with him, and in him,” our whole life is lifted to the Father.
Apollos was taught the Way more accurately. In the Mass we are taught first by the Word and then fed by the Bread; the table of the Word and the table of the Eucharist form one act of worship.
outline: Opening
Ask: when did someone take you aside and correct you kindly? How did it feel?
Point 1 · Strengthening all the disciples
A missionary who goes back.
Point 2 · They took him aside
Priscilla, Aquila and the humble scholar.
Point 3 · The Father himself loves you
Asking in Jesus' name.
Closing image
Mary in the upper room, hands open in prayer, the apostles around her.
Take-home line
“The Father himself loves you.”
live: Strengthen someone
Visit, phone or message one person whose faith is weak or tired, simply to encourage them.
Correct in private
If you must correct someone today, do it as Priscilla and Aquila did: privately, gently, with the aim of helping.
Ask in his name
Bring one need to the Father today, beginning: Father, in the name of Jesus your Son, and ending with: your will be done.
fathers: St Jerome (in substance)
Ignorance of the Scriptures is ignorance of Christ. Apollos was mighty in the Scriptures, and so he could show from them that Jesus is the Messiah.
St John Chrysostom (in substance)
See how Apollos, eloquent and learned, was not ashamed to be taught by a tentmaker and his wife. He learned, and so he was able to teach more powerfully.
St Augustine (in substance)
Whatever we ask that is against our salvation we do not ask in the Saviour's name. To ask in the name of Jesus is to ask what belongs to our salvation, and that the Father gives.
magis: Catechism 2614
When Jesus openly entrusts to his disciples the mystery of prayer to the Father, he reveals to them what their prayer and ours must be: asking in his name.
Catechism 2666
The name of Jesus contains all: God and man and the whole economy of creation and salvation. To pray “Jesus” is to invoke him and to call him within us.
Dei Verbum 25 (Vatican II, 1965)
All the faithful are urged to learn by frequent reading of the Scriptures “the surpassing worth of knowing Christ Jesus,” for ignorance of the Scriptures is ignorance of Christ.
Catechism 965
After her Son's Ascension, Mary aided the beginnings of the Church by her prayers; with the apostles she implored the gift of the Spirit.
Christifideles Laici 49 (St John Paul II, 1988)
Women and men together share in the mission of the Church; the gifts of women are needed for the life and growth of the Christian community.
saints: The Supplication to Our Lady of Pompeii

On 8 May (and on the first Sunday of October) many Catholics recite at noon the Supplication to Our Lady of the Rosary of Pompeii, composed by Bartolo Longo, a lawyer who returned to the faith and built the shrine at Pompeii. He was canonized in October 2025.
This week

9 May: THE ASCENSION OF THE LORD (in India); World Communications Day. 10 May: St John of Avila (optional). 11 May: Easter weekday. 12 May: Sts Nereus and Achilleus; St Pancras (optional). 13 May: Our Lady of Fatima (optional).
2027-05-08.prayer: Father, you love us because we have loved your Son and believed that he came from you. In his name we come to you, trusting that you hear us, and we ask above all for the gift of your Holy Spirit. Make us like Paul, strengthening the disciples; like Priscilla and Aquila, teaching the Way gently and truly; like Apollos, burning with zeal and humble enough to learn. With Mary, who prayed with the apostles while they waited, we wait for the Spirit and for the joy you promised to make complete. As your Son goes to you, let our hearts follow him. Through Christ our Lord. Alleluia. Amen.

2027-05-10.title: Monday of the Seventh Week of Easter
readings: Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you became believers?
Sing to God, O kingdoms of the earth (or: Alleluia)
Take courage; I have conquered the world
2027-05-10.alt: Easter weekday. The paschal candle burns beside the ambo; the Alleluia is sung before the Gospel; the Regina Caeli (Queen of Heaven) replaces the Angelus until Pentecost. Liturgical colour: white. Optional memorial of St John of Avila, priest and doctor of the Church (in the General Roman Calendar since 2021). The days between the Ascension and Pentecost: the novena to the Holy Spirit continues.
2027-05-10.verse: I have said this to you, so that in me you may have peace. In the world you face persecution. But take courage; I have conquered the world!
theo: Paul arrives in Ephesus and meets “some disciples,” about twelve of them. Something about them makes him ask a direct question: “Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you became believers?” Their answer is startling: “No, we have not even heard that there is a Holy Spirit.” They had been baptized “into John's baptism,” the baptism of repentance that prepared the way for the Messiah. They were sincere; they had begun the journey; but they had stopped at the door. Paul explains gently: “John baptized with the baptism of repentance, telling the people to believe in the one who was to come after him, that is, in Jesus.” They are baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus, and “when Paul had laid his hands on them, the Holy Spirit came upon them, and they spoke in tongues and prophesied.” It is a small Pentecost in Ephesus, like the one in Samaria (Acts 8:14–17) and in the house of Cornelius (Acts 10:44–48). The Church has always seen here the two moments of Christian initiation: Baptism, and the laying on of hands that we call Confirmation.

The question Paul asked those twelve is worth asking ourselves in this week before Pentecost. Many of us were baptized as babies and confirmed as children. We have heard that there is a Holy Spirit; we say it every Sunday in the Creed. But do we live as people who have received him? Do we pray to him, listen to him, expect anything of him? Paul spent three months in the synagogue, “arguing persuasively about the kingdom of God.” The Spirit makes the Church speak. The Psalm sings of the God who rises up and scatters his enemies, “Father of orphans and protector of widows,” who “gives the desolate a home to live in”: that is what the Spirit does in the Church, making a home for the lonely and a family for the orphaned.

In the Gospel the disciples, at the end of the Last Supper, think at last that they understand: “Yes, now you are speaking plainly … by this we believe that you came from God.” Jesus answers with a sad, loving realism: “Do you now believe? The hour is coming, indeed it has come, when you will be scattered, each one to his home, and you will leave me alone.” Within hours they would run away. Yet Jesus is not bitter: “I am not alone because the Father is with me.” And his last words before the great prayer of John 17 are words of courage: “In the world you face persecution. But take courage; I have conquered the world!” He says this before the cross, as if the victory were already won, because it is. St John of Avila, whom the Church remembers today, knew persecution from within the Church itself: as a young priest he was denounced to the Inquisition and spent about a year in prison. There, he said, he learned more of the mystery of Christ than in all his studies. He came out without bitterness, and became the great preacher of Andalusia and a guide of saints.
conn: Ephesus.
Paul's base for more than two years (Acts 19:10), from which the Gospel spread through the province of Asia. Tradition also links Ephesus with St John the Apostle and with the Blessed Virgin Mary.
“Some disciples.”
Luke uses the word for believers, but they knew only John's baptism, like Apollos in Saturday's reading. Disciples of John the Baptist were found well beyond Palestine.
John's baptism.

A baptism of repentance, preparing for the Messiah (Luke 3:3, 16). Christian Baptism is baptism “in the name of the Lord Jesus,” into his death and Resurrection, with the gift of the Spirit (Romans 6:3–4).
The laying on of hands.

A gesture of blessing and of handing on the Spirit (Acts 8:17; 1 Timothy 4:14; Hebrews 6:2). In the Latin Church it is completed in Confirmation by the anointing with chrism and the words: Be sealed with the Gift of the Holy Spirit.
About twelve.
Perhaps a quiet echo of the Twelve: a new beginning of the Church in Ephesus.
Psalm 68.
An ancient processional hymn of God marching from Sinai to his sanctuary. Verse 18, “You ascended the high mount, leading captives,” is quoted in Ephesians 4:8 of Christ's Ascension.
“I have conquered the world.”
The Greek nenikēka is in the perfect tense: a victory already won and still in force. 1 John 5:4 takes it up: “this is the victory that conquers the world, our faith.”
St John of Avila (about 1499–1569).

A Spanish secular priest, the “Apostle of Andalusia.” He wrote Audi, filia on the spiritual life, guided St John of God, St Francis Borgia and others, and was consulted by St Teresa of Avila. Canonized in 1970, declared a Doctor of the Church by Benedict XVI in 2012; patron of the secular clergy of Spain.
altar: The Spirit who came on the twelve at Ephesus is called down at every Mass. In the epiclesis the priest stretches out his hands over the bread and wine, as Paul laid his hands on the disciples, and asks the Father to send the Holy Spirit so that they may become the Body and Blood of Christ.

St John of Avila taught priests to celebrate Mass as men in love with the Eucharist; he said (in substance) that the priest should be so united to Christ in the sacrifice that his whole life becomes an offering.
outline: Opening
Ask: if someone asked you, have you received the Holy Spirit? what would you answer?
Point 1 · We have not even heard
Twelve disciples at the door.
Point 2 · Paul laid his hands on them
Baptism, Confirmation, and a little Pentecost.
Point 3 · Take courage
The Lord who has conquered the world.
Closing image
A circle of new believers in Ephesus, Paul's hands on their heads, and their faces bright with prayer.
Take-home line
“Take courage; I have conquered the world!”
live: Remember your Confirmation
Find out the date of your Confirmation, or ask your parents. Thank God for it today, and pray the prayer: Come, Holy Spirit.
Pray to the Spirit by name
Each day until Pentecost, ask the Holy Spirit for one of his seven gifts: wisdom, understanding, counsel, fortitude, knowledge, piety, fear of the Lord.
Take courage
Face one difficulty today that you have been avoiding, saying: Jesus, you have conquered the world; give me courage.
fathers: St Cyril of Jerusalem (Mystagogical Catecheses, in substance)

Do not think that the holy chrism is plain ointment. As the bread of the Eucharist after the invocation of the Holy Spirit is no longer simple bread, so this holy oil after the invocation is the gift of Christ and of the Holy Spirit.
St Ambrose (On the Mysteries, in substance)

Remember that you have received the spiritual seal, the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, the Spirit of counsel and fortitude, the Spirit of knowledge and piety, the Spirit of holy fear. Keep what you have received.
St Augustine (in substance)
The Lord says: I have conquered the world. Rejoice, then, for if he conquered, we too conquer in him. He did not say: you will not be troubled, but: take courage.
magis: Catechism 1288

From that time on the apostles, in fulfilment of Christ's will, imparted to the newly baptized by the laying on of hands the gift of the Spirit that completes the grace of Baptism (Acts 8:15–17; 19:5–6).
Catechism 1302–1303

Confirmation brings an increase and deepening of baptismal grace: it unites us more firmly to Christ, increases the gifts of the Holy Spirit in us, and gives us strength to spread and defend the faith.
Lumen Gentium 11 (Vatican II, 1964)
By Confirmation the faithful are more perfectly bound to the Church and endowed with the special strength of the Holy Spirit, so that they are more strictly obliged to spread and defend the faith.
Catechism 1808
Fortitude ensures firmness in difficulties and constancy in the pursuit of the good: “In the world you have tribulation; but be of good cheer, I have overcome the world.”
Benedict XVI, Apostolic Letter on St John of Avila (7 October 2012)
A master of evangelizers and of priests, whose doctrine of the love of God and of the Eucharist remains a light for the new evangelization.
saints: St John of Avila (optional memorial)

Born in Almodóvar del Campo, Spain, he studied at Salamanca and Alcalá, gave away his inheritance to the poor, and longed to be a missionary in Mexico, but was kept in Andalusia, where he preached for some forty years. He founded schools and colleges, renewed the clergy, and died at Montilla on 10 May 1569.
St Damien of Molokai

A Belgian priest of the Congregation of the Sacred Hearts who served the people with leprosy on Molokai in Hawaii, caught the disease himself and died in 1889. He was canonized in 2009; in the United States he is remembered on 10 May.
2027-05-10.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, you told your disciples: take courage, I have conquered the world. We confess that we too are often afraid, and that we know the Holy Spirit only a little. Send him upon us as he came on the disciples at Ephesus when Paul laid his hands on them. Renew in us the grace of our Baptism and Confirmation; give us his gifts of wisdom and fortitude; and make us witnesses who speak boldly of the kingdom of God. Through the prayers of St John of Avila, give your Church holy priests who love the Eucharist and preach your Word with fire. In you may we have peace. You live and reign for ever and ever. Alleluia. Amen.

2027-05-11.title: Tuesday of the Seventh Week of Easter
readings: I may finish my course and the ministry that I received from the Lord Jesus
Sing to God, O kingdoms of the earth (or: Alleluia)
Father, glorify your Son so that the Son may glorify you
2027-05-11.alt: Easter weekday. The paschal candle burns beside the ambo; the Alleluia is sung before the Gospel; the Regina Caeli (Queen of Heaven) replaces the Angelus until Pentecost. Liturgical colour: white. From today until Thursday the Gospels are taken from the prayer of Jesus at the Last Supper (John 17), the “priestly prayer.” The novena to the Holy Spirit continues.
2027-05-11.verse: And this is eternal life, that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent.
theo: Paul is on his way to Jerusalem, hurrying to arrive before Pentecost (Acts 20:16). His ship stops at Miletus, a port about fifty kilometres south of Ephesus, and he sends for the elders of the Ephesian church. When they arrive he speaks to them as a father who knows he will not see his children again. This is the only speech in Acts that Paul gives to Christian leaders, and it is his farewell. He looks back first: “You yourselves know how I lived among you the entire time from the first day that I set foot in Asia, serving the Lord with all humility and with tears.” He reminds them of the trials he endured, including plots by those who opposed him, and of how he held nothing back: “I did not shrink from doing anything helpful, proclaiming the message to you and teaching you publicly and from house to house.” His message was simple and complete: “repentance toward God and faith toward our Lord Jesus,” to Jews and Greeks alike.

Then he looks ahead: “as a captive to the Spirit, I am on my way to Jerusalem, not knowing what will happen to me there, except that the Holy Spirit testifies to me in every city that imprisonment and persecutions are waiting for me.” Paul does not know the details, only the direction. And he is at peace: “I do not count my life of any value to myself, if only I may finish my course and the ministry that I received from the Lord Jesus, to testify to the good news of God's grace.” The word “course” is the runner's track; Paul sees his life as a race to be run to the end. He can say, with a clear conscience, “I did not shrink from declaring to you the whole purpose of God.” Not a selection of pleasant truths, but the whole of it. The Psalm gives thanks to the God “who daily bears us up,” and to whom “belongs escape from death”: that is the confidence with which Paul walks towards chains.

In the Gospel we hear the beginning of the great prayer of Jesus. “He looked up to heaven and said, ‘Father, the hour has come; glorify your Son so that the Son may glorify you.’” The hour is the cross, and Jesus calls it glory: the moment when the love of the Father and the Son is most fully shown. Then he defines eternal life, not as endless time but as a relationship: “this is eternal life, that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent.” To know, in the Bible, is to love and be united. Jesus can say what Paul will echo at Miletus: “I glorified you on earth by finishing the work that you gave me to do.” And he prays for his disciples: “I am asking on their behalf … because they are yours … And now I am no longer in the world, but they are in the world, and I am coming to you.” These are words of the Ascension. Jesus goes to the Father, and he leaves his friends in the world, held in his prayer. Paul at Miletus, handing his flock to God, is praying the same prayer in his own way.
conn: Miletus.
An ancient Ionian port at the mouth of the river Maeander, south of Ephesus. Paul chose not to go into Ephesus itself, perhaps to save time or to avoid trouble (Acts 20:16).
The elders.
In Greek presbyteroi; in verse 28 Paul also calls them episkopoi, overseers, and tells them to shepherd the church of God. From these words come our words priest and bishop.
“With tears.”
Paul speaks of his tears twice in this speech (Acts 20:19, 31) and also in his letters (2 Corinthians 2:4; Philippians 3:18). His ministry was not cold administration but love that wept.
“From house to house.”
The first Christians met in homes (Acts 2:46; Romans 16:5). Paul taught both in public places and in family gatherings.
“A captive to the Spirit.”
Literally “bound in the Spirit.” Before he is bound with chains in Jerusalem, Paul is already bound by obedience to the Spirit.
“Finish my course.”
An image from the athletic games. Near the end of his life Paul will write: “I have finished the race, I have kept the faith” (2 Timothy 4:7).
The priestly prayer.

The name given to John 17 since the sixteenth-century Lutheran theologian David Chytraeus, but its content was recognized by the Fathers: Jesus, as High Priest, consecrates himself and prays for his disciples and for all who will believe.
“Glorify.”
In John, glory (doxa) is the visible radiance of God's love. The cross is the hour of glory because there love is shown without limit (John 12:23–24; 13:31–32).
“To know.”
In biblical language knowledge is personal communion, as in Jeremiah 9:24 and Hosea 6:6. Eternal life begins now, in knowing and loving God.
altar: In the priestly prayer Jesus offers himself to the Father for his disciples. At every Mass that same offering is made present: the Son glorifies the Father by giving himself, and we, joined to him, are offered with him.

Paul said he did not shrink from declaring the whole purpose of God. The Mass, too, holds nothing back: the Lord gives us his whole self, Body and Blood, soul and divinity, so that we may know him, and in knowing him have eternal life.
outline: Opening
Ask: if you knew you were seeing your family or parish for the last time, what would you say to them?
Point 1 · Serving the Lord with humility and tears
Paul's look back at Ephesus.
Point 2 · If only I may finish my course
Walking towards Jerusalem in the Spirit.
Point 3 · This is eternal life
Jesus' prayer for his own as he goes to the Father.
Closing image
Elders kneeling on the beach at Miletus, praying with Paul, then watching his ship sail away.
Take-home line
“This is eternal life, that they may know you.”
live: Hold nothing back
Think of one truth or kindness you have kept from someone because it was uncomfortable. Offer it today, gently.
Run your course
Look at one duty you are tempted to leave unfinished. Finish it today, as an offering to the Lord.
Know him
Spend ten minutes today with John 17:1–11, not to study it but to listen to Jesus praying for you.
fathers: St Augustine (in substance)

This is eternal life: to know God. The knowledge that saves is not the knowledge of many things, but the knowledge of God that is joined to love. We shall be fully happy when we see him as he is; even now we begin to live by knowing him.
St John Chrysostom (in substance)
See how Paul, about to depart, does not boast of miracles but of tears and labours. He shows the elders a shepherd who wept for his flock day and night; this is the model he leaves them.
St Gregory the Great (Pastoral Rule, in substance)
The shepherd must not keep silent out of fear or flattery. He must not hide the truth from those entrusted to him, but declare the whole counsel of God, with discretion and love.
magis: Catechism 2746–2747
When his hour came, Jesus prayed to the Father; his prayer at the Last Supper, the priestly prayer, embraces the whole economy of creation and salvation, his death and Resurrection.
Catechism 2750

The priestly prayer of Jesus fulfils, from within, the great petitions of the Lord's Prayer: concern for the Father's name, zeal for his kingdom, the accomplishment of his will, and deliverance from evil.
Catechism 1551
The ministerial priesthood is a service. It is entirely related to Christ and to the faithful; it depends on Christ and his unique priesthood.
Catechism 217
God is truthful when he reveals himself; his teaching is true instruction, and the Son came into the world “to testify to the truth.”
Spe Salvi 27 (Benedict XVI, 2007)
Whoever does not know God, even though he may entertain all kinds of hopes, is ultimately without hope; true life is relationship with him who is the source of life.
saints: St Ignatius of Laconi

A Capuchin lay brother of Sardinia (1701–1781) who for some forty years went begging alms for his friary through the streets of Cagliari. Known for his gentleness and his care for the poor and sick, he was canonized in 1951. The Capuchins keep his memory on 11 May.
A note on the calendar
From 1956 to 1969 the feast of Sts Philip and James was kept on 11 May; since the calendar reform of 1969 it has been celebrated on 3 May.
2027-05-11.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, when your hour came, you lifted up your eyes to heaven and prayed for your friends. Pray for us now, as you go to the Father. Teach us that eternal life is to know the only true God and you whom he has sent; let us know you, love you and be one with you. Give us the heart of Paul, who served you with humility and tears, held nothing back from your people, and ran his course to the end. Bless all pastors of your Church, that they may shepherd your flock faithfully and declare the whole purpose of God. Keep us in your name while we remain in the world, and send us your Holy Spirit, for whom we wait with Mary. You live and reign for ever and ever. Alleluia. Amen.

2027-05-12.title: Wednesday of the Seventh Week of Easter · Sts Nereus and Achilleus; St Pancras
readings: Keep watch over yourselves and over all the flock, of which the Holy Spirit has made you overseers
Sing to God, O kingdoms of the earth (or: Alleluia)
Sanctify them in the truth; your word is truth
2027-05-12.alt: Easter weekday of the seventh week (Year I), in the days between the Ascension and Pentecost. In India the Ascension was celebrated on Sunday 9 May. Until Pentecost one of the Prefaces of the Ascension or of Easter is said, the paschal candle burns beside the ambo, and the Regina Caeli (Queen of Heaven) replaces the Angelus. Many parishes pray the novena to the Holy Spirit in these days, as the apostles prayed with Mary in the upper room. Liturgical colour: white. Optional memorials: Sts Nereus and Achilleus, martyrs, and St Pancras, martyr (colour red if one of their Masses is said). Lectionary Psalm 68:29–30, 33–35a, 35bc–36ab = NRSV 68:28–29, 32–35.
2027-05-12.verse: Sanctify them in the truth; your word is truth.
theo: Paul is on his last journey to Jerusalem, and he knows what waits for him there: “imprisonment and persecutions.” He does not have time to go back to Ephesus, where he had worked for three years, so he sends for the elders of that church to meet him at the port of Miletus. Today we hear the second half of his farewell, the only speech in Acts that Paul gives to Christian leaders. It is a pastor's last will. “Keep watch over yourselves and over all the flock, of which the Holy Spirit has made you overseers, to shepherd the church of God that he obtained with the blood of his own Son.” The Church is not their property; it was bought at the price of Christ's blood, and the Holy Spirit placed them in charge. Paul is honest about the danger: “savage wolves will come in among you,” and some “even from your own group will come distorting the truth.” Then he commends them “to God and to the message of his grace,” and points to his own example: “I coveted no one's silver or gold or clothing,” he worked with his own hands, and he quotes a saying of the Lord found in no Gospel: “It is more blessed to give than to receive.” The scene ends on the shore with tears. “He knelt down with them all and prayed. There was much weeping among them all; they embraced Paul and kissed him,” grieving most because they would not see his face again. The Psalm lifts the sadness into praise: “Sing to God, O kingdoms of the earth.” The God who “gives power and strength to his people” will keep the flock when the shepherd has gone.

In the Gospel we hear the heart of the prayer Jesus offered at the Last Supper, a farewell even deeper than Paul's. He is going to the Father, and he prays for those he leaves behind: “Holy Father, protect them in your name that you have given me, so that they may be one, as we are one.” He does not ask for an escape: “I am not asking you to take them out of the world, but I ask you to protect them from the evil one.” Disciples are not meant to hide from the world, but neither are they meant to belong to it. And then the great petition: “Sanctify them in the truth; your word is truth.” To be sanctified is to be set apart for God, made holy, and sent: “As you have sent me into the world, so I have sent them into the world.” The martyrs remembered today were sent in this way. Nereus and Achilleus were soldiers in Rome. Pope St Damasus, in an inscription he wrote for their tomb in the catacomb of Domitilla, says (in substance) that they had served a cruel order, but suddenly believed, threw down their shields and weapons, and gladly bore witness to the triumph of Christ. St Pancras was a boy of about fourteen, put to death in Rome on the Via Aurelia, probably in the persecution of Diocletian around 304. Soldiers and a teenager: the prayer of Jesus, “protect them from the evil one,” was answered in them not by sparing their lives but by keeping their faith.
outline: Opening
Ask: if you had to say goodbye to the people you love most, what would your last words be?
Point 1 · Keep watch over the flock
A Church bought with the blood of Christ and entrusted by the Spirit.
Point 2 · More blessed to give
Paul's hands and the Lord's saying.
Point 3 · Sanctify them in the truth
In the world, not of it, and sent.
Take-home line
“Sanctify them in the truth; your word is truth.”
live: Pray for your shepherds (Acts 20:28)
Name your parish priest and your bishop in prayer today, and ask the Holy Spirit to keep them watchful and faithful.
Give before you receive (Acts 20:35)
Do one act of giving today that no one will repay: time, help, money or a kind word.
2027-05-12.prayer: Holy Father, your Son prayed for us on the night before he died: keep us in your name and make us one. Protect us from the evil one, and sanctify us in the truth, for your word is truth. Watch over the shepherds of your Church, whom the Holy Spirit has made overseers of the flock bought by the blood of Christ. By the prayers of Sts Nereus, Achilleus and Pancras, who laid down their weapons and their lives for Christ, give us courage to belong to you in the middle of the world. Come, Holy Spirit, as we wait with Mary for Pentecost. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.
altar: Paul reminds the elders that the Church was obtained “with the blood of his own Son.” At every Mass that price is placed before our eyes: the chalice of the Blood of Christ, poured out for the Church. The Eucharist is the food that keeps the flock one and holy in the truth.

2027-05-13.title: Thursday of the Seventh Week of Easter · Our Lady of Fatima
readings: Keep up your courage! You must bear witness also in Rome
Protect me, O God, for in you I take refuge (or: Alleluia)
That they may become completely one
2027-05-13.alt: Easter weekday of the seventh week (Year I), in the days between the Ascension and Pentecost. In India the Ascension was celebrated on Sunday 9 May. Until Pentecost one of the Prefaces of the Ascension or of Easter is said, the paschal candle burns beside the ambo, and the Regina Caeli (Queen of Heaven) replaces the Angelus. Many parishes pray the novena to the Holy Spirit in these days, as the apostles prayed with Mary in the upper room. Liturgical colour: white. Optional memorial of Our Lady of Fatima (white), added to the General Roman Calendar by St John Paul II in 2002; in India it is often kept with special devotion in parishes and shrines dedicated to her.
2027-05-13.verse: As you, Father, are in me and I am in you, may they also be in us, so that the world may believe that you have sent me.
theo: Paul has been arrested in the Temple in Jerusalem, and the Roman tribune, who “wanted to find out what Paul was being accused of,” brings him before the council. Paul looks at the assembly and sees two groups. The Sadducees, the priestly party, held that there is no resurrection, no angel, no spirit; the Pharisees believed in all three. So Paul cries out: “Brothers, I am a Pharisee, a son of Pharisees. I am on trial concerning the hope of the resurrection of the dead.” This is not a trick. It is the heart of his message: Jesus is risen, and in him the hope of Israel for the resurrection has begun to come true. The council divides, and some scribes of the Pharisees even say, “We find nothing wrong with this man.” Luke is careful: the quarrel is a debate within Israel about Israel's own hope, not a story of one people against another. The meeting ends in uproar, and the soldiers drag Paul to the barracks. Then, in the night, comes the real word of the day: “the Lord stood near him and said, ‘Keep up your courage! For just as you have testified for me in Jerusalem, so you must bear witness also in Rome.’” The Psalm puts that night into a prayer: “I keep the Lord always before me; because he is at my right hand, I shall not be moved.” And it ends with the hope Paul preached: “You show me the path of life. In your presence there is fullness of joy.”

In the Gospel Jesus lifts his eyes beyond the Upper Room, beyond the apostles, to us: “I ask not only on behalf of these, but also on behalf of those who will believe in me through their word, that they may all be one.” Every Christian who has ever believed through the preaching of the apostles was in that prayer. The unity he asks for is not a mere agreement; it is a share in the life of the Holy Trinity: “As you, Father, are in me and I am in you, may they also be in us.” And it has a purpose: “so that the world may believe that you have sent me.” Divided Christians make the Gospel hard to believe; Christians who love one another make it shine. Today the Church also remembers Our Lady of Fatima. On 13 May 1917, during the First World War, three shepherd children of Portugal, Lucia dos Santos and her cousins Francisco and Jacinta Marto, saw a Lady at the Cova da Iria who asked them to pray the Rosary every day for peace and to offer prayers and sacrifices for sinners. The Church approved the apparitions in 1930. On 13 May 1981 St John Paul II was shot in St Peter's Square; he believed (in substance) that a mother's hand had guided the bullet, and a year later he went to Fatima to give thanks. Francisco and Jacinta were canonised there by Pope Francis on 13 May 2017. Mary's message at Fatima is the Gospel's own: prayer, conversion, and the peace that comes when hearts are made one in her Son.
outline: Opening
Ask: when everything around you is in uproar, who stands near you in the night?
Point 1 · Keep up your courage
The Lord stands by Paul between Jerusalem and Rome.
Point 2 · The hope of the resurrection
The path of life and the fullness of joy.
Point 3 · That they may all be one
Jesus prays for us, and Mary at Fatima asks for prayer and peace.
Take-home line
“That they may all be one … so that the world may believe.”
live: Courage in the night (Acts 23:11)
Bring to the Lord tonight the situation that frightens you most, and listen for his word: Keep up your courage.
Pray for peace with Mary
Pray one decade of the Rosary today for peace in the world and for the unity of Christians, as Our Lady asked at Fatima.
2027-05-13.prayer: Lord Jesus, risen from the dead, you stood beside Paul in the night and said: Keep up your courage. Stand beside us in our fears and keep us steady, for you are at our right hand. You prayed to the Father for all who would believe through the apostles' word: make us one, as you and the Father are one, so that the world may believe. Through the prayers of Our Lady of Fatima, Mother of mercy, give us hearts converted, faithful in prayer and eager for peace. Come, Holy Spirit. Amen.
altar: Jesus prayed for unity on the night he gave us the Eucharist. St Paul would later write: “Because there is one bread, we who are many are one body.” Every Holy Communion is an answer to the prayer of John 17: the one Body of Christ makes us one body. At Fatima the children were also taught to adore the Lord in the Blessed Sacrament and to make reparation for the indifference he receives there.

2027-05-14.title: Saint Matthias, Apostle
readings: The lot fell on Matthias; and he was added to the eleven apostles
He raises the poor from the dust, to make them sit with the princes of his people (or: Alleluia)
You did not choose me but I chose you
2027-05-14.alt: Feast. The Gloria is said. The readings of Friday of the Seventh Week of Easter (Acts 25:13b–21; John 21:15–19) give way to those of the feast. St Matthias was kept on 24 February until the reform of the calendar in 1969, which moved him to 14 May, close to the days between the Ascension and Pentecost when he was chosen. Liturgical colour: red.
2027-05-14.verse: You did not choose me but I chose you. And I appointed you to go and bear fruit, fruit that will last,
theo: Of all the apostles, Matthias is the one we know least, and yet his feast falls at exactly the right moment. The Lord has ascended; the disciples have gone back to Jerusalem and are praying in the upper room “together with certain women, including Mary the mother of Jesus.” In those days of waiting, Peter stands up among about a hundred and twenty believers. There is a wound in the Twelve. Judas, who “was numbered among us and was allotted his share in this ministry,” has gone “to his own place.” Peter reads the tragedy in the light of the Psalms: “Let his homestead become desolate,” and “Let another take his position of overseer.” The number twelve is not a detail. Jesus chose twelve to stand for the twelve tribes of Israel, the whole People of God gathered anew, and he promised that they would sit on thrones judging those tribes (Luke 22:30). Before the Spirit comes and the Church goes out to the nations, the circle must be complete.

What kind of man must fill the empty place? Peter names the condition: “one of the men who have accompanied us during all the time that the Lord Jesus went in and out among us, beginning from the baptism of John until the day when he was taken up from us.” Above all, “one of these must become a witness with us to his resurrection.” An apostle is not chosen for his talents or his eloquence, but because he was with Jesus and has seen him risen. Two names are put forward: “Joseph called Barsabbas, who was also known as Justus, and Matthias.” Then the whole community prays: “Lord, you know everyone's heart. Show us which one of these two you have chosen.” They cast lots, an ancient way in Israel of leaving the decision to God (“The lot is cast into the lap, but the decision is the Lord's alone,” Proverbs 16:33), and “the lot fell on Matthias; and he was added to the eleven apostles.” It is the last time lots are used in the New Testament. After Pentecost the Church will discern by the Holy Spirit, by prayer and by the laying on of hands.

The Psalm sings what happened to Matthias: “He raises the poor from the dust, and lifts the needy from the ash heap, to make them sit with princes, with the princes of his people.” An unknown disciple, who had followed Jesus quietly from the Jordan to the Mount of Olives without ever being named, is suddenly placed among the foundations of the Church. The book of Revelation will say that the wall of the holy city “has twelve foundations, and on them are the twelve names of the twelve apostles of the Lamb.” Matthias's name is written there. Joseph Barsabbas was not chosen, and we hear no complaint from him; he too is part of the story, a reminder that God's choice is never a rejection of the one who serves elsewhere.

The Gospel tells us where every apostolic call begins: “You did not choose me but I chose you. And I appointed you to go and bear fruit, fruit that will last.” Matthias did not campaign for the place; the Lord, who knows every heart, chose him. And the choice is an act of friendship: “I do not call you servants any longer … but I have called you friends.” The heart of the apostle's work is the commandment of love: “love one another as I have loved you. No one has greater love than this, to lay down one's life for one's friends.” Of Matthias's later life we know almost nothing for certain. Eusebius records a tradition that he was one of the Seventy whom Jesus sent out (Luke 10:1). Ancient accounts send him to preach in Judea, in Cappadocia, or on the shores of the Black Sea, and say he died a martyr; the Abbey of St Matthias at Trier in Germany has honoured relics believed to be his since the Middle Ages.
