What is certain is enough: he was with Jesus, he saw him risen, he was chosen by the Lord, and he received the Holy Spirit with the others at Pentecost. His name means “gift of the Lord.”
conn: About a hundred and twenty.
In Jewish custom a community of a hundred and twenty men could have its own council. Luke may be hinting that the little group in the upper room is already the new Israel, ready to act.
Judas's end.

Acts 1:18–19 and Matthew 27:3–10 tell of Judas's death and of the field called Hakeldama, Field of Blood, in two different ways. The Lectionary omits these verses; Peter's point is not the gruesome detail but the empty place in the Twelve.
The Psalms quoted.
Psalm 69:25 (“Let his homestead become desolate”) and Psalm 109:8 (“Let another take his position of overseer”). The Greek word for that position, episkopē, later gives us the word bishop.
The Twelve.

Jesus chose twelve “to be with him, and to be sent out” (Mark 3:14). They stand for the twelve tribes of Israel. When James the brother of John was killed (Acts 12:2), no one was chosen to replace him: the circle of witnesses had been completed, and the Church was now founded.
Casting lots.
Israel used lots to divide the land (Joshua 18:6), to choose the priests' duties (1 Chronicles 24:5; Luke 1:9) and to discern God's will. The stones were shaken in a vessel until one fell out.
Barsabbas called Justus.
“Son of the Sabbath,” perhaps because he was born on a Sabbath; Justus was his Latin name. A Judas called Barsabbas, perhaps his brother, appears later as a leader in Jerusalem (Acts 15:22).
Matthias.
A short form of Mattathias, Hebrew Mattithiah, “gift of the Lord.” He is never mentioned again in the New Testament after Acts 1:26.
Friends, not servants.

In the ancient world the “friends of the king” were his trusted counsellors, who knew his plans. Abraham was called the friend of God (Isaiah 41:8; James 2:23). Jesus gives that title to all his disciples.
The date.
The older Roman calendar kept St Matthias on 24 February (25 in a leap year). The Eastern Churches honour him on 9 August. The reform of 1969 moved the Roman feast to 14 May.
altar: The apostles chose Matthias while they were waiting for the Spirit in prayer, and he was immediately counted among those who “devoted themselves to the apostles' teaching and fellowship, to the breaking of bread and the prayers.” The Eucharist we celebrate today rests on that apostolic foundation; in the Eucharistic Prayer the Church names the apostles, and in the Roman Canon Matthias is named among the martyrs after the consecration.

“No one has greater love than this, to lay down one's life for one's friends.” At the altar Jesus does not only tell us this; he gives his own Body and Blood for his friends, and makes us capable of loving as he loved.
outline: Opening
Show a team photograph with one empty place. Ask: what does it take to fill that place?
Point 1 · One must become a witness
The Twelve made whole before Pentecost.
Point 2 · Lord, you know everyone's heart
Prayer and the lot: leaving the choice to God.
Point 3 · You did not choose me
The call as a gift of friendship.
Point 4 · From the dust to the princes
An unknown disciple among the foundations.
Closing image
Twelve names carved on the foundation stones of the holy city, one of them Matthias.
Take-home line
“You did not choose me but I chose you.”
live: Be a witness
Tell one person this week, simply and in your own words, why you believe that Jesus is risen.
Pray before you decide
Before an important decision this week, pray as the apostles did: Lord, you know everyone's heart; show me what you have chosen.
Serve without being seen
Like Matthias, who followed Jesus for years without being named, do one service in your parish that no one will notice.
Pray for vocations
Pray today for those whom the Lord is choosing as priests and religious, especially in your own parish and family.
fathers: St John Chrysostom (in substance)

See how Peter does everything with the common consent: nothing by his own authority alone, nothing by command. He was the first of the apostles, yet he made the whole community share in the choice. And they prayed first, because they wanted God to make the choice, not themselves.
St Augustine (in substance)
You did not choose me: here is grace beyond words. What were we before Christ chose us, if not wicked? He did not choose us because we were good; he chose us so that we might become good.
St Clement of Alexandria (in substance)
Matthias taught, so it was handed down, that we must fight against the flesh and not give in to it, and must make the soul grow through faith and knowledge.
St Augustine (in substance)
A lot is not something evil: in a matter where human beings are uncertain, it points to the will of God.
magis: Catechism 765
The Lord gave his community a structure: the Twelve with Peter as their head, representing the twelve tribes of Israel.
Catechism 857–860
The Church is apostolic: built on the foundation of the apostles, guarding their teaching, and guided by their successors.
Catechism 861–862
The apostles took care to appoint successors; the bishops have by divine institution taken the place of the apostles as shepherds of the Church.
Lumen Gentium 19–20
Vatican II: Christ established the apostles as a college; the mission entrusted to them will last until the end of the world.
Catechism 1823
Jesus makes charity the new commandment: “As the Father has loved me, so have I loved you; abide in my love.”
saints: St Matthias, Apostle

A disciple who followed Jesus from his baptism to the Ascension, chosen by lot to take the place of Judas among the Twelve (Acts 1:26). Traditions place his preaching in Judea and further afield and say he died a martyr; relics believed to be his are venerated at Trier and in Rome. Patron of Trier.
This week

15 May: Saturday of the Seventh Week of Easter, the last weekday of Easter; the Vigil of Pentecost in the evening. 16 May: PENTECOST SUNDAY. 17 May: The Blessed Virgin Mary, Mother of the Church (memorial); Ordinary Time resumes. 18 May: St John I (optional). 20 May: St Bernardine of Siena (optional). 21 May: St Christopher Magallanes and companions (optional). 22 May: St Rita of Cascia (optional).
2027-05-14.prayer: O God, who assigned Saint Matthias a place in the college of Apostles, grant us, through his intercession, that, rejoicing at your love for us, we may merit to be numbered among the elect. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, who lives and reigns with you in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, for ever and ever. Amen. Let us also pray: Lord Jesus, you did not wait for us to choose you; you chose us and called us your friends. As you chose Matthias to be a witness of your resurrection, make us witnesses in our homes and workplaces. Teach us to pray before we decide, to serve without seeking a name, and to love one another as you have loved us. With Mary and the apostles we wait for your Spirit: come, Holy Spirit, and fill the empty places in our hearts and in your Church. Amen.

2027-05-15.title: Saturday of the Seventh Week of Easter
readings: He lived there two whole years and welcomed all who came to him, proclaiming the kingdom of God
The upright shall behold his face (or: Alleluia)
This is the disciple who is testifying to these things and has written them, and his testimony is true
2027-05-15.alt: Easter weekday of the seventh week (Year I), in the days between the Ascension and Pentecost. In India the Ascension was celebrated on Sunday 9 May. Until Pentecost one of the Prefaces of the Ascension or of Easter is said, the paschal candle burns beside the ambo, and the Regina Caeli (Queen of Heaven) replaces the Angelus. Many parishes pray the novena to the Holy Spirit in these days, as the apostles prayed with Mary in the upper room. Liturgical colour: white. This is the last weekday of the Easter season. In the evening the Vigil Mass of Pentecost is celebrated, in its simple form or as an extended vigil with several readings (Genesis 11:1–9; Exodus 19; Ezekiel 37:1–14; Joel 2:28–32, numbered 3:1–5 in some Bibles; Romans 8:22–27; John 7:37–39). Today both the Acts of the Apostles and the Gospel of John, read through the fifty days, come to their last page.
2027-05-15.verse: Jesus said to him, “If it is my will that he remain until I come, what is that to you? Follow me!”
theo: For fifty days the Church has read the Acts of the Apostles, from the Ascension at Jerusalem to the shipwreck at Malta. Today we reach the last page, and it ends in Rome. Paul has arrived as a prisoner, but a strange kind of prisoner: “Paul was allowed to live by himself, with the soldier who was guarding him.” Three days later he calls together the leaders of the Jewish community of Rome. He speaks to them as “brothers,” and he insists that he has “done nothing against our people or the customs of our ancestors,” and that he has “no charge to bring against my nation.” Then he says why he wears a chain: “it is for the sake of the hope of Israel that I am bound with this chain.” Paul never stopped being a son of Israel; the risen Messiah is, for him, the fulfilment of Israel's own hope, not its rejection. And the book ends with a picture rather than a conclusion: “He lived there two whole years at his own expense and welcomed all who came to him, proclaiming the kingdom of God and teaching about the Lord Jesus Christ with all boldness and without hindrance.” Luke does not tell us how Paul's trial ended, or how he died. The last word of Acts in Greek is akōlytōs, “without hindrance.” The apostle is in chains, but the word of God is not. The story of the Church is left open, for us to continue. The Psalm gives the reason for that boldness: “The Lord is in his holy temple; the Lord's throne is in heaven,” and “the upright shall behold his face.”

The Gospel of John ends in the same open way. On the shore of the lake the risen Jesus has just asked Peter three times, “Do you love me?” and told him how he would one day glorify God by his death. Peter turns, sees the beloved disciple following them, and asks a very human question: “Lord, what about him?” Jesus answers gently but firmly: “If it is my will that he remain until I come, what is that to you? Follow me!” Each disciple has his own road. Peter will die a martyr; John, tradition tells us, will live long and die in peace. Comparison is a waste of time; what matters is following. Then the evangelist steps forward: “This is the disciple who is testifying to these things and has written them, and we know that his testimony is true.” The Gospel rests on the witness of one who reclined next to Jesus at the supper and stood at the foot of the cross with Mary. And it ends with a smile: “if every one of them were written down, I suppose that the world itself could not contain the books that would be written.” Tonight, at the Vigil of Pentecost, the Church will hear Jesus cry out: “Let anyone who is thirsty come to me.” The last weekday of Easter ends where the novena began, in the upper room, waiting with Mary for the gift that will write the rest of the story in us.
outline: Opening
Ask: how would you feel if your favourite book ended in the middle of a sentence?
Point 1 · For the hope of Israel
Paul in chains in Rome, still a son of his people.
Point 2 · Without hindrance
The open ending of Acts and the word that cannot be chained.
Point 3 · What is that to you? Follow me!
Each disciple's own road, and the true witness of John.
Take-home line
“Follow me!”
live: Stop comparing (John 21:22)
When you catch yourself comparing your life with someone else's today, say quietly: what is that to me? Lord, I will follow you.
Prepare for Pentecost
Tonight or tomorrow morning, spend ten minutes in silence and ask the Holy Spirit for the one gift you need most. If you can, join the Vigil of Pentecost in your parish.
2027-05-15.prayer: Lord Jesus, you told Peter: What is that to you? Follow me! Deliver us from comparing ourselves with others, and give us the grace to follow you on the road you have chosen for each of us. Like Paul in Rome, let us proclaim your kingdom with boldness, even when we are bound; like the beloved disciple, let us bear true witness to what we have seen of your love. As Easter draws to its close, we wait with Mary and the apostles: send us your Holy Spirit, the Advocate, the giver of life. Come, Holy Spirit. Amen.
altar: Paul in Rome “welcomed all who came to him.” The risen Lord does the same at every altar: whoever comes to him in faith he will never drive away. Tonight's Vigil and tomorrow's Mass of Pentecost will celebrate the Spirit who, at every Eucharist, is called down upon the gifts so that they become the Body and Blood of Christ, and upon us so that we become one body in him.

2027-05-17.title: The Blessed Virgin Mary, Mother of the Church
readings: I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your offspring and hers (or: Acts 1:12–14, All these were constantly devoting themselves to prayer, together with Mary the mother of Jesus)
Glorious things are spoken of you, O city of God
Woman, here is your son. Here is your mother
2027-05-17.alt: Memorial, kept on the Monday after Pentecost since Pope Francis inscribed it in the General Roman Calendar (decree of the Congregation for Divine Worship, 11 February 2018). The readings of the memorial are proper and are used today in place of those of Monday of the Seventh Week in Ordinary Time (Sirach 1:1–10; Mark 9:14–29). In the first reading, Acts 1:12–14 may be read instead of Genesis. With the Easter season ended, Ordinary Time resumes today with the Seventh Week (Year I), and the Angelus replaces the Regina Caeli. Liturgical colour: white (from tomorrow, green).
2027-05-17.verse: When Jesus saw his mother and the disciple whom he loved standing beside her, he said to his mother, “Woman, here is your son.” Then he said to the disciple, “Here is your mother.”
theo: The day after Pentecost the Church turns to the one who was in the upper room when the Spirit came, and calls her by a name that sums up her place in God's plan: Mother of the Church. The first reading takes us back to the beginning, to the garden after the first sin. The Lord God calls: “Where are you?” Adam hides, afraid; he blames the woman, and the woman blames the serpent. Then God speaks to the serpent the first promise of salvation in the Bible, which the Fathers called the Protoevangelium, the first Gospel: “I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your offspring and hers; he will strike your head, and you will strike his heel.” A woman and her offspring will stand against the power of evil, and the offspring will crush its head. The reading ends with a name: “The man named his wife Eve, because she was the mother of all living.” Christian tradition has seen in Mary the New Eve. St Irenaeus wrote (in substance) that the knot of Eve's disobedience was untied by Mary's obedience; what the virgin Eve bound by unbelief, the Virgin Mary loosed by faith. Eve became the mother of all the living in the order of nature; Mary, by her faith and her share in her Son's work, becomes the mother of all who live in grace. If Acts 1:12–14 is read instead, we see the apostles after the Ascension “constantly devoting themselves to prayer, together with certain women, including Mary the mother of Jesus”: the Church at prayer, with the Mother in its midst. The Psalm sings of Zion, the mother city where every people is born: “Glorious things are spoken of you, O city of God,” and “All my springs are in you.”

The Gospel brings us to Calvary. “Standing near the cross of Jesus were his mother, and his mother's sister, Mary the wife of Clopas, and Mary Magdalene.” In the hour of his death Jesus looks at his mother and at the disciple whom he loved: “Woman, here is your son.” Then to the disciple: “Here is your mother.” “And from that hour the disciple took her into his own home.” He calls her “Woman,” as he did at Cana, the name that recalls the woman of Genesis. The beloved disciple is not named, so that every disciple can stand in his place. Jesus does not only provide for his widowed mother; from the cross he gives her as mother to all whom he loves, and gives them to her as children. Then, “knowing that all was now finished,” he says “I am thirsty,” and “It is finished,” and “gave up his spirit.” Finally a soldier pierces his side, “and at once blood and water came out.” The Fathers saw in that blood and water the sacraments of the Eucharist and Baptism, and the Church herself born from the side of Christ, as Eve was formed from the side of Adam. At the foot of the cross, Mary stands at the birth of the Church; in the upper room she prays at its Pentecost. St Paul VI solemnly declared her Mother of the Church on 21 November 1964, at the Second Vatican Council, on the day the Council approved its teaching on the Church, Lumen Gentium, whose last chapter is about her. St Augustine had written (in substance): Mary is the mother of the members of Christ, because by her love she cooperated so that the faithful might be born in the Church.
outline: Opening
Ask: who taught you your first prayer? For most of us it was a mother. Today the whole Church thanks God for her Mother.
Point 1 · The woman and her offspring
The first promise in Eden; Mary, the New Eve.
Point 2 · Here is your mother
Jesus' gift from the cross to every beloved disciple.
Point 3 · With Mary in prayer
The Church born from the pierced side, gathered with Mary in the upper room.
Take-home line
“Here is your mother.”
live: Take her into your home (John 19:27)
Give Mary a place in your home today: pray the Angelus at noon, the first time since Easter, or light a candle before her picture and pray one decade of the Rosary as a family.
Be a child of the Church
Do one thing today for your parish, your mother in faith: help a priest or sister, visit a sick parishioner, or simply thank someone who serves.
2027-05-17.prayer: O God, Father of mercies, whose Only Begotten Son, as he hung upon the Cross, chose the Blessed Virgin Mary, his Mother, to be our Mother also, grant, we pray, that with her loving help your Church may be more fruitful day by day and, exulting in the holiness of her children, may draw to her embrace all the families of the peoples. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, who lives and reigns with you in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, for ever and ever. Amen. Let us also pray: Lord Jesus, from the cross you gave us your Mother; like the beloved disciple, we take her into our homes. Holy Mary, Mother of the Church, who prayed with the apostles for the Holy Spirit, pray for us now as we begin again the ordinary days of the year, that we may do whatever your Son tells us. Amen.
altar: From the pierced side of Christ came blood and water, and the Church has always seen there the sacraments that build her up: Baptism and the Eucharist. Mary stood by the cross when that blood was shed; at every Mass the same sacrifice is made present on the altar, and the Church, with Mary, stands beside it. In the Eucharistic Prayer we name her first among the saints: “the glorious ever-Virgin Mary, Mother of our God and Lord, Jesus Christ.”

2027-05-18.title: Tuesday of the Seventh Week in Ordinary Time · St John I
readings: My child, when you come to serve the Lord, prepare yourself for testing
Commit your life to the Lord, and he will help you
Whoever wants to be first must be last of all and servant of all
2027-05-18.alt: Weekday of Ordinary Time, Week 7 (Year I). Ordinary Time resumed on the Monday after Pentecost; the Angelus has again taken the place of the Regina Caeli, and the Paschal candle now stands by the baptismal font. Liturgical colour: green. Optional memorial: St John I, pope and martyr (colour red if his Mass is said). Two days after Pentecost the weekday readings return to the Book of Sirach and to the Gospel of Mark, where they paused before Lent.
2027-05-18.verse: He sat down, called the twelve, and said to them, “Whoever wants to be first must be last of all and servant of all.”
theo: After the great feasts of Easter and Pentecost, the Church takes us back to the school of daily life, and the teacher she chooses is Jesus ben Sira, a wise man of Jerusalem who wrote about two hundred years before Christ. His first lesson for anyone who wants to belong to God is honest and a little startling: “My child, when you come to serve the Lord, prepare yourself for testing.” Faith is not an insurance policy against trouble. Ben Sira does not promise an easy road; he promises a faithful God. “Set your heart right and be steadfast, and do not be impetuous in time of calamity. Cling to him and do not depart.” Then comes the image that has comforted believers for centuries: “For gold is tested in the fire, and those found acceptable, in the furnace of humiliation.” The goldsmith does not put gold in the fire to destroy it but to make it pure. Three times the reading repeats “You who fear the Lord”: wait for his mercy, trust in him, hope for good things. And it ends with a challenge to look at history: “Consider the generations of old and see: has anyone trusted in the Lord and been disappointed?” The answer the whole Bible gives is no, “for the Lord is compassionate and merciful; he forgives sins and saves in time of distress.” The Psalm adds its counsel: “Trust in the Lord, and do good.”

In the Gospel Jesus is walking through Galilee, quietly, “for he was teaching his disciples.” For the second time he tells them plainly what lies ahead: “The Son of Man is to be betrayed into human hands, and they will kill him, and three days after being killed, he will rise again.” This is the testing Ben Sira spoke of, and Jesus walks into it first. “But they did not understand what he was saying and were afraid to ask him.” While their Master speaks of the cross, the disciples are busy with another question. At Capernaum he asks them, “What were you arguing about on the way?” Nobody answers, “for on the way they had argued with one another who was the greatest.” Jesus does not scold them. He sits down, as a teacher does, and gives them a new measure of greatness: “Whoever wants to be first must be last of all and servant of all.” Then he takes a little child, in that world a person with no rank or rights, puts the child in the middle of them, and holds the child in his arms: “Whoever welcomes one such child in my name welcomes me.” Today the Church remembers St John I, an elderly pope who in 526 died in a prison at Ravenna after being sent on a difficult mission by a suspicious king. He did not seek the first place; he accepted the furnace, and was found to be gold.
outline: Opening
Ask: when trouble comes, do I take it as a sign that God has left me?
Point 1 · Prepare yourself for testing
Gold is purified in the fire; God is faithful in the furnace.
Point 2 · Who was the greatest?
The disciples argue about rank while Jesus speaks of the cross.
Point 3 · A child in his arms
To welcome the least is to welcome Christ and the Father.
Take-home line
“Whoever wants to be first must be last of all and servant of all.”
live: Hold on in the fire (Sirach 2:3)
Name one trial you are carrying now and pray each morning this week: Lord, I cling to you; do not let me depart from you.
Serve the one with no rank (Mark 9:35–37)
Do one hidden service today for someone who cannot repay you: a child, a domestic worker, an elderly neighbour.
2027-05-18.prayer: Lord our God, compassionate and merciful, you test your servants as gold is tested in the fire, and you never forsake those who trust in you. Keep our hearts steadfast in every trial. Lord Jesus, you walked to your cross as the servant of all; cure us of the desire to be the greatest, and teach us to welcome the little ones in your name. Through the prayers of St John I, who suffered in prison for the Church, make us faithful to the end. Amen.
altar: At every Mass the Son of Man who was “betrayed into human hands” gives himself into our hands. The One who said “servant of all” is present on the altar as the Lamb offered for all, and he comes to the smallest and least worthy of us in Holy Communion, as he once took a child into his arms.

2027-05-19.title: Wednesday of the Seventh Week in Ordinary Time
readings: O Lord, great peace have they who love your law
Whoever is not against us is for us
2027-05-19.alt: Weekday of Ordinary Time, Week 7 (Year I). Ordinary Time resumed on the Monday after Pentecost; the Angelus has again taken the place of the Regina Caeli, and the Paschal candle now stands by the baptismal font. Liturgical colour: green. No memorial is assigned to this day in the General Roman Calendar; a Mass of the Holy Spirit, still close to Pentecost, or a votive Mass may be chosen.
2027-05-19.verse: But Jesus said, “Do not stop him; for no one who does a deed of power in my name will be able soon afterward to speak evil of me. Whoever is not against us is for us.”
theo: Ben Sira speaks of Wisdom as a mother and a teacher: “Wisdom teaches her children and gives help to those who seek her. Whoever loves her loves life, and those who seek her from early morning are filled with joy.” Wisdom here is far more than cleverness. She is the way God's own mind shapes a human life, and to serve her is to serve God: “Those who serve her minister to the Holy One; the Lord loves those who love her.” Then the reading becomes very honest about how Wisdom educates. She does not hand out her secrets on the first day. “For at first she will walk with them on tortuous paths; she will bring fear and dread upon them, and will torment them by her discipline until she trusts them.” Every good teacher, every good parent, knows this. Trust is built through testing, and only then “she will come straight back to them again and gladden them, and will reveal her secrets to them.” The Christian reads this page with new eyes, for St Paul calls Christ crucified “the power of God and the wisdom of God.” The Wisdom that walks with us on crooked paths has a face and a name. The Psalm sings the fruit of that long schooling: “Great peace have those who love your law; nothing can make them stumble.”

The Gospel is short and sharp. John, the son of Zebedee, the one whom Jesus called a “son of thunder,” brings a report that he expects will please his Master: “Teacher, we saw someone casting out demons in your name, and we tried to stop him, because he was not following us.” Notice the words: not following “us.” John is guarding the borders of the group. Jesus answers with surprising openness: “Do not stop him; for no one who does a deed of power in my name will be able soon afterward to speak evil of me. Whoever is not against us is for us.” The same thing had happened to Moses in the desert, when Eldad and Medad prophesied outside the tent of meeting and Joshua wanted them silenced; Moses answered, “Would that all the Lord's people were prophets.” Jesus does not deny that there is one Church, built on the apostles, and at once he warns against causing the little ones to stumble. But he refuses a jealous spirit that cannot rejoice when good is done in his name by others. The Second Vatican Council teaches that many elements of sanctification and truth are found outside the visible structure of the Catholic Church, gifts that belong to the Church of Christ and impel towards unity (Lumen Gentium 8). Wisdom, after all, teaches her children to recognise her work wherever it appears.
outline: Opening
Ask: when someone outside my group does good, am I glad or a little jealous?
Point 1 · Wisdom teaches her children
To love Wisdom is to love life; Christ is the Wisdom of God.
Point 2 · Tortuous paths
Wisdom tests before she trusts, then gladdens and reveals.
Point 3 · Not following us
Jesus refuses a jealous spirit: whoever is not against us is for us.
Take-home line
“Whoever is not against us is for us.”
live: Seek her early (Sirach 4:12)
Give the first ten minutes of tomorrow morning to the word of God, before the phone and the news.
Rejoice in others' good (Mark 9:39)
Name one good work done by another parish, Church or group, and thank God for it aloud today.
2027-05-19.prayer: God of wisdom, you teach your children by paths we do not always understand, and you gladden those who persevere. Make us lovers of your wisdom, which is Christ your Son. Heal our hearts of the jealousy that wants to keep goodness for ourselves; teach us to rejoice wherever your name is honoured and your works are done, and lead all who believe in Christ into the unity he prayed for. Amen.
altar: In the Eucharist the Wisdom of God becomes food: Christ, “the power of God and the wisdom of God,” gives himself to us under the signs of bread and wine. The one table of the altar is also our deepest prayer for the unity of all who bear his name.

2027-05-20.title: Thursday of the Seventh Week in Ordinary Time · St Bernardine of Siena
readings: Do not delay to turn back to the Lord
Blessed are they who hope in the Lord
It is better for you to enter life maimed than to have two hands and to go to hell
2027-05-20.alt: Weekday of Ordinary Time, Week 7 (Year I). Ordinary Time resumed on the Monday after Pentecost; the Angelus has again taken the place of the Regina Caeli, and the Paschal candle now stands by the baptismal font. Liturgical colour: green. Optional memorial: St Bernardine of Siena, priest (white). In some countries the bishops have adopted, on this Thursday after Pentecost, the feast of Our Lord Jesus Christ, the Eternal High Priest; it is not assumed here for India.
2027-05-20.verse: Do not delay to turn back to the Lord, and do not postpone it from day to day.
theo: Ben Sira today writes a list of things we must never say. “Do not rely on your wealth, or say, ‘I have enough.’” “Do not say, ‘Who can have power over me?’” “Do not say, ‘I sinned, yet what has happened to me?’ for the Lord is slow to anger.” Each sentence names a false security. Money that makes us think we need nobody, strength that makes us think we answer to nobody, and, most subtle of all, a kind of presumption on God's patience: nothing happened when I sinned, so it cannot matter. Ben Sira goes further: “Do not be so confident of forgiveness that you add sin to sin. Do not say, ‘His mercy is great, he will forgive the multitude of my sins.’” God's mercy is real and vast, but it is the mercy of a holy God, never permission to keep sinning. And so the urgent counsel: “Do not delay to turn back to the Lord, and do not postpone it from day to day.” The sinner always means to repent tomorrow. Ben Sira asks: why not today? The Psalm paints the two ways: the one who delights in the law of the Lord is “like trees planted by streams of water,” while the wicked are “like chaff that the wind drives away.”

The Gospel continues the teaching Jesus gave at Capernaum. It opens with a promise so small it is easy to miss: “whoever gives you a cup of water to drink because you bear the name of Christ will by no means lose the reward.” No kindness done for Christ is ever wasted. Then the tone becomes severe. To cause one of “these little ones who believe” to stumble is so grave that a millstone around the neck would be better. Jesus speaks of cutting off a hand or a foot, tearing out an eye, rather than being thrown into “hell, where their worm never dies, and the fire is never quenched.” The Church has never taken this as a command to injure the body; it is the vivid language of a teacher who wants us to see that nothing, not even what is dearest to us, is worth losing eternal life for. Whatever leads us into sin, a habit, a phone, a friendship, a place, must be cut away decisively. And he ends with salt: “Have salt in yourselves, and be at peace with one another.” Today the Church remembers St Bernardine of Siena (1380–1444), the Franciscan who preached across Italy with this same urgency, calling crowds to conversion and teaching them to love the Holy Name of Jesus. He did not let people postpone; he told them that today is the day.
outline: Opening
Ask: what am I planning to change “tomorrow”?
Point 1 · Do not say “I have enough”
False securities: wealth, strength, presumption on mercy.
Point 2 · Do not delay
Conversion belongs to today, not tomorrow.
Point 3 · A cup of water and the salt of peace
Cut away what makes us stumble; no kindness for Christ is lost.
Take-home line
“Do not delay to turn back to the Lord.”
live: Turn today (Sirach 5:7)
Name one sin or habit you keep postponing, and take one concrete step against it before tonight; if needed, plan your confession for this week.
Give a cup of water (Mark 9:41)
Offer a drink, a meal or a kind word today to someone who serves the Church or the poor.
2027-05-20.prayer: Holy and merciful God, you are slow to anger and rich in mercy; do not let us presume on your patience. Give us the grace to turn back to you today, without delay, and to cut away whatever leads us into sin. Through the prayers of St Bernardine, who preached the Holy Name of Jesus with burning love, write that name on our hearts, so that we may have salt in ourselves and be at peace with one another. Amen.
altar: The mercy Ben Sira warns us not to presume upon is offered to us in its fullness at the altar, where Christ's Body is given and his Blood is poured out “for the forgiveness of sins.” To receive him worthily is to turn back to the Lord today; and every Communion sends us out with salt, to be peacemakers.

2027-05-21.title: Friday of the Seventh Week in Ordinary Time · St Christopher Magallanes and Companions
readings: Faithful friends are a sturdy shelter: whoever finds one has found a treasure
Guide me, Lord, in the way of your commands
What God has joined together, let no one separate
2027-05-21.alt: Weekday of Ordinary Time, Week 7 (Year I). Ordinary Time resumed on the Monday after Pentecost; the Angelus has again taken the place of the Regina Caeli, and the Paschal candle now stands by the baptismal font. Liturgical colour: green. Optional memorial: St Christopher Magallanes, priest, and companions, martyrs (red). Today is the centenary of his arrest (21 May 1927); he was shot four days later, on 25 May 1927.
2027-05-21.verse: So they are no longer two, but one flesh. Therefore what God has joined together, let no one separate.
theo: Ben Sira writes one of the finest pages on friendship in all literature. He begins with the pleasant side: “Pleasant speech multiplies friends, and a gracious tongue multiplies courtesies.” Be kind, and many will be kind to you. But then he becomes a careful realist. “Let those who are friendly with you be many, but let your advisers be one in a thousand. When you gain friends, gain them through testing, and do not trust them hastily.” He describes the fair-weather friend with a sharp pen: there are friends “who sit at your table, but they will not stand by you in time of trouble,” and when you are brought low, “they turn against you, and hide themselves from you.” And then comes the praise of the true friend: “Faithful friends are a sturdy shelter: whoever finds one has found a treasure. Faithful friends are beyond price; no amount can balance their worth. Faithful friends are life-saving medicine; and those who fear the Lord will find them.” The secret of good friendship, he says, is the fear of the Lord: “as they are, so are their neighbors also.” Those who belong to God become faithful, and they attract faithful friends. On the night before he died Jesus would say to his disciples: “I have called you friends.” He is the friend who stays in the time of trouble.

In the Gospel the Pharisees test Jesus: “Is it lawful for a man to divorce his wife?” In his time there was a lively debate among Jewish teachers about the grounds for divorce, some strict and some very lenient; but in practice it was the husband who could send his wife away. Jesus goes behind the debate to the beginning: “from the beginning of creation, ‘God made them male and female.’ ‘For this reason a man shall leave his father and mother and be joined to his wife, and the two shall become one flesh.’ So they are no longer two, but one flesh. Therefore what God has joined together, let no one separate.” The permission of Moses was given “because of your hardness of heart”; the plan of God is a covenant of faithful love that lasts for life. Then, in the house, Jesus says plainly that remarriage after divorce is adultery, for wife and husband alike, which in that world was itself a defence of women. The Church holds this teaching faithfully (CCC 1614–1615, 1640), and with the same faithfulness she accompanies with tenderness those whose marriages have broken, never treating them as outsiders (Amoris Laetitia 243). Marriage, like friendship, is God's work, and both are made strong by the fear of the Lord. Today we honour St Christopher Magallanes, a parish priest of Jalisco in Mexico, arrested exactly a hundred years ago today, on his way to celebrate Mass, and shot without trial with Fr Agustín Caloca on 25 May 1927. He had opposed armed revolt and preached peace; before he died he forgave his executioners. He was a faithful friend of Christ to the end.
outline: Opening
Ask: who stood by me in my worst time, and whom have I stood by?
Point 1 · Faithful friends are a treasure
Tested friendship, rooted in the fear of the Lord.
Point 2 · From the beginning
Marriage as God made it: two become one flesh.
Point 3 · Hardness of heart and a new heart
Christ gives the grace to love faithfully; the martyrs show the cost.
Take-home line
“What God has joined together, let no one separate.”
live: Be a sturdy shelter (Sirach 6:14)
Call or visit a friend who is going through a hard time and simply stay with them.
Pray for marriages (Mark 10:9)
Pray today by name for one married couple you know, especially one that is struggling, and for one person whose marriage has broken.
2027-05-21.prayer: Lord Jesus, faithful friend, you call us friends and never desert us in the time of trouble. Give us faithful friends and make us faithful friends to others. Bless the marriages of our families; renew in husbands and wives the love that you joined together from the beginning, and console with your tenderness all whose marriages have been wounded. Through the prayers of St Christopher Magallanes and his companions, who loved you even unto death, give us hearts of flesh and steadfast love. Amen.
altar: In the Eucharist Christ gives himself as the Bridegroom to his Bride, the Church: “This is my body, which is given for you.” Every Christian marriage draws its strength from this faithful, self-giving love, and every martyr, like St Christopher Magallanes, who was arrested on his way to offer Mass, shows that to love Christ is to be ready to give one's life with him.

2027-05-22.title: Saturday of the Seventh Week in Ordinary Time · St Rita of Cascia
readings: The Lord created human beings out of earth, and made them in his own image
The Lord's kindness is everlasting to those who fear him
Whoever does not receive the kingdom of God as a little child will never enter it
2027-05-22.alt: Weekday of Ordinary Time, Week 7 (Year I). Ordinary Time resumed on the Monday after Pentecost; the Angelus has again taken the place of the Regina Caeli, and the Paschal candle now stands by the baptismal font. Liturgical colour: green. Optional memorial: St Rita of Cascia, religious (white). Where St Rita is not kept, the memorial of the Blessed Virgin Mary on Saturday may be celebrated. Tomorrow is the Solemnity of the Most Holy Trinity.
2027-05-22.verse: Let the little children come to me; do not stop them; for it is to such as these that the kingdom of God belongs.
theo: Ben Sira today meditates on the first pages of Genesis, and he holds together two truths about us that are easy to separate. The first is humility: “The Lord created human beings out of earth, and makes them return to it again. He gave them a fixed number of days.” We are dust, and our days are counted. The second is dignity: he “granted them authority over everything on the earth. He endowed them with strength like his own, and made them in his own image.” God gave us “discretion and tongue and eyes, ears and a mind for thinking,” filled us “with knowledge and understanding,” and “showed them good and evil.” Why? So that we might see his works and praise him: “they will praise his holy name, to proclaim the grandeur of his works.” Then Ben Sira moves from creation to covenant: “He established with them an eternal covenant, and revealed to them his decrees. Their eyes saw his glorious majesty,” a memory of Sinai, and he gave each one “commandment … concerning the neighbor.” To be made in God's image is to be made for praise and for love of neighbour. The Psalm adds the tenderness that makes this bearable: “As a father has compassion for his children, so the Lord has compassion for those who fear him. For he knows how we were made; he remembers that we are dust.”

The Gospel shows us that compassion in action. “People were bringing little children to him in order that he might touch them; and the disciples spoke sternly to them.” Perhaps they thought the Master had more important work than blessing babies. Mark uses a strong word for Jesus' reaction: “he was indignant.” Only here in the Gospels is Jesus said to be indignant with his own disciples. “Let the little children come to me; do not stop them; for it is to such as these that the kingdom of God belongs. Truly I tell you, whoever does not receive the kingdom of God as a little child will never enter it.” A child does not earn a gift; a child receives it with open hands. That is how the Kingdom is entered: not by achievement but by trust. “And he took them up in his arms, laid his hands on them, and blessed them.” The Church has always seen in this scene a reason to bring even infants to Baptism (CCC 1250–1252). Today we may honour St Rita of Cascia (1381–1457), wife, mother, widow and Augustinian nun, whom many in Kerala and across India call upon in desperate situations. She lived through a hard marriage, the murder of her husband and the death of her two sons, and she answered violence with forgiveness and prayer. Like a child, she kept receiving everything from God's hands, even when those hands seemed to hold only thorns.
outline: Opening
Ask: do I come to God as a child who receives, or as a worker who wants to be paid?
Point 1 · Dust and image
Made from earth, made in God's image, made for praise.
Point 2 · He remembers that we are dust
The Father's compassion for his fragile children.
Point 3 · Let the children come
Receive the Kingdom with open hands; St Rita's trust in sorrow.
Take-home line
“Whoever does not receive the kingdom of God as a little child will never enter it.”
live: Praise with your senses (Sirach 17:6–10)
Take five minutes today simply to look at something beautiful in creation and thank God for your eyes, ears and mind.
Bring the children (Mark 10:14)
Bless your children or grandchildren tonight with the sign of the cross on their foreheads; if you have none, pray for the children of your street by name.
2027-05-22.prayer: Lord God, you formed us from the dust of the earth and made us in your image; you remember that we are dust and you have compassion on us as a father on his children. Give us the heart of a little child, to receive your Kingdom with open hands. Through the prayers of St Rita, who answered violence with forgiveness and trusted you in every sorrow, bring peace to our homes, and grant us what seems impossible, if it is your will. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.
altar: At the altar we come as children. Nothing we bring earns the gift; we hold out our hands, and the Lord who took the children in his arms gives us himself, his Body and Blood, as a father feeds his little ones. “Lord, I am not worthy” is the prayer of a child who knows that everything is grace.

2027-05-24.title: Monday of the Eighth Week in Ordinary Time
readings: Turn back to the Lord and forsake your sins (Lectionary numbering: Sirach 17:20–24)
Let the just exult and rejoice in the Lord
Go, sell what you own, and give the money to the poor; then come, follow me
2027-05-24.alt: Weekday of Ordinary Time, Week 8 (Year I). Liturgical colour: green. The Lectionary cites the first reading as Sirach 17:20–24; in the NRSV and in the Malayalam POC Bible the same verses are numbered 17:24–29. Today Salesian communities and many parishes in India honour Mary, Help of Christians; Pope Benedict XVI asked that 24 May also be a World Day of Prayer for the Church in China, under the protection of Our Lady of Sheshan.
2027-05-24.verse: Jesus looked at them and said, “For mortals it is impossible, but not for God; for God all things are possible.”
theo: Ben Sira today speaks to anyone who has wandered away from God, and his tone is full of hope. “Yet to those who repent he grants a return, and he encourages those who are losing hope.” God does not merely allow a return; he grants it, opens the road, and even comes to meet those whose courage is failing. Then the invitation, in three urgent verbs: “Turn back to the Lord and forsake your sins; pray in his presence and lessen your offense. Return to the Most High and turn away from iniquity.” Ben Sira, who wrote before the full revelation of the resurrection, adds a reason drawn from life itself: the living give thanks, the dead are silent, so “those who are alive and well sing the Lord's praises.” Today, while we have breath, is the time to return. And he ends with a cry of wonder: “How great is the mercy of the Lord, and his forgiveness for those who return to him!” The Psalm gives the experience of one who has made that return: “While I kept silence, my body wasted away … Then I acknowledged my sin to you … and you forgave the guilt of my sin.” Hiding sin makes us sick; confessing it heals. “Happy are those whose transgression is forgiven.”

The Gospel tells of a man who runs up to Jesus and kneels before him: “Good Teacher, what must I do to inherit eternal life?” He is sincere, eager, respectful. Jesus points him first to God, “No one is good but God alone,” and then to the commandments, especially those about the neighbour. “Teacher, I have kept all these since my youth.” And then comes one of the most tender lines in the Gospels: “Jesus, looking at him, loved him.” Out of that love comes the invitation: “You lack one thing; go, sell what you own, and give the money to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; then come, follow me.” The man “was shocked and went away grieving, for he had many possessions.” He did not lose the love of Jesus; he lost the courage to accept it. Jesus then turns to the disciples: “How hard it will be for those who have wealth to enter the kingdom of God! … It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle.” The disciples are astounded: “Then who can be saved?” And Jesus answers with the sentence that is the hope of every one of us: “For mortals it is impossible, but not for God; for God all things are possible.” Not everyone is called to sell everything, but every disciple is called to hold nothing more tightly than Christ. The rich man went away; Ben Sira tells us the door of return is always open. Today, as many honour Mary, Help of Christians, we ask her to help us let go of whatever keeps us from following her Son, and we pray, as the Church asks, for the Catholics of China.
outline: Opening
Ask: what is the one thing I would find hardest to give up for Jesus?
Point 1 · He grants a return
God opens the road home and encourages those losing hope.
Point 2 · Looking at him, loved him
The love of Jesus comes before the challenge.
Point 3 · For God all things are possible
What is impossible for us, grace makes possible.
Take-home line
“For God all things are possible.”
live: Return and confess (Psalm 32:5)
Make a quiet examination of conscience tonight, and plan to receive the sacrament of Reconciliation this week.
Loosen your grip (Mark 10:21)
Give away one possession you are attached to, or give a generous gift to the poor this week, as an act of trust in Jesus.
2027-05-24.prayer: Merciful Father, how great is your mercy and your forgiveness for those who return to you. Open for us the road home, and encourage us when we are losing hope. Lord Jesus, you looked at the rich man and loved him; look at us with the same love, and give us the courage to let go of whatever we hold more tightly than you. Mary, Help of Christians, help us to follow your Son; and protect the Church in China and all who suffer for their faith. For you, O God, all things are possible. Amen.
altar: The Lord who “looked at him and loved him” looks at us from the altar. He who had no possessions on the cross gives us the only treasure that lasts, himself, in his Body and Blood. To receive him is to receive the grace that makes the impossible possible: a heart that can let go and follow.

2027-05-25.title: Tuesday of the Eighth Week in Ordinary Time · St Bede the Venerable; St Gregory VII; St Mary Magdalene de' Pazzi
readings: Give to the Most High as he has given to you, and as generously as you can afford
To the upright I will show the saving power of God
who will not receive a hundredfold now in this age … with persecutions … and in the age to come eternal life
2027-05-25.alt: Weekday of Ordinary Time, Week 8 (Year I). Three optional memorials may be kept today: St Bede the Venerable, priest and doctor of the Church; St Gregory VII, pope; St Mary Magdalene de' Pazzi, virgin. The first reading is given in NRSV numbering (Lectionary Sirach 35:1–12 = NRSV 35:1–15). Liturgical colour: green (white if a memorial is kept).
2027-05-25.verse: With every gift show a cheerful face, and dedicate your tithe with gladness. Give to the Most High as he has given to you, and as generously as you can afford.
theo: Ben Sira, the wise teacher of Jerusalem, wrote about two centuries before Christ, when the Temple sacrifices were offered every day. He loved the Temple, and he does not mock the sacrifices. But he wants his students to understand what makes an offering pleasing to God. He begins with a surprising list: “The one who keeps the law makes many offerings; one who heeds the commandments makes an offering of well-being. The one who returns a kindness offers choice flour, and one who gives alms sacrifices a thank offering.” Kindness repaid, alms given, a commandment kept: each of these is already an offering laid on God's altar. “To keep from wickedness is pleasing to the Lord, and to forsake unrighteousness is an atonement.” Then he turns to the gifts themselves, and his advice is warm and practical: “Do not appear before the Lord empty-handed.” “Be generous when you worship the Lord, and do not stint the first fruits of your hands. With every gift show a cheerful face, and dedicate your tithe with gladness.” The measure is simple: “Give to the Most High as he has given to you, and as generously as you can afford. For the Lord is the one who repays, and he will repay you sevenfold.” And one warning: “Do not offer him a bribe, for he will not accept it.” God cannot be bought. The Psalm says the same thing in God's own voice: “Not for your sacrifices do I rebuke you,” but “offer to God a sacrifice of thanksgiving,” for “those who bring thanksgiving as their sacrifice honor me.”

In the Gospel Peter speaks for all the Twelve. They have just watched a rich young man walk away sad, and heard Jesus say how hard it is for the wealthy to enter the kingdom. Peter blurts out: “Look, we have left everything and followed you.” There is a question hidden in the sentence: and what will we get? Jesus does not scold him. He answers with a promise that is both generous and honest: “there is no one who has left house or brothers or sisters or mother or father or children or fields, for my sake and for the sake of the good news, who will not receive a hundredfold now in this age.” The hundredfold is real: the one who leaves a family for Christ finds brothers and sisters and mothers in every Christian community, houses opened in every town. But Jesus adds two words no salesman would add: “with persecutions.” And then the true reward: “in the age to come eternal life.” Ben Sira said God repays sevenfold; Jesus says a hundredfold. You cannot outgive God. St Bede the Venerable, whom the Church remembers today, gave his whole life from the age of seven to the monastery of Jarrow in northern England. He never travelled far, yet through his books he taught all of Europe. Tradition says that on his last day he finished dictating a passage of St John's Gospel in English and died singing “Glory be to the Father.” That is the cheerful face Ben Sira asks for, kept to the end.
outline: Opening
Ask: when you put money in the collection, or give your time, what does your face look like?
Point 1 · Every good deed is an offering
Kindness repaid and alms given are sacrifices pleasing to God.
Point 2 · With a cheerful face
Give as God has given you, gladly, without trying to bribe him.
Point 3 · A hundredfold, with persecutions
Jesus' honest promise to those who leave all for him.
Take-home line
“Give to the Most High as he has given to you.”
live: Give with gladness (Sirach 35:11)
Choose one gift today, money, time or help, and give it with a smile, without telling anyone.
Count the hundredfold (Mark 10:30)
Tonight name three people God has given you as brothers and sisters in faith, and thank him for each.
2027-05-25.prayer: Most High God, everything we have has come from your hand. Teach us to give back to you as you have given to us, generously and with a cheerful face, not to buy your favour but to thank you for it. Lord Jesus, you promised a hundredfold to all who leave everything for your sake; give us courage when following you costs us something, and keep our eyes on the life of the age to come. Through the prayers of St Bede the Venerable, may we serve you gladly to our last breath. Amen.
altar: At every Mass the priest says: blessed are you, Lord God of all creation, for through your goodness we have received the bread and wine we offer you. We bring back to God what he first gave us, and he returns it a hundredfold: the bread becomes the Body of Christ, the wine his Blood, and our small offering is united to the one perfect sacrifice of his Son.

2027-05-26.title: Saint Philip Neri, Priest
readings: Then they will know, as we have known, that there is no God but you, O Lord
Show us, O Lord, the light of your kindness
The Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life a ransom for many
2027-05-26.alt: Memorial. Wednesday of the Eighth Week in Ordinary Time (Year I). The weekday readings are given here (first reading in NRSV numbering); the proper first reading of the memorial, Philippians 4:4–9, “Rejoice in the Lord always,” may be used instead. St Philip Neri, the Apostle of Rome, founded the Congregation of the Oratory. Liturgical colour: white.
2027-05-26.verse: For the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life a ransom for many.
theo: The first reading is a prayer, one of the most fervent in the Wisdom books. Ben Sira's people are small and pressed on every side by powerful nations, and he cries out: “Have mercy upon us, O God of all, and put all the nations in fear of you.” But his deepest wish is not revenge. It is that the nations should come to know the true God: “As you have used us to show your holiness to them, so use them to show your glory to us. Then they will know, as we have known, that there is no God but you, O Lord.” Israel's suffering and Israel's rescue are meant to become a lesson for the whole world. Then the prayer grows tender: “Gather all the tribes of Jacob,” “Have mercy, O Lord, on the people called by your name, on Israel, whom you have named your firstborn,” “Have pity on the city of your sanctuary, Jerusalem.” And he ends with a line that the Church can pray at every Mass: “Hear, O Lord, the prayer of your servants, according to your goodwill toward your people, and all who are on the earth will know that you are the Lord, the God of the ages.” The Psalm, from a time of national disaster, prays in the same spirit: “Help us, O God of our salvation, for the glory of your name; deliver us, and forgive our sins, for your name's sake.”

In the Gospel Jesus is walking ahead of his disciples on the road up to Jerusalem, and “they were amazed, and those who followed were afraid.” For the third time he tells them plainly what will happen: he will be handed over, condemned, mocked, flogged and killed, “and after three days he will rise again.” And at that very moment James and John come with a request: “Grant us to sit, one at your right hand and one at your left, in your glory.” They are thinking of thrones; he is thinking of a cross. “You do not know what you are asking. Are you able to drink the cup that I drink?” They answer bravely, “We are able,” and in time they will: James will be the first of the Twelve to die for Christ. The other ten are angry, perhaps because they wanted the same seats. So Jesus gathers them all and turns the world upside down: among the nations, rulers “lord it over them,” “but it is not so among you; but whoever wishes to become great among you must be your servant, and whoever wishes to be first among you must be slave of all. For the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life a ransom for many.” St Philip Neri, whom we remember today, could have had honours in the Rome of the popes. He refused the cardinal's hat more than once. He spent his life hearing confessions, visiting the sick in the hospitals, walking with young men from church to church, and making people laugh so that pride would have no room. He showed that the greatness Jesus speaks of can be joyful.
outline: Opening
Ask: if Jesus asked you today, “What do you want me to do for you?”, what would you say?
Point 1 · That all may know you
Ben Sira prays that God's people may become a light for the nations.
Point 2 · The cup and the thrones
James and John ask for glory; Jesus offers a share in his cup.
Point 3 · Not to be served but to serve
Greatness turned upside down, lived with joy by St Philip Neri.
Take-home line
“The Son of Man came not to be served but to serve.”
live: Pray for the nations (Sirach 36:5)
Pray today for one country where Christ is not yet known, that its people may come to know the true God.
Take the lowest place (Mark 10:44)
Do one humble task at home or at work today that nobody else wants to do, and do it cheerfully.
saints: St Philip Neri (1515–1595)

Born in Florence, he came to Rome as a young man and lived for years as a layman, praying in the catacombs and caring for pilgrims and the sick. At Pentecost 1544, according to his own account, he felt the love of the Holy Spirit enter his heart like a ball of fire. Ordained priest in 1551, he gathered people for prayer, Scripture, music and conversation in a room above the church, the Oratory, from which the Congregation of the Oratory was born (approved 1575). Known for his humour, his long hours in the confessional and his care for the young, he is called the Apostle of Rome. He died on 26 May 1595 and was canonised in 1622.
2027-05-26.prayer: O God, who never cease to bestow the glory of holiness on the faithful servants you raise up for yourself, graciously grant that the Holy Spirit may kindle in us that fire with which he wonderfully filled the heart of Saint Philip Neri. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, who lives and reigns with you in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, for ever and ever. Amen. Let us also pray: Lord Jesus, you came not to be served but to serve. Deliver us from the wish for the first seats, and give us joy in the lowest place, so that all the earth may know that you are Lord. Amen.
altar: The cup Jesus asked James and John about is the cup he lifts at every Mass: “This is the cup of my Blood, the Blood of the new and eternal covenant, which will be poured out for you and for many.” Here the Son of Man still serves us, giving his life as a ransom, and those who drink from this cup are sent out to serve as he did.

2027-05-27.title: Thursday of the Eighth Week in Ordinary Time · St Augustine of Canterbury
readings: By the word of the Lord his works are made; who could ever tire of seeing his glory?
By the word of the Lord the heavens were made
My teacher, let me see again. Go; your faith has made you well
2027-05-27.alt: Weekday of Ordinary Time, Week 8 (Year I). St Augustine of Canterbury, bishop, may be remembered (optional memorial). Where the Solemnity of the Most Holy Body and Blood of Christ is kept on Thursday (as at the Vatican and in many countries), it is celebrated today; in India the Latin Church keeps it on Sunday 30 May. Liturgical colour: green (white if the memorial is kept).
2027-05-27.verse: Then Jesus said to him, “What do you want me to do for you?” The blind man said to him, “My teacher, let me see again.”
theo: Near the end of his book Ben Sira lifts his eyes from human affairs and begins a great hymn to the Creator: “I will now call to mind the works of the Lord, and will declare what I have seen. By the word of the Lord his works are made; and all his creatures do his will.” He looks at the sun, which “looks down on everything with its light,” and says, “the work of the Lord is full of his glory.” He confesses that even the angels, God's “holy ones,” cannot tell all his wonders. Then he turns inward: God “searches out the abyss and the human heart; he understands their innermost secrets.” Nothing is hidden from him; “he is from all eternity one and the same,” and “he needs no one to be his counselor.” What moves Ben Sira most is the order and harmony of things: “All things come in pairs, one opposite the other, and he has made nothing incomplete. Each supplements the virtues of the other. Who could ever tire of seeing his glory?” Day and night, sea and land, male and female, rain and sunshine: each completes the other. The Psalm sings the same wonder: “By the word of the LORD the heavens were made, and all their host by the breath of his mouth,” “for he spoke, and it came to be; he commanded, and it stood firm.” Christians hear in these lines the whole Trinity at work: the Father who speaks, the Word through whom all things were made, and the Breath, the Spirit, who gives life.

In the Gospel the same powerful Word walks on a dusty road out of Jericho. Jesus is on his last journey to Jerusalem, and a large crowd is with him. By the roadside sits “Bartimaeus son of Timaeus, a blind beggar.” He cannot see the works of God that Ben Sira praised, not even the sun. But he can hear, and when he hears that Jesus of Nazareth is passing, he shouts: “Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me!” Many tell him to be quiet. Beggars are supposed to sit still and not disturb important people. “But he cried out even more loudly.” And then: “Jesus stood still.” The one through whom the heavens were made stops for a blind man. “Call him here.” The crowd that was silencing him now says, “Take heart; get up, he is calling you.” Bartimaeus throws off his cloak, perhaps the only thing he owned, the cloak spread on the ground to catch coins, and springs up. Jesus asks him the very question he asked James and John a few verses earlier: “What do you want me to do for you?” They had asked for seats of glory. Bartimaeus asks for the one thing he needs: “My teacher, let me see again.” “Go; your faith has made you well.” And the healed man does not go away; he “followed him on the way,” up the road to Jerusalem and the cross. His cry has become one of the great prayers of Christians, the Jesus Prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me. Today the Church also remembers St Augustine of Canterbury, the monk sent by Pope St Gregory the Great to bring the Gospel to the English, who landed in Kent in 597. He too had to throw off his fears: on the way, his monks were so afraid of the journey that they wanted to turn back, but Gregory sent them on with encouragement, and Augustine became the first Archbishop of Canterbury.
outline: Opening
Ask: if Jesus stopped in front of you today and asked, “What do you want me to do for you?”, what would you answer?
Point 1 · Who could tire of his glory?
Ben Sira praises the Creator who made all things by his word and searches every heart.
Point 2 · He cried out even more loudly
Bartimaeus will not be silenced; Jesus stands still.
Point 3 · Let me see again, and follow
The healed man throws off his cloak and follows Jesus on the way.
Take-home line
“What do you want me to do for you?”
live: Look and praise (Sirach 42:25)
Step outside today for two minutes, look at the sky or a tree, and say: Lord, your work is full of your glory.
Pray the cry of Bartimaeus (Mark 10:47)
Repeat slowly today, especially when you are worried: Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me.
2027-05-27.prayer: Lord God, by your word the heavens were made, and all their host by the breath of your mouth. Your works are full of your glory, and you search the depths of every heart. Open our eyes to see your wonders. Lord Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on us; when the crowd tells us to be silent, give us courage to cry out more loudly; and when you call us, help us to throw off our cloak and follow you on the way. Through the prayers of St Augustine of Canterbury, make us bold messengers of the Gospel. Amen.
altar: The Word by whom all things were made, who stood still for Bartimaeus, stands still for us at this altar. Under the appearance of bread and wine he is truly present, Body and Blood, soul and divinity. Before Communion we pray with the centurion, Lord, I am not worthy; and with Bartimaeus we may add: let me see you, and follow you on the way.

2027-05-28.title: Friday of the Eighth Week in Ordinary Time
readings: These also were godly men, whose righteous deeds have not been forgotten
The Lord takes delight in his people
My house shall be called a house of prayer for all the nations. Have faith in God
2027-05-28.alt: Weekday of Ordinary Time, Week 8 (Year I). Liturgical colour: green.
2027-05-28.verse: Whenever you stand praying, forgive, if you have anything against anyone; so that your Father in heaven may also forgive you your trespasses.
theo: Ben Sira now begins the longest section of his book, a hymn in praise of the ancestors of Israel, from Enoch and Noah to the high priest Simon of his own day. He opens with a famous line: “Let us now sing the praises of famous men, our ancestors in their generations.” He names kings, counsellors, prophets, musicians and wise teachers. But then he does something tender. He remembers those whom nobody remembers: “But of others there is no memory; they have perished as though they had never existed; they have become as though they had never been born.” And he insists that they too count before God: “But these also were godly men, whose righteous deeds have not been forgotten; their wealth will remain with their descendants, and their inheritance with their children's children.” Their goodness lives on in their families: “Their descendants stand by the covenants; their children also, for their sake. Their offspring will continue forever, and their glory will never be blotted out.” Every family in our parishes has such people: a grandmother who taught the rosary, a father who worked hard and never cheated, a teacher who lived the faith quietly. No book records their names, but their goodness is not forgotten, and we are living on their inheritance. The Psalm sings with joy: “the LORD takes pleasure in his people; he adorns the humble with victory.”

The Gospel is one of the most dramatic in St Mark. Jesus enters Jerusalem and the Temple, looks around at everything, and leaves for Bethany. The next morning he sees a fig tree “in leaf,” goes to look for fruit and finds “nothing but leaves, for it was not the season for figs.” He says, “May no one ever eat fruit from you again.” Then he enters the Temple and drives out the sellers and buyers, overturns the tables of the money changers and quotes two prophets: “Is it not written, ‘My house shall be called a house of prayer for all the nations’? But you have made it a den of robbers.” The next morning the disciples see the fig tree “withered away to its roots.” Mark places the cleansing of the Temple between the two halves of the fig tree story, like a filling in a sandwich, so that each explains the other. Jesus is acting like the prophets of old, who used signs to wake people up. A tree full of leaves but without fruit is a picture of worship full of activity but without prayer, justice and faith. This is not a judgment on the Jewish people; Jesus loved the Temple, called it “my house,” and the Church teaches that he honoured it (Catechism 584). It is a warning to every place of worship and every heart, including our own parishes. Then Jesus tells the disciples what real fruit looks like: “Have faith in God.” Faith that moves mountains, prayer that trusts, and above all forgiveness: “Whenever you stand praying, forgive, if you have anything against anyone; so that your Father in heaven may also forgive you your trespasses.” A house of prayer is a house of forgiveness.
outline: Opening
Ask: who in your family, now gone to God, taught you the faith without ever being famous?
Point 1 · Not forgotten
Ben Sira praises the godly whom no one remembers; their goodness lives on in their children.
Point 2 · Leaves without fruit
The fig tree and the Temple: worship busy with activity but empty of prayer.
Point 3 · A house of prayer and forgiveness
Have faith in God, and when you pray, forgive.
Take-home line
“Whenever you stand praying, forgive.”
live: Remember the forgotten (Sirach 44:10)
Pray today for one person in your family history whose goodness you inherited, and thank God for them.
Forgive before you pray (Mark 11:25)
Before your evening prayer, name one person you hold something against, and forgive them from your heart.
2027-05-28.prayer: Lord God, you take delight in your people and you do not forget the righteous deeds of those whom the world forgets. We thank you for the godly men and women who handed on the faith to us. Lord Jesus, you came to your Father's house looking for fruit; do not find our hearts full of leaves only. Make our churches houses of prayer for all the nations, strengthen our faith in God, and teach us to forgive whenever we stand to pray, so that our Father in heaven may forgive us. Amen.
altar: Before we come to the altar, the Lord asks us to be reconciled: in the Our Father we pray, forgive us our trespasses as we forgive those who trespass against us, and we exchange the sign of peace. The Eucharist is the fruit the Lord looks for in his house: the one sacrifice of Christ, offered by a people reconciled with God and with one another.

2027-05-29.title: Saturday of the Eighth Week in Ordinary Time · St Paul VI, Pope
readings: While I was still young, before I went on my travels, I sought wisdom openly in my prayer
The precepts of the Lord give joy to the heart
By what authority are you doing these things?
2027-05-29.alt: Weekday of Ordinary Time, Week 8 (Year I). St Paul VI, pope, may be remembered (optional memorial, inscribed in the General Roman Calendar in 2019). A Mass of the Blessed Virgin Mary on Saturday may also be celebrated. First reading and psalm in NRSV numbering. Liturgical colour: green (white if a memorial is kept).
2027-05-29.verse: More to be desired are they than gold, even much fine gold; sweeter also than honey, and drippings of the honeycomb.
theo: The Book of Sirach ends with a short autobiography in the form of a poem. The old teacher looks back and tells his students how he found wisdom. It began with thanksgiving: he blesses the name of the Lord who rescued him in time of trouble. Then he remembers his youth: “While I was still young, before I went on my travels, I sought wisdom openly in my prayer. Before the temple I asked for her, and I will search for her until the end.” Wisdom is not first a set of clever ideas; it is something asked for in prayer, before God's house. He uses the image of a vine: “From the first blossom to the ripening grape my heart delighted in her; my foot walked on the straight path; from my youth I followed her steps.” Growth was slow but steady: “I inclined my ear a little and received her, and I found for myself much instruction. I made progress in her; to him who gives wisdom I will give glory.” It also took effort: “My soul grappled with wisdom, and in my conduct I was strict.” And the fruit was purity of heart: “I directed my soul to her, and in purity I found her.” The Psalm praises God's law in the same spirit: “the precepts of the LORD are right, rejoicing the heart; the commandment of the LORD is clear, enlightening the eyes,” “sweeter also than honey, and drippings of the honeycomb.” As schools in Kerala and across India prepare to reopen, these lines are a prayer for every student: seek wisdom on your knees, and keep seeking her to the end.

In the Gospel Jesus is walking in the Temple the day after he drove out the traders, and the chief priests, the scribes and the elders come with a sharp question: “By what authority are you doing these things? Who gave you this authority to do them?” It is a fair question for the guardians of the Temple to ask. Jesus answers with a question of his own: “Did the baptism of John come from heaven, or was it of human origin? Answer me.” The leaders discuss it among themselves. If they say from heaven, he will ask why they did not believe John; if they say of human origin, they fear the crowd, “for all regarded John as truly a prophet.” So they answer, “We do not know.” And Jesus says, “Neither will I tell you by what authority I am doing these things.” Jesus is not playing a clever game. John had pointed to Jesus; anyone who accepted John's witness would already know where Jesus' authority came from. But the question cannot be answered by calculation, by asking what is safe to say. It needs a heart that seeks the truth, as Ben Sira sought wisdom. This is not a judgment on a whole people; these were particular men in a particular moment, and the same temptation to measure the truth by what others will think lives in every one of us. Today the Church may remember St Paul VI, the pope who guided the Second Vatican Council to its end. He knew the weight of authority, and he used it as a servant: in 1964 he laid the papal tiara on the altar of St Peter's as a gift for the poor, and in the same year he came to Bombay for the International Eucharistic Congress, the first pope ever to visit India. He wrote that people today listen more willingly to witnesses than to teachers (Evangelii Nuntiandi 41, in substance). Authority in the Church is credible when it is a witness to the truth.
outline: Opening
Ask: when you have to decide what is true, do you ask “What is right?” or “What will people think?”
Point 1 · Sought in prayer from youth
Ben Sira found wisdom by asking for it before God's house and following her steps.
Point 2 · Sweeter than honey
God's law rejoices the heart and enlightens the eyes.
Point 3 · By what authority?
An answer that needs a heart open to the truth, not a calculation.
Take-home line
“I sought wisdom openly in my prayer.”
live: Ask for wisdom (Sirach 51:13)
Before you begin your work or study today, pray: Lord, give me wisdom for this task.
Say what is true (Mark 11:33)
Today, when it would be easier to say “I do not know” to avoid trouble, speak the truth kindly and simply.
2027-05-29.prayer: Lord God, giver of wisdom, from our youth teach us to seek you in prayer and to follow wisdom's steps until the end. Make your precepts sweeter to us than honey, and let your commandment enlighten our eyes. Lord Jesus, your authority comes from the Father; give us hearts that seek the truth and do not measure it by the fear of others. Through the prayers of St Paul VI, may all who hold authority in the Church be humble servants and faithful witnesses. Amen.
altar: Ben Sira asked for wisdom “before the temple.” We come before the altar where Wisdom himself, the eternal Word made flesh, gives us his Body and Blood. Here the question “By what authority?” is answered: by the authority of the Son who loved us to the end and offers himself to the Father for us.

2027-05-31.title: The Visitation of the Blessed Virgin Mary
readings: The King of Israel, the Lord, is in your midst
Great in your midst is the Holy One of Israel
Why has this happened to me, that the mother of my Lord comes to me?
2027-05-31.alt: Feast. Gloria; no Creed. The readings are proper to the feast and replace those of Monday of the Ninth Week in Ordinary Time. Either Zephaniah 3:14–18a or Romans 12:9–16 may be read as the first reading; the responsorial psalm is the canticle of Isaiah 12. Since 1969 the Visitation is kept on 31 May, between the Annunciation (25 March) and the Birth of St John the Baptist (24 June); it closes the month of May, dedicated to Mary. Liturgical colour: white.
2027-05-31.verse: And blessed is she who believed that there would be a fulfillment of what was spoken to her by the Lord.
theo: On the last day of the month of Mary the Church follows a young woman on a journey. The prophet Zephaniah, writing in a dark time for Jerusalem, suddenly breaks into a song of joy addressed to “daughter Zion”: “Sing aloud, O daughter Zion; shout, O Israel! Rejoice and exult with all your heart, O daughter Jerusalem!” The reason for the joy is a presence: “The king of Israel, the LORD, is in your midst; you shall fear disaster no more.” And again: “Do not fear, O Zion; do not let your hands grow weak. The LORD, your God, is in your midst, a warrior who gives victory; he will rejoice over you with gladness, he will renew you in his love; he will exult over you with loud singing as on a day of festival.” The Hebrew for “in your midst” can also mean “within you,” “in your womb.” The Church has always heard in these words the voice of the angel to Mary: “Greetings, favored one! The Lord is with you” (Luke 1:28), a greeting that in Greek begins with the word “Rejoice,” and then: do not be afraid. Mary is the true daughter Zion, and the Lord is now, literally, within her. The responsorial psalm, the song of Isaiah 12, carries the same joy: “Shout aloud and sing for joy, O royal Zion, for great in your midst is the Holy One of Israel.” Where the second option is read, St Paul's words in Romans 12 sound like a portrait of what Mary does in today's Gospel: “Let love be genuine,” “extend hospitality to strangers,” “Rejoice with those who rejoice,” “do not be haughty, but associate with the lowly.”

Then the Gospel. Mary has just heard the angel's message, and has heard too that her elderly relative Elizabeth, “who was said to be barren,” is in her sixth month. Her first response to the gift of God is not to stay at home and wonder, but to go and serve: “In those days Mary set out and went with haste to a Judean town in the hill country.” It was a journey of perhaps four days on foot, from Nazareth in the north to the hills near Jerusalem, where tradition places the village of Ein Karem. Mary carries the Son of God within her, hidden and very small, and she brings him to another home. St Luke tells the story with words that echo the Old Testament account of the Ark of the Covenant being brought into the hill country of Judah (2 Samuel 6).
