pm.resp: Commit your life to the Lord, and he will help you.
interc: For all who are being tested by illness, loss or failure, that they may cling to the Lord and not lose hope.
For the Pope and all bishops, that like St John I they may serve faithfully under pressure.
For Christians imprisoned for their faith.
For children who are neglected, abused or trafficked, and for all who protect them.
For our group, that we may stop measuring ourselves against one another and learn to serve.
pm.close: Father, you are compassionate and merciful, and you save in time of distress. Make us servants of all, after the pattern of your Son, who lives and reigns for ever and ever. Amen.

quick: Ben Sira: Wisdom teaches her children; whoever loves her loves life.
Wisdom first walks with us on hard paths and tests us, then gladdens us and reveals her secrets.
John tried to stop a man casting out demons in Jesus' name; Jesus said: do not stop him; whoever is not against us is for us.
2027-05-19.action: Thank God today, by name, for one good work done by people outside your own circle.
2027-05-19.question: Do I guard the borders of my group more carefully than I rejoice in God's work?

family.explain: The disciples saw a man doing good things in Jesus' name, but he was not one of their group, so they told him to stop. Jesus said: do not stop him. If someone does good in my name, he is on our side. God is happy whenever good is done, and we should be happy too.
family.intention: We pray for unity among all Christians, and for all people who help the poor and the sick.
family.ask: Ask: “Is there a family, a school or a group we sometimes speak badly about? Can we find one good thing about them today?”

illus: An illustration

In the Kerala floods of August 2018, fishermen from the coastal villages of Kollam, Alappuzha and Thiruvananthapuram brought their own boats inland and rescued many thousands of people from flooded homes. Nobody asked the stranded families whether they were Hindu, Muslim or Christian, or which party they voted for; the fishermen simply pulled people into the boats. A parish priest in Chengannur said afterwards: that week I learned that the hand that lifts you out of the water is never on the wrong side.

pm.open: Lord Jesus, Wisdom of God, teach us your ways and give us hearts glad at every good done in your name. Amen.
share: Whoever loves her loves life (Sirach 4:12). Do I seek God's wisdom, or only information and advice?
At first she will walk with them on tortuous paths (Sirach 4:17). How has a hard season taught me something I could not learn otherwise?
Whoever is not against us is for us (Mark 9:40). Whom have I been quick to treat as an outsider?
pm.resp: O Lord, great peace have they who love your law.
interc: For the unity of all Christians, that we may grow towards the one Church Christ willed.
For teachers, parents and formators, that they may guide with wisdom and patience.
For all who do good outside the Church, that the Spirit may lead them to the fullness of truth.
For young people facing hard paths in study or work, that they may not give up.
For our group, that jealousy and rivalry may have no place among us.
pm.close: Father, your Son is our wisdom and our peace. Make us glad at every sign of your Kingdom, through Christ our Lord. Amen.

quick: Ben Sira: do not trust in wealth or strength, and do not presume on God's mercy to keep sinning.
Do not delay to turn back to the Lord; do not put it off from day to day.
Jesus: a cup of water given in his name is rewarded; cut off whatever causes you to sin; have salt and be at peace.
2027-05-20.action: Take one concrete step today against a sin you keep postponing.
2027-05-20.question: Which conversion have I been putting off until tomorrow?
kidsaint: St Bernardine of Siena

Bernardine lived in Italy six hundred years ago. When he was twenty, a terrible sickness came to his city, and he and his friends looked after the sick in the hospital day and night. Later he became a Franciscan preacher and travelled from town to town. He carried a board with the letters IHS, the first letters of the name of Jesus in Greek, shining like the sun, and taught everyone to love that holy name. Lesson: say the name of Jesus with love many times a day.

family.explain: Jesus says that even a cup of water given to someone because they belong to him will never be forgotten by God. Small kind things matter to Jesus. He also says that if something makes us do wrong again and again, we must throw it away, like a bad habit.
family.intention: We pray for anyone in our family who needs to come back to God, and for people who have no clean drinking water.
family.ask: Ask: “Is there one bad habit our family should stop starting from today? What small kindness can we do instead?”

illus: An illustration

A story told about St Bernardine: after one of his sermons against gambling, people in a city burned their dice and playing cards in the square. A man who made playing cards for a living came to him in distress: you have ruined my trade. Bernardine is said to have drawn the sign of the Holy Name, the letters IHS surrounded by rays of the sun, and told him to make and sell that instead. The man did, and the tablets of the Holy Name spread through Italy. Whether every detail is exact or not, the point is sound: conversion does not only remove what is bad; it makes room for something better.

pm.open: Lord Jesus, we do not want to delay any longer. Turn our hearts to you today. Amen.
share: Do not rely on your wealth, or say, “I have enough” (Sirach 5:1). Where do I feel I do not need God?
Do not delay to turn back to the Lord (Sirach 5:7). What conversion have I been postponing?
Have salt in yourselves, and be at peace with one another (Mark 9:50). With whom do I need to make peace?
pm.resp: Blessed are they who hope in the Lord.
interc: For all who keep putting off their return to God, that they may hear his call today.
For those who are led into sin by others, and for the little ones who have been scandalised.
For preachers of the Gospel, that like St Bernardine they may call people to conversion with love.
For families and communities divided by quarrels, that they may be at peace with one another.
For our group, that we may give a cup of water to all who serve in Christ's name.
pm.close: Father, you are patient with sinners and you wait for our return. Make us turn to you today, through Jesus, whose name is above every name. Amen.

quick: Ben Sira: test your friends; faithful friends are a sturdy shelter, a treasure, a life-saving medicine.
The Pharisees ask about divorce; Jesus points to the beginning: God made them male and female, and the two become one flesh.
What God has joined together, let no one separate; St Christopher Magallanes, arrested a century ago today, forgave his executioners.
2027-05-21.action: Stand by one friend or family member who is going through a hard time today.
2027-05-21.question: Am I the kind of friend Ben Sira describes, one who stays when trouble comes?
kidsaint: St Christopher Magallanes

Christopher was a priest in a village in Mexico a hundred years ago. He loved his people, built schools and helped young men become priests. At that time the government closed the churches, and priests could be arrested. On his way to say Mass, Christopher was caught, and a few days later he was shot. Before he died, he gave away what he had to the soldiers and forgave them. Lesson: a friend of Jesus forgives, even when it is very hard.

family.explain: God made man and woman to love each other, and when they marry, God joins them together like two hands folded in prayer. Jesus says: what God has joined together, nobody should separate. Our family is something God has made, and we look after it by loving, forgiving and staying together.
family.intention: We pray for our parents and grandparents, for all married couples, and for families who are hurting because of separation.
family.ask: Ask: “What can each of us do this week to make our home a sturdy shelter for one another?”

illus: An illustration

A couple in Kottayam celebrated their fiftieth wedding anniversary. At the parish lunch a young man asked the husband for the secret of fifty years together. He laughed: there were years we did not like each other very much. But every night we prayed the Rosary together, and you cannot pray the Rosary with someone and stay angry for long. His wife added: and we decided early that the word divorce would never be used in our house, not even as a joke. Ben Sira would have called them faithful friends.

pm.open: Lord Jesus, faithful friend, make us faithful in friendship and in marriage. Amen.
share: Faithful friends are a sturdy shelter (Sirach 6:14). Who has been a shelter for me, and have I thanked them?
There are friends who sit at your table, but they will not stand by you in time of trouble (Sirach 6:10). What kind of friend am I when others are in trouble?
What God has joined together, let no one separate (Mark 10:9). How can I support the marriages around me?
pm.resp: Guide me, Lord, in the way of your commands.
interc: For all married couples, that they may grow in faithful love.
For couples in crisis and for those whose marriages have broken, that they may find support and the tenderness of the Church.
For young people preparing for marriage.
For Christians persecuted for their faith today, through the prayers of St Christopher Magallanes and companions.
For our group, that we may be faithful friends to one another.
pm.close: Father, from the beginning you made man and woman for each other. Keep our families in your faithful love, through Christ our Lord. Amen.

quick: Ben Sira: God made us from earth and in his image, gave us senses and mind to praise him, and taught us to care for our neighbour.
The Lord has compassion on us as a father on his children; he remembers that we are dust.
Jesus, indignant with his disciples, blesses the children: the Kingdom belongs to such as these; receive it as a little child.
2027-05-22.action: Bless a child tonight with the sign of the cross, or pray for one child by name.
2027-05-22.question: Am I trying to earn God's love, or am I receiving it like a child?
kidsaint: St Rita of Cascia

Rita lived in a small village in Italy. She married a man who was often angry and rough, but she was patient and kind, and prayed for him. After he died, she became a nun. People say that when she was dying in winter, she asked for a rose from her old garden, and a rose was found blooming in the snow. That is why she is often shown with roses. Lesson: patient love and prayer can change hard hearts.

family.explain: Some parents brought their little children to Jesus so that he could bless them. The disciples said: go away, the Master is busy! Jesus was not happy with the disciples. He said: let the children come to me. Then he hugged them and blessed them. Jesus always has time for children.
family.intention: We pray for all children, especially those who are sick, poor, or far from their parents, and for families going through difficult times, through the prayers of St Rita.
family.ask: Ask: “Can we bless each other tonight before sleeping, making a small cross on each other's foreheads?”

illus: An illustration

In many parishes of Kerala, on the evening before a child's first day of school, a grandmother takes the child on her lap, makes the sign of the cross on the little forehead with her thumb and whispers a prayer. One grandmother in Thodupuzha did this for every grandchild for forty years. When the eldest, now a doctor working abroad, came home for her funeral, he said: I have forgotten many things she taught me, but I have never forgotten the feel of her thumb on my forehead. It taught me that I was blessed before I had done anything at all.

pm.open: Father, we come to you as little children. Hold us and bless us. Amen.
share: The Lord created human beings out of earth (Sirach 17:1). How do I accept the limits of my life and body?
He remembers that we are dust (Psalm 103:14). Do I believe that God is patient with my weakness?
Whoever does not receive the kingdom of God as a little child will never enter it (Mark 10:15). What does it mean for me to receive like a child?
pm.resp: The Lord's kindness is everlasting to those who fear him.
interc: For all children, that they may be loved, protected and brought to Jesus.
For parents and grandparents who pass on the faith.
For families suffering violence or quarrels, through the prayers of St Rita.
For all who face situations that seem impossible, that they may not lose hope.
For our group, that we may receive God's gifts with the trust of children.
pm.close: Father, you have compassion on your children. Make us small and trusting before you, through Christ our Lord. Amen.

quick: Ben Sira: God grants a return to those who repent; turn back to the Lord; how great is his mercy.
A rich man asks Jesus about eternal life; Jesus, looking at him, loves him and invites him to sell all, give to the poor and follow.
The man goes away grieving; Jesus says: for mortals it is impossible, but not for God; for God all things are possible.
2027-05-24.action: Give away one thing you are attached to, or make a generous gift to the poor this week.
2027-05-24.question: What do I hold more tightly than I hold Jesus?

family.explain: A man who had lots of money and things came running to Jesus. Jesus looked at him with love and said: give your things to the poor, and come with me. But the man went away sad, because he loved his things too much. Jesus loves us too, and he wants our hearts to love him more than any toy or phone or money.
family.intention: We pray for poor families who have very little, for the Church in China, and, through Mary Help of Christians, for all who are in trouble.
family.ask: Ask: “Is there something in our house we could give to someone who needs it more than we do?”

illus: An illustration

A young software engineer in Bengaluru, with a good salary and a new car, began volunteering on Sundays at a home for abandoned elderly people run by sisters. After a year he sold the car, bought a scooter, and used the difference to pay for medicines at the home. His friends thought he had gone mad. He said: I am not a hero. Jesus did not ask me to sell everything. He only asked me to stop holding the car more tightly than I hold him. Now I sleep better.

pm.open: Lord Jesus, look at us with love, and give us hearts that let go and follow you. Amen.
share: To those who repent he grants a return (Sirach 17:24). Where do I need to come back to God?
Jesus, looking at him, loved him (Mark 10:21). Can I believe that Jesus looks at me with love, even before I change?
For God all things are possible (Mark 10:27). Which impossible situation in my life do I need to hand over to God?
pm.resp: Let the just exult and rejoice in the Lord.
interc: For all who have drifted away from God, that they may find the road of return open.
For the rich and powerful, that they may use their wealth for the poor.
For the Catholics of China, that they may live their faith in peace and in communion with the whole Church.
Through Mary, Help of Christians, for young people, especially those helped by the Salesian family.
For our group, that we may hold nothing more tightly than Christ.
pm.close: Father, for you all things are possible. Take our hearts and make them wholly yours, through Christ our Lord. Amen.

quick: Ben Sira teaches that keeping the commandments, repaying kindness and giving alms are offerings pleasing to God.
Give to God as he has given to you, generously and with a cheerful face; God cannot be bribed, but he repays sevenfold.
Jesus promises those who leave everything for him a hundredfold now, with persecutions, and eternal life in the age to come.
2027-05-25.action: Give one gift today, of money, time or help, quietly and with a smile.
2027-05-25.question: When I give to God or to others, do I give gladly, or with a long face?
kidsaint: St Bede the Venerable

When Bede was only seven years old, his family took him to a monastery in England, and he lived there all his life. He loved to study, to pray and to sing. He wrote many books about the Bible and about the history of the Church in England, so people call him the father of English history. On the last day of his life he was still helping a young monk to write, and he died singing Glory be to the Father. Lesson: use the gifts God gives you to help others learn about him, every day of your life.

family.explain: Ben Sira was a wise teacher long ago. He said: when you give something to God, give it with a happy face! God gave us everything, our home, our food, our family, so we should give back gladly. Jesus told Peter that anyone who gives up something for him will get back a hundred times more, a big family of brothers and sisters in the Church.
family.intention: We pray for the poor who will receive our alms, and for people who are treated badly because they follow Jesus.
family.ask: Ask: “What is one thing our family can give this week, with a smile?”

illus: An illustration

A parish priest in Alappuzha used to watch the collection basket go round at Sunday Mass. He noticed that a fisherwoman who sold fish at the market every morning always dropped in her coin with a little smile and a sign of the cross. One day he asked her why. She said: Father, God gave me the sea and the fish and the strength to carry the basket; this is only a little of his own money that I am giving back to him. The priest said later that her coin taught him more about Sirach 35 than any commentary. (An illustrative story.)

pm.open: Lord God, everything we have is yours. Teach us to give back to you gladly, and keep us faithful to Jesus whatever it costs. Amen.
share: One who gives alms sacrifices a thank offering (Sirach 35:4). Which of my ordinary good deeds could I offer to God as a sacrifice today?
With every gift show a cheerful face (Sirach 35:11). Is there something I give, at home or in the parish, with a grumbling heart?
Look, we have left everything and followed you (Mark 10:28). What has following Jesus cost me, and what have I received in return?
pm.resp: To the upright I will show the saving power of God.
interc: For the Church, that her members may give generously and gladly to the poor and to the work of the Gospel.
For Christians who suffer persecution for the name of Jesus, especially in India and across Asia.
For priests and religious who have left home and family for Christ, that they may find the hundredfold he promised.
For teachers and scholars, through the prayers of St Bede, that they may serve the truth.
For our group, that we may never try to bargain with God, but trust his generosity.
pm.close: Father, you are never outdone in generosity. Accept the offering of our lives, and give us joy in serving you. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

quick: Ben Sira prays that God would gather his people and show his glory, so that all nations may know there is no God but the Lord.
James and John ask for the best seats in Christ's glory; Jesus asks if they can drink his cup.
Whoever wishes to be great must be a servant, for the Son of Man came to serve and to give his life as a ransom for many.
2027-05-26.action: Do one humble task today that nobody else wants to do, cheerfully and without mentioning it.
2027-05-26.question: Am I looking for the first seat, or for the chance to serve?
kidsaint: St Philip Neri

Philip lived in Rome a long time ago and he was full of joy. He loved to tell jokes, play with children and sing. Sometimes he did funny things on purpose, like shaving only half his beard, so that people would laugh at him and he would not become proud. He looked after poor people and sick people, and he listened to people's confessions for hours. Children loved him. He used to tell them: be good, if you can! Lesson: being holy does not mean being sad; Jesus wants us to serve others with a happy heart.

family.explain: Two of Jesus' friends, James and John, asked him: when you are king, can we sit in the best chairs beside you? Jesus said: in my kingdom the greatest person is the one who serves others. I did not come to be served, but to serve. St Philip Neri lived like that: he helped the poor and sick, and he did it with a big smile.
family.intention: We pray for people who serve in our parish, and for those in hospitals who need someone to visit them.
family.ask: Ask: “Who in our family serves everyone else the most? How can we help that person today?”

illus: An illustration

A story is told of St Philip Neri and a woman who loved to gossip. She came to confession and he gave her a strange penance: take a chicken, pluck its feathers as you walk through the streets, and come back to me. She did it. Then he said: now go back and pick up every feather. She cried that it was impossible, the wind had carried them everywhere. Exactly, said Philip; so it is with the words you have spoken about others. (A traditional story, told in many forms.) Serving others begins with how we speak of them.

pm.open: Lord Jesus, you came not to be served but to serve. Fill us with the joy of the Holy Spirit, as you filled St Philip Neri, and teach us to serve. Amen.
share: Then they will know, as we have known, that there is no God but you, O Lord (Sirach 36:5). Does my life help anyone come to know God?
Grant us to sit, one at your right hand and one at your left (Mark 10:37). In what ways do I still look for honour and the first place?
Whoever wishes to become great among you must be your servant (Mark 10:43). Whom could I serve this week, and how?
pm.resp: Show us, O Lord, the light of your kindness.
interc: For the Pope, the bishops and all who hold authority in the Church, that they may lead as servants.
For rulers and leaders of nations, that they may not lord it over their people.
For the Congregation of the Oratory and all who work with young people, through the prayers of St Philip Neri.
For the sick in hospitals and the lonely, that someone may visit them with joy.
For our group, that we may seek the lowest place and serve one another gladly.
pm.close: Father, your Son gave his life as a ransom for many. Give us his spirit of service, and the joy that filled St Philip Neri. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

quick: Ben Sira praises the Creator: all his works are made by his word, full of his glory, and nothing in the human heart is hidden from him.
Blind Bartimaeus cries out to Jesus, Son of David, and will not be silenced; Jesus stops and calls him.
Asked what he wants, he says, Let me see again; healed by his faith, he follows Jesus on the way.
2027-05-27.action: Pray the cry of Bartimaeus ten times today: Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me.
2027-05-27.question: What would I really ask Jesus for, if he stopped in front of me today?
kidsaint: St Augustine of Canterbury

Augustine was a monk in Rome. One day Pope Gregory asked him to take some monks and travel far away to England to tell the people there about Jesus. On the way the monks heard scary stories about England and wanted to go back! But the Pope wrote them a letter: be brave, keep going. They went on, and the king of Kent listened to them and was baptised, with many of his people. Augustine became the first Archbishop of Canterbury. Lesson: when we are afraid to do something good for Jesus, we can ask him for courage and keep going.

family.explain: Bartimaeus could not see. He sat by the road begging. When Jesus came by, he shouted: Jesus, have mercy on me! People said: be quiet! But he shouted louder. Jesus stopped and called him. Bartimaeus jumped up, threw off his coat and ran to Jesus. Jesus asked: what do you want? He said: I want to see! And Jesus healed him. Then Bartimaeus followed Jesus.
family.intention: We pray for people who are blind or have poor eyesight, and for doctors and nurses who care for them.
family.ask: Ask: “If Jesus asked you today, what do you want me to do for you, what would you say?”

illus: An illustration

A Russian book of the nineteenth century, The Way of a Pilgrim, tells of a poor wanderer who heard in church St Paul's words, “pray without ceasing,” and set out to learn how. An old monk taught him to repeat the prayer of Bartimaeus and the tax collector: Lord Jesus Christ, have mercy on me. He walked across Russia praying it with every breath, and found that it filled his heart with peace and love for everyone he met. The cry of a blind beggar outside Jericho became a school of prayer for millions.

pm.open: Lord Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on us. Open our eyes to see your glory and our hearts to follow you. Amen.
share: The work of the Lord is full of his glory (Sirach 42:16). Where have I seen God's glory in creation this week?
Many sternly ordered him to be quiet, but he cried out even more loudly (Mark 10:48). What voices try to silence my prayer, and how do I respond?
What do you want me to do for you? (Mark 10:51). What do I truly want to ask Jesus for today?
pm.resp: By the word of the Lord the heavens were made.
interc: For the Church, that she may always stop, like Jesus, for those who cry out by the roadside.
For the blind and visually impaired, and for eye hospitals and their staff.
For those who are silenced or ignored in our society, that their voice may be heard.
For missionaries who are afraid on their journey, through the prayers of St Augustine of Canterbury.
For our group, that we may follow Jesus on the way after he has healed us.
pm.close: Father, your Son stood still for a blind beggar and gave him sight. Open the eyes of our hearts, that we may follow him on the way. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

quick: Ben Sira praises the ancestors and remembers the godly whom no one remembers: their righteous deeds are not forgotten.
Jesus curses a fig tree with leaves but no fruit, and cleanses the Temple: my house shall be a house of prayer for all the nations.
He teaches his disciples to have faith in God and to forgive whenever they pray.
2027-05-28.action: Forgive one person today before you say your evening prayers.
2027-05-28.question: Is my prayer full of leaves only, or does it bear the fruit of faith and forgiveness?

family.explain: Jesus saw a fig tree with lots of leaves but no fruit. Then he went into the Temple and saw people buying and selling and making noise, instead of praying. He said: God's house is a house of prayer! He taught his friends: have faith in God, and when you pray, forgive anyone who has hurt you.
family.intention: We pray for our grandparents and great-grandparents who handed on the faith to us, living and departed.
family.ask: Ask: “Is there anyone in our family we need to forgive before we pray tonight?”

illus: An illustration

In an old family compound in Kottayam there was a huge mango tree, planted, the family said, by a great-grandmother on the day of her wedding. Every May it was heavy with fruit, and the children of the whole neighbourhood came to share it. Nobody now living had met that great-grandmother, and no book recorded her name. But every year, eating the mangoes, the grandmother of the house would say: this is her fruit, still feeding us; say a Hail Mary for her soul. Ben Sira would have understood: their righteous deeds have not been forgotten. (An illustrative story.)

pm.open: Father, you take delight in your people. Make our hearts fruitful with faith and forgiveness, and our church a true house of prayer. Amen.
share: These also were godly men, whose righteous deeds have not been forgotten (Sirach 44:10). Whose quiet goodness has shaped my faith?
He found nothing but leaves (Mark 11:13). Where is my religious life busy but without fruit?
Whenever you stand praying, forgive (Mark 11:25). Whom do I need to forgive before I can pray with a clean heart?
pm.resp: The Lord takes delight in his people.
interc: For our parish, that it may be a house of prayer for all, welcoming the poor and the stranger.
For grandparents and the elderly who hand on the faith, and for all our departed ancestors.
For those who find it hard to forgive, and for families divided by old quarrels.
For good relations between Christians and the Jewish people, who first loved the Temple of the Lord.
For our group, that our prayer may bear fruit in faith and mercy.
pm.close: Father, your Son cleansed your house and taught us to pray with faith and to forgive. Make us fruitful branches for your glory. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

quick: At the end of his book Ben Sira tells how he sought wisdom in prayer from his youth and found her in purity of heart.
God's law is sweeter than honey and enlightens the eyes.
Asked by what authority he acts, Jesus asks about John's baptism; the leaders, afraid of the crowd, say: We do not know.
2027-05-29.action: Before any study or work today, pray: Lord, give me wisdom.
2027-05-29.question: Do I decide what is true by asking what is right, or by asking what others will think?
kidsaint: St Paul VI

Paul VI was the Pope about fifty years ago. He was the first Pope to travel by aeroplane to many countries, and in 1964 he came to India, to Bombay, for a big celebration of Jesus in the Eucharist. Huge crowds came to see him. He loved the poor so much that he gave away the Pope's beautiful crown, the tiara, to help them, and he gave the car he used in Bombay to Mother Teresa for her work. Lesson: the more important you are, the more you should serve others.

family.explain: A wise man in the Bible tells us: when I was young I prayed to God and asked him for wisdom. Wisdom means knowing what is good and right and doing it. The psalm says that God's words are sweeter than honey! Soon school will start again. Let us ask God to make us wise, not only clever.
family.intention: We pray for children and students preparing for the new school year, and for their teachers.
family.ask: Ask: “What is the difference between being clever and being wise?”

illus: An illustration

When St Paul VI landed in Bombay in December 1964 for the International Eucharistic Congress, he was the first pope ever to set foot in India. Huge crowds of Christians, Hindus, Muslims and others lined the roads. In one of his talks he spoke of the people of India as seekers of God, and he prayed for peace and for the hungry. Before leaving he gave the white car he had used during the visit to Mother Teresa; she raffled it and used the money for her work among people with leprosy. The pope's authority became a gift for the poorest.

pm.open: Lord, giver of wisdom, open our hearts to your truth and make your word sweeter to us than honey. Amen.
share: While I was still young, before I went on my travels, I sought wisdom openly in my prayer (Sirach 51:13). Do I ask God for wisdom before my decisions?
The precepts of the Lord are right, rejoicing the heart (Psalm 19:8). Which commandment of God has brought me joy rather than burden?
We do not know (Mark 11:33). When have I avoided the truth because I feared what others would think?
pm.resp: The precepts of the Lord give joy to the heart.
interc: For the Pope and the bishops, that their authority may always be a service and a witness, through the prayers of St Paul VI.
For students and teachers as the new academic year begins.
For young people seeking their path in life, that they may seek wisdom in prayer.
For all who are afraid to speak the truth, that they may receive courage.
For our group, that God's word may be sweeter to us than honey.
pm.close: Father, you give wisdom to those who ask. Make us humble seekers of your truth and faithful witnesses of your Son. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

quick: Zephaniah calls daughter Zion to rejoice because the Lord, the King of Israel, is in her midst.
Carrying Jesus in her womb, Mary goes with haste to serve Elizabeth, and the child in Elizabeth's womb leaps for joy.
Elizabeth blesses Mary as the mother of my Lord, and Mary sings the Magnificat: my soul magnifies the Lord.
2027-05-31.action: Visit or call someone who needs help this week, and do it promptly and joyfully.
2027-05-31.question: Do I carry Jesus to others, or keep my faith to myself?
catechism: Mary is truly the Mother of God.
The Magnificat, song of Mary and of the Church.
The Hail Mary and Mary as the Ark of the Covenant.
kidsaint: St Elizabeth

Elizabeth was Mary's relative. She and her husband Zechariah had waited many, many years for a baby, and now, when they were old, God gave them a son, John the Baptist! When Mary came to visit, Elizabeth felt her baby jump for joy inside her, and she knew at once that Mary was carrying Jesus. She said to Mary: blessed are you among women! We still say her words every time we pray the Hail Mary. Lesson: God sees those who wait patiently, and he fills them with joy.
2027-05-31.special: Feast of the Visitation of the Blessed Virgin Mary. Gloria; no Creed. Proper readings: Zephaniah 3:14–18a or Romans 12:9–16; Isaiah 12; Luke 1:39–56. Close of the month of May.
term: Magnificat

The song of Mary in Luke 1:46–55, named from its first word in Latin, Magnificat anima mea Dominum, my soul magnifies the Lord. It praises God who lifts up the lowly and fills the hungry, and is sung every evening at Vespers, the Evening Prayer of the Church.

family.explain: After the angel's visit, Mary heard that her old relative Elizabeth was going to have a baby. Mary did not wait; she hurried over the hills to help her. When Mary said hello, the baby inside Elizabeth jumped for joy, because Jesus was inside Mary! Elizabeth said: blessed are you among women! Mary stayed three months to help her.
family.intention: We pray for mothers who are expecting a baby, for elderly people who need help, and for all who serve the sick.
family.ask: Ask: “Who can we visit or help this week, the way Mary helped Elizabeth?” End the month of May by praying the Rosary together tonight.

illus: An illustration

In a hill village in Idukki a young mother in the last months of her own pregnancy heard that her elderly neighbour had fallen and could not leave her bed. Her family told her to rest. Instead she went every morning, slowly, up the steep path with a flask of kanji and a clean towel, and sat with the old woman, praying the Rosary with her. The neighbour said afterwards: when she came through the door, I felt as if Our Lady herself had come in. That is what the Visitation looks like in our hills. (An illustrative story.)

pm.open: Holy Spirit, who filled Elizabeth and moved Mary to go with haste, fill us now with joy and readiness to serve. With Mary we say: my soul magnifies the Lord. Amen.
share: The Lord, your God, is in your midst (Zephaniah 3:17). Do I live with the joy of one in whom God dwells?
Mary set out and went with haste (Luke 1:39). Is there a visit or a service I keep putting off?
He has looked with favor on the lowliness of his servant (Luke 1:48). Where has God lifted me up when I felt small?
pm.resp: Great in your midst is the Holy One of Israel.
interc: For the Church, that like Mary she may go out in haste to serve the poor and the forgotten.
For expectant mothers, especially those who are alone or afraid, and for their unborn children.
For the elderly and housebound, that they may be visited and cared for.
For the hungry and the lowly, that the Lord may fill them with good things through our generosity.
For our group, that we may carry Christ to every home we enter, as Mary did.
pm.close: Father, you inspired the Virgin Mary to visit Elizabeth. Make us attentive to the Spirit and ready to serve, that with Mary we may magnify your name for ever. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

homily: Dear friends, a few weeks ago we heard Jesus say, I am the vine, you are the branches. Today he tells us what flows through that vine: love. As the Father has loved me, so I have loved you; abide in my love (John 15:9). The Father loves the Son; the Son loves us; and we are asked to love one another with that same love.

In the first reading Peter does something new. He enters the house of Cornelius, a Roman officer, a Gentile. Cornelius falls at his feet, and Peter says: stand up; I am only a mortal (Acts 10:26). Then Peter says: I truly understand that God shows no partiality (Acts 10:34). And while he is still speaking, the Holy Spirit falls on everyone in that house. God did not wait for the Church's committee to decide. He poured out his love first.

St John says it in three words: God is love (1 John 4:8). Not that God has some love, but that love is what God is. And this love began with him: not that we loved God but that he loved us and sent his Son (1 John 4:10). We do not earn God's love by being good. We become good because we are loved.

Then Jesus gives the measure: love one another as I have loved you (John 15:12). Not as much as is convenient, not only those who love us back. As I have loved you. And how did he love? No one has greater love than this, to lay down one's life for one's friends (John 15:13). Every mother who sits up at night with a sick child, every husband who forgives, every young person who stands by a friend in trouble, lives a small part of this love.

And then the most beautiful word: I do not call you servants any longer; I have called you friends (John 15:15). We are not servants waiting for orders. We are friends to whom Jesus has told everything. You did not choose me but I chose you. He chose you. Today. Here.

In this month of May, let us stay close to Mary, who knew this love better than anyone. Next Sunday, in India, we will celebrate the Ascension; then we will wait with Mary for the Holy Spirit. Let us open our hearts, our homes and our parish to everyone, as Peter opened his to Cornelius, and let our love be the fruit that lasts. Alleluia. Amen.
kids: Children, who is your best friend? Jesus says: you are my friends! Not my servants, my friends. He tells us everything his Father told him, and he loves us so much that he gave his life for us on the cross.

And Jesus asks us: love one another as I have loved you. That means being kind even to children who are different from us, who speak another language or who have no friends. Let us say: Jesus, my friend, help me to love like you!

homily: Dear friends, when we think of St Paul we imagine a great preacher in a crowded city square. Today's reading shows us something else: a man sitting in a workshop in Corinth, stitching leather for tents. Because he was of the same trade, he stayed with Aquila and Priscilla, and they worked together (Acts 18:3).

Paul could have asked the Christians to support him. Often he refused. He wanted no one to think the Gospel was a business. So he worked with his hands by day and preached by night and on the sabbath. His workshop became a chapel, and his customers heard about Jesus while they waited for their tents.

Not everyone listened. Some in the synagogue opposed him. Paul shook out his clothes, a sign that he had done his part. But see where he went: to the house next door. He did not slam the door; he stayed close. And the official of the synagogue himself, Crispus, believed with his whole household (Acts 18:8). Never give up on anyone.

In the Gospel Jesus prepares his friends for a time of sorrow: a little while, and you will no longer see me. You will weep and mourn, but your pain will turn into joy (John 16:20). Not replaced by joy; turned into joy. God does not throw away our tears. He changes them, as he changed Good Friday into Easter.

Today, in many countries, Christians celebrate the Ascension, the day the apostles stopped seeing Jesus with their eyes. In India we will celebrate it on Sunday. But we are all living in that little while now: we do not see him, yet we believe, we work, we wait.

So take your work today, your kitchen, your field, your office, your studies, and offer it to Christ. Take your sorrows and give them to him too. In his time, every pain offered to him will turn into joy, a joy no one can take from you. Alleluia. Amen.
kids: Children, St Paul had a job! He made tents with his friends Aquila and Priscilla. While he worked, he told people about Jesus.
Jesus said: you will be sad for a little while, but then your sadness will turn into joy. When you feel sad, tell Jesus. He can turn your sad face into a smiling face!

homily: Dear friends, have you ever stood at an airport and watched a plane carry away someone you love? You stand at the glass and watch until it is only a dot, and then it disappears into the clouds. You keep looking a little longer. Then someone touches your shoulder: come, let us go home.

That is what happened to the apostles on the Mount of Olives. Jesus blessed them, and as they were watching, he was lifted up, and a cloud took him out of their sight (Acts 1:9). They kept staring. And two men in white touched their shoulders, so to speak: Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking up toward heaven? (Acts 1:11).

First, the Ascension tells us where Jesus has gone. Not to some planet far away. The cloud in the Bible is the sign of God's glory. Jesus has entered the glory of God, and he has taken our human nature with him: his risen body, with his wounds, now sits at the right hand of the Father (Ephesians 1:20). A man like us is in the heart of God. That is our future too. Where the Head has gone, the Body will follow.

Second, the Ascension tells us that Jesus has not left us. St Paul says God made him the head over all things for the church, which is his body (Ephesians 1:22–23). The Head is in heaven; the Body is here. You are that Body. And Mark tells us something wonderful: they went out and proclaimed the good news everywhere, while the Lord worked with them (Mark 16:20). He sits at the right hand of God and at the same time works with us. He is not further away; he is nearer, because he is no longer in one place but with every disciple everywhere.

Third, the Ascension gives us a job. Go into all the world and proclaim the good news to the whole creation (Mark 16:15). You will be my witnesses to the ends of the earth (Acts 1:8). The angels did not let the apostles stand and stare. Our faith is not only looking up; it is also going out.

Today is World Communications Day. Two thousand years ago the apostles walked on dusty roads. Today the ends of the earth are in your pocket, on your phone. What do you send and forward? Rumours, gossip, anger? Or hope, truth, and the Good News? Every Christian with a phone can be a witness, like St Carlo Acutis, the teenager who used the internet to spread love for the Eucharist.

Finally, the apostles did not rush out at once. Jesus told them to wait for the Holy Spirit. So they went back to Jerusalem and prayed, together with Mary the mother of Jesus (Acts 1:14). We are in those days now. In this Mass the ascended Lord comes down to us in his Body and Blood. Let us receive him, lift up our hearts to where he is, and with Mary pray every day this week: Come, Holy Spirit. Alleluia. Amen.
kids: Children, forty days after Easter, Jesus went up to heaven. A cloud hid him. His friends kept looking up at the sky, and two angels said: why are you looking up? Jesus will come back! Now go and tell everybody about him.
Jesus is in heaven with the Father, and he is also with us every day, especially in Holy Communion. Let us look up and say: Jesus, I love you; and then go and be kind to someone!

opts.a: A life worthy of the calling
intro: In the alternative second reading Paul draws a practical lesson from the Ascension: the risen Lord has gone up and given gifts, so we must live in unity and build up his body.

points.apply: Practise patience with one difficult person this week.

sub: One Lord, one faith, one baptism.
One God and Father of all.
points.apply: Pray for unity in your family, parish and the whole Church.

sub: The psalm of the ascending King.
points.apply: Offer your parish one gift of your time or talent.

concl: The ascended Lord pours out gifts so that his body on earth may grow in unity.
We honour his Ascension by living worthy of our calling.
opts.resolve: This week I will practise patience, pray for unity, and offer my parish one gift.
homily: Dear brothers and sisters, the Ascension can seem far from daily life. Jesus goes up; we stay here. But St Paul draws a very practical lesson from it. Writing from prison, he says: I therefore, the prisoner in the Lord, beg you to lead a life worthy of the calling to which you have been called (Ephesians 4:1).

What does such a life look like? With all humility and gentleness, with patience, bearing with one another in love, making every effort to maintain the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace (Ephesians 4:2–3). The prophet Micah had said the same: to do justice, and to love kindness, and to walk humbly with your God (Micah 6:8). The ascended Lord is not honoured by staring at the sky but by patience in the kitchen, in the office and in the parish committee.

Paul continues: there is one body and one Spirit… one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all (Ephesians 4:4–6). Israel prayed every day: hear, O Israel, the LORD is our God, the LORD alone (Deuteronomy 6:4). Because God is one, his people must be one. Every quarrel in the Church wounds the body whose Head has ascended into heaven.

Then Paul quotes a psalm about a king going up in triumph: when he ascended on high he made captivity itself a captive; he gave gifts to his people (Ephesians 4:8; Psalm 68:18). The ascended Christ does not leave us empty-handed. The gifts he gave were that some would be apostles, some prophets, some evangelists, some pastors and teachers, to equip the saints for the work of ministry, for building up the body of Christ (Ephesians 4:11–12). Every Christian has received a gift for others.

So let us celebrate the Ascension by living worthy of our calling. Be patient with one difficult person. Pray and work for unity. Offer your parish one gift: teaching catechism, singing in the choir, visiting the sick, cleaning the church. And at this Mass, receive the ascended Lord who gives himself as the greatest gift of all. Alleluia. Amen.

intro: Paul prays that the eyes of our hearts may be enlightened to see the hope to which God has called us. The Ascension shows us that hope: Christ in glory, praying for us, and coming again.

points.apply: Ask the Holy Spirit each morning this week: open the eyes of my heart.

points.h: He lives to intercede for us
points.apply: Pray through Christ for someone in great need.

points.h: He will come in the same way
points.apply: Put right one thing you would not want him to find undone.

concl: The ascended Christ is our hope: he is in glory, he prays for us, and he will return.
With enlightened hearts we live in that hope.
opts.resolve: This week I will pray each morning for enlightened eyes and live ready for the Lord's return.
homily: Dear friends, in today's second reading St Paul prays a beautiful prayer for us. He asks that God may give us a spirit of wisdom and revelation, so that, with the eyes of your heart enlightened, you may know what is the hope to which he has called you (Ephesians 1:17–18). The Ascension is about hope, and hope needs eyes of the heart to see it.

Our physical eyes saw the cloud take Jesus away. The eyes of the heart see more. They see that the man Jesus, with his wounded and risen body, now sits at the right hand of the Father. The psalm had foretold it: the LORD says to my lord, sit at my right hand (Psalm 110:1). The psalmist prayed: open my eyes, so that I may behold wondrous things (Psalm 119:18). Let us ask for those eyes today.

What is Jesus doing at the right hand of the Father? The Letter to the Hebrews answers: he is able for all time to save those who approach God through him, since he always lives to make intercession for them (Hebrews 7:25). At this very moment Jesus is praying for you. He shows the Father his wounds and presents your name. When we pray through Christ our Lord, as the Church does at the end of her prayers, we join a prayer that is already rising in heaven.

And the angels promised the apostles: this Jesus, who has been taken up from you into heaven, will come in the same way as you saw him go into heaven (Acts 1:11). Daniel had seen one like a human being coming with the clouds of heaven (Daniel 7:13). Christ will come again in glory to judge the living and the dead. We do not know the day. So the hope of the Ascension is also a call to be ready.

So let us lift the eyes of our hearts. Let us remember that Jesus prays for us. Let us live each day so that we would be glad to see him come. And at this Mass, where the ascended Lord comes to us hidden in bread, let us receive a foretaste of the glory to which he has called us. Alleluia. Amen.

Dear brothers and sisters, happy birthday! Today is the birthday of the Church. Fifty days ago we sang the Alleluia of Easter; today we sing it for the last time in this season, and we celebrate the great gift that Easter was for: the Holy Spirit.

Look at the apostles before Pentecost. They had seen the risen Lord, they had eaten with him, they had watched him ascend. And yet they were still in one room, waiting. Then, when the day of Pentecost had come, suddenly from heaven there came a sound like the rush of a violent wind, and tongues as of fire rested on each of them. All of them were filled with the Holy Spirit (Acts 2:2–4). The same frightened men opened the doors and went out into the street to proclaim the deeds of God.

And what happened outside? People from every nation heard them, each in their own native language. At Babel human pride divided languages and scattered people. At Pentecost God's gift gathered them. Notice: the Spirit did not make everyone speak one language. He made the one Gospel understood in many. Here in India we know what that means. In our country the same Mass is offered and the same Gospel proclaimed in many languages, and it is one faith, one Lord, one Spirit.

St Paul tells us that the Spirit is not only for great events. No one can say Jesus is Lord except by the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 12:3). Every time you pray, even a simple Jesus, I love you, the Spirit is praying in you. And he gives gifts to each one: there are varieties of gifts, but the same Spirit (1 Corinthians 12:4). The gift of teaching, of caring for the sick, of music, of patience with old parents, of making peace. Each is given for the common good. Nobody in the Church is useless; nobody is without a gift.

In the Gospel we go back to Easter evening. The doors are locked; the disciples are afraid. Jesus comes, shows his wounds, and says: Peace be with you. Then he breathed on them and said, Receive the Holy Spirit (John 20:22). Just as God breathed life into Adam at the beginning, the risen Christ breathes new life into his Church. And the first gift of that breath is forgiveness: if you forgive the sins of any, they are forgiven them. Every confession is a little Pentecost, a breath of new life.

Finally, remember who was in the upper room: Mary, the Mother of Jesus, praying with the apostles. The Spirit who overshadowed her at Nazareth now fills the whole Church. Let us ask her to pray with us today. What doors are locked in our lives? What fears keep us silent? Where do we need forgiveness, healing, warmth? Let us pray with the whole Church: Come, Holy Spirit. Heal what is wounded, warm what is cold, guide what has gone astray. Send forth your Spirit, and renew the face of the earth. Amen. Alleluia, alleluia!
kids: Children, today is the birthday of the Church! Fifty days after Easter, the friends of Jesus were praying with Mary. Suddenly, whoosh, a sound like a strong wind! And little flames like fire came on each of them. It was the Holy Spirit! They were not scared any more, and they told everybody about Jesus.
The Holy Spirit lives in you too, from your Baptism. He helps you pray, be kind and be brave. Let us say together: Come, Holy Spirit, fill my heart with your love!

opts.a: The gifts and the fruit of the Spirit
intro: The Spirit who came at Pentecost comes to each of us in Baptism and Confirmation. He brings gifts that strengthen us and fruit that others can see.

sub: Knowledge, piety, fear of the Lord.
points.apply: Each day this week, ask for one of the seven gifts by name.
Ask a family member which fruit of the Spirit you most need.

sub: Peter and John lay on hands.
points.apply: Find out the date of your Confirmation and pray for your sponsor.

concl: The Spirit gives gifts to make us strong and fruit to make us like Christ.
What began at Pentecost continues in every Confirmation.
opts.resolve: This week I will pray daily for the gifts of the Spirit and work on one fruit of the Spirit.
homily: Dear brothers and sisters, at Pentecost the Holy Spirit came upon the apostles with wind and fire. But the Spirit did not come only once, long ago. He comes to every Christian in Baptism and, in a special way, in Confirmation. Today let us look at what he brings: gifts and fruit.

Isaiah foretold the Messiah: the spirit of the LORD shall rest on him, the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and the fear of the LORD (Isaiah 11:2). From this passage the Church names seven gifts: wisdom, understanding, counsel, fortitude, knowledge, piety and fear of the Lord. The Spirit who rested on Christ now rests on us. To each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good (1 Corinthians 12:7).

The gifts make us strong. The fruit shows that the Spirit lives in us. Paul writes: the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, generosity, faithfulness, gentleness, and self-control (Galatians 5:22–23). God had promised: I will put my spirit within you (Ezekiel 36:27). If someone wants to know whether the Spirit lives in me, they should not look for wonders but for this fruit. Am I patient? Am I kind? Can I control my tongue?

In the Acts of the Apostles, when the people of Samaria had been baptised, Peter and John came and laid their hands on them, and they received the Holy Spirit (Acts 8:17). That is the root of our sacrament of Confirmation. Joel had promised: I will pour out my spirit on all flesh (Joel 2:28). The bishop's hand and the holy chrism seal us with the Spirit, to make us witnesses of Christ.

So today let us thank God for our Confirmation. If you were never confirmed, speak to the parish priest. Pray each day this week for one of the seven gifts. Ask someone at home which fruit you most need, and work on it. And at this Mass, let us pray: Come, Holy Spirit, fill the hearts of your faithful. Alleluia. Amen.

opts.a: Father of the poor, best of consolers
intro: Before the Gospel today the Church sings the Golden Sequence, Veni, Sancte Spiritus. It calls the Spirit father of the poor and best of consolers. These titles are a whole teaching on the Spirit.

sub: The Spirit anointed Jesus for the poor.
points.apply: Visit or help one poor person this week in the power of the Spirit.

sub: Rest in labour, comfort in tears.
He stays with us for ever.
points.apply: Console one grieving or lonely person this week.
Before every task this week, pray: Come, Holy Spirit.

concl: The Holy Spirit comes to the poor, consoles the sorrowful and gives life to all.
Without him we can do nothing; with him all things are made new.
opts.resolve: This week I will begin every task with Come, Holy Spirit, and console one person who suffers.
homily: Dear friends, today the Church sings one of her most beautiful prayers, the Golden Sequence: Come, Holy Spirit. It gives the Spirit tender names. Let us reflect on three of them.

First, the Sequence calls him father of the poor. In the synagogue at Nazareth Jesus read from Isaiah: the Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me to bring good news to the poor (Luke 4:18; Isaiah 61:1). The Spirit loves to come where hands are empty. The proud and self-sufficient have no room for him. If you feel poor today, in money, in strength, in faith, you are exactly where the Spirit likes to come.

Second, he is called the best of consolers, rest in our labour, coolness in the heat, comfort in our tears. Jesus promised: I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Advocate, to be with you forever (John 14:16). The prophet had heard God say: comfort, O comfort my people (Isaiah 40:1). The Holy Spirit is God's comfort living in us. He does not always take the sorrow away, but he never leaves us alone in it.

Third, the Sequence admits that without the Spirit there is nothing in us, nothing that is not harmful. The psalm says the same: when you take away their breath, they die and return to their dust. When you send forth your spirit, they are created (Psalm 104:29–30). Even our prayer depends on him: the Spirit helps us in our weakness; for we do not know how to pray as we ought (Romans 8:26). Every good thing we do begins with his breath.

So let us make the Sequence our prayer this week. Before every task, say: Come, Holy Spirit. Visit someone poor and console someone in tears, so that through us the Spirit may be father of the poor and consoler of the sorrowful. And at this Mass, let us ask him to send forth his Spirit and renew our hearts. Alleluia, alleluia! Amen.

Dear friends, the first thing most of us learned as children in church was not a prayer but a gesture. Our mother or grandmother took our small hand and made it touch the forehead, the chest, the left shoulder and the right: in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Today the Church celebrates what that gesture means: the Most Holy Trinity.

We cannot fully understand God. If we could, he would be smaller than our minds. But God has not left us in the dark. In the first reading Moses tells Israel: ask from one end of heaven to the other: has anything so great as this ever happened? The God who spoke from the fire, who rescued his people from Egypt, is the one true God. So acknowledge today and take to heart that the Lord is God in heaven above and on the earth beneath; there is no other (Deuteronomy 4:39). We Christians believe in one God, not three.

But Jesus has shown us the inner life of this one God. He calls God his Father. He promises the Holy Spirit. And St Paul tells us that this Spirit has been given to us: you have received a spirit of adoption. When we cry, “Abba! Father!” it is that very Spirit bearing witness with our spirit that we are children of God (Romans 8:15–16). Think of that. The Spirit, inside you, praying to the Father with the words of the Son. You are not outside the Trinity looking in; you have been brought inside.

In the Gospel the risen Jesus sends the disciples: go therefore and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit (Matthew 28:19). Notice that some of them doubted. Jesus sent them anyway. He does not wait for perfect people. Neither should we wait until we have perfect faith before we share it.

What does the Trinity mean for our daily life? God is a communion of love: the Father loves the Son, the Son loves the Father, and the Holy Spirit is their love in Person. We are made in that image. A family where husband and wife forgive each other, where children are welcomed, where the old are cared for, is a small picture of God. A parish where people of different backgrounds pray and serve together is a picture of God. Selfishness, division, loneliness by choice, these are not God's image.

And finally, Jesus gives the promise that ends Matthew's Gospel: remember, I am with you always, to the end of the age (Matthew 28:20). In every Mass he keeps that promise, coming to us in his Body and Blood. So today, let us make the sign of the cross slowly, with love, and let us live as children of the Father, brothers and sisters of the Son, and temples of the Holy Spirit. Glory be to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit. Amen.
kids: Children, let us make the sign of the cross together, slowly: in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Amen. There is one God, and God is three Persons: the Father who made us, Jesus the Son who saved us, and the Holy Spirit who lives in our hearts.

God is like a family of love that never ends. When you were baptised, God made you part of his family! So every time you make the sign of the cross, you can say: thank you, God, for making me your child.

opts.a: Heirs of God, not slaves of fear
intro: Paul tells the Romans that those led by the Spirit are children of God, and if children, then heirs. The Trinity is not only a mystery to believe but a family that makes us heirs.

sub: As he led Israel in the desert.
points.apply: Before each decision this week, ask the Spirit to lead you.
Name one fear and hand it over to the Father in prayer.
Offer one suffering this week united with Christ.

concl: Through the Son and in the Spirit we become heirs of the Father.
Children of God need not live in fear.
opts.resolve: This week I will let the Spirit lead my decisions and hand my fears to the Father.
homily: Dear brothers and sisters, the mystery of the Holy Trinity can seem far above us. But St Paul shows us that the Trinity is not only something to think about; it is a family into which we have been brought. For all who are led by the Spirit of God are children of God (Romans 8:14).

Led by the Spirit. Isaiah remembered how God guided Israel in the desert: the spirit of the LORD gave them rest. Thus you led your people (Isaiah 63:14). The Spirit is not only a gift we received at Baptism; he is a guide who walks with us each day. When we must decide something about work, family, marriage or money, we can ask: Holy Spirit, lead me.

Paul continues: for you did not receive a spirit of slavery to fall back into fear (Romans 8:15). Many Christians live as if God were a harsh master waiting to punish them. But we are not slaves; we are sons and daughters. When Israel stood trapped at the Red Sea, Moses said: do not be afraid, stand firm, and see the deliverance that the LORD will accomplish for you today (Exodus 14:13). Children of the Father can face life without fear.

And then the greatest promise: if children, then heirs, heirs of God and joint heirs with Christ, if, in fact, we suffer with him so that we may also be glorified with him (Romans 8:17). What do we inherit? Not land or money, but God himself, the life of the Trinity for ever. The path to that inheritance passes through suffering with Christ. But God promises: when you pass through the waters, I will be with you (Isaiah 43:2).

So today let us live as heirs, not slaves. Let the Spirit lead you. Hand your fears to the Father. Unite your sufferings with the Son. And when we make the sign of the cross at this Mass, let us remember that we are signed with the name of the family to which we belong. Glory be to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit. Amen.

intro: Every prayer of the Church is shaped by the Trinity: to the Father, through the Son, in the Holy Spirit. Today we learn to pray as the Church prays.

points.h: To the Father, through the Son, in the Spirit
sub: The pattern of the Church's prayer.
The great Doxology of the Mass.
points.apply: Pay attention to the endings of the prayers at the Mass this Sunday.
Pray the Glory Be slowly after every decade of the Rosary this week.
Teach a child to make the sign of the cross and pray the Glory Be.

concl: Our prayer is a share in the life of the Trinity.
We pray to the Father, through the Son, in the Spirit, and live what we pray.
opts.resolve: This week I will pray the Glory Be with attention and teach it to a child.
homily: Dear friends, have you ever noticed how the prayers at Mass end? The priest prays to the Father, and then concludes: through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, who lives and reigns with you in the unity of the Holy Spirit. Every prayer of the Church has this shape: to the Father, through the Son, in the Spirit. St Paul explains why: for through him both of us have access in one Spirit to the Father (Ephesians 2:18).

We do not pray to a distant God from outside. Through Jesus, and with the Holy Spirit in our hearts, we pray from inside the family of God. Even creation was made this way: by the word of the LORD the heavens were made, and all their host by the breath of his mouth (Psalm 33:6). The Father creates through his Word and by his Breath. At the end of the Eucharistic Prayer, the priest lifts the Body and Blood of Christ and sings: through him, and with him, and in him, O God, almighty Father, in the unity of the Holy Spirit, all glory and honour is yours. And we answer with the great Amen.

Isaiah saw the Lord in the temple, and the seraphim crying: holy, holy, holy is the LORD of hosts; the whole earth is full of his glory (Isaiah 6:3). John heard the same song in heaven (Revelation 4:8). We sing it at every Mass in the Sanctus. This is prayer that asks for nothing; it simply adores. The Glory Be is the same kind of prayer. We say it so quickly. Let us learn to say it slowly, with love.

Jesus sent his disciples to baptise in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, and also: teaching them to obey everything that I have commanded you (Matthew 28:20). Moses had said: keep his statutes and his commandments… for your own well-being and that of your descendants after you (Deuteronomy 4:40). Prayer to the Trinity must become a life of love: in our families, in forgiveness, in care for one another.

So this week, let us listen carefully to the prayers at the Mass. Let us say the Glory Be slowly. And let us teach a child to make the sign of the cross and to pray: Glory be to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit, as it was in the beginning, is now, and ever shall be, world without end. Amen.

Dear brothers and sisters, today the Church kneels in wonder before the greatest gift Jesus left us: his own Body and Blood. In many of our parishes the Blessed Sacrament will be carried through the streets this evening, with candles, flowers, songs and children in white. We do this because we believe that the small white Host is not a thing but a Person: Jesus Christ, the Son of God.

In the first reading Moses stands at the foot of Mount Sinai. The people promise: all that the Lord has spoken we will do. Moses takes the blood of the sacrifice, dashes half of it on the altar and half on the people, and says: see the blood of the covenant (Exodus 24:8). For the people of the Bible, blood is life. The same life touches God's altar and God's people. Now they are one family. That is a covenant.

But that covenant was written in the blood of animals, and the people did not keep their promise. So God made a new covenant. The Letter to the Hebrews says: Christ entered once for all into the Holy Place, not with the blood of goats and calves, but with his own blood (Hebrews 9:12). And his blood does what animal blood could never do: it purifies our conscience from dead works to worship the living God (Hebrews 9:14). It washes not our skin but our heart.

Then the Gospel. In the upper room Jesus takes bread and says: take; this is my body. He takes the cup and says: this is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many (Mark 14:22, 24). The apostles remembered Moses. What Moses sprinkled, Jesus gives to drink, and it is his own blood. He did not say: this is a picture of my body. He said: this is my body. And the Church believes him. The bread becomes his Body, the wine becomes his Blood. It still looks like bread, it still tastes like wine, but it is the Lord.

If we truly believe this, it will change how we come to Mass. We will come on time. We will prepare our hearts, and go to confession when we have sinned seriously. We will receive him with reverence, and say Amen with faith. And we will not run away after Communion, but stay a few moments to thank him. As the Psalm says: what shall I return to the Lord for all his bounty to me? I will lift up the cup of salvation.

Finally the Gospel says: when they had sung the hymn, they went out (Mark 14:26). Jesus went out to give his life. Today we go out in procession, carrying him through our streets, so that our neighbours may see the One who loves them. And when we go home, we carry him too, in our hearts. Let us become what we receive: the Body of Christ, broken and shared for the world. Amen.
kids: Children, at the Last Supper Jesus took bread and said: this is my body. Then he took the cup and said: this is my blood. Jesus loves us so much that he wants to come right into our hearts! At Mass the bread and wine become Jesus himself. It still looks like bread, but it is really Jesus.

So when you see the Host lifted up at Mass, or carried in the procession today, say quietly in your heart: My Lord and my God! And if you have made your First Holy Communion, when you receive Jesus, say thank you to him with all your heart.

opts.a: A large room, furnished and ready
intro: Before the Last Supper Jesus sent two disciples to prepare a room. Today he asks us to prepare a place for him: in our churches, in our homes and in our hearts.

points.h: Where do you want us to go?
sub: Jesus has already chosen the place.
points.apply: Ask Jesus in prayer where he wants to meet you this week.

points.h: Follow the man with the jar
sub: A strange sign in the city.
points.apply: Follow one instruction of the Church you have been neglecting.
Keep the Eucharistic fast carefully and come to Mass early to prepare.

concl: The Lord who gives himself in the Eucharist asks for a prepared place.
A heart made ready receives him with faith and love.
opts.resolve: This week I will prepare for Communion with prayer, confession if needed, and the Eucharistic fast.
homily: Dear brothers and sisters, today's Gospel begins not with the Last Supper itself but with the preparations. On the first day of Unleavened Bread, when the Passover lamb is sacrificed, his disciples said to him: where do you want us to go and make the preparations for you to eat the Passover? (Mark 14:12). They asked. Jesus had already chosen the place.

The Book of Proverbs pictures Wisdom building her house and setting her table, and calling: come, eat of my bread and drink of the wine I have mixed (Proverbs 9:5). Jesus is the Wisdom of God. He has prepared the table long before we arrive. But he wants us to prepare too. Each Sunday the question of the disciples is ours: Lord, where do you want me to meet you?

Jesus gives a strange sign: go into the city, and a man carrying a jar of water will meet you; follow him (Mark 14:13). In those days men rarely carried water jars; it was the work of women. The disciples had to obey before they understood. Isaiah had called: everyone who thirsts, come to the waters (Isaiah 55:1). Sometimes the way to the Eucharist is through simple obedience: to the Sunday obligation, to the one-hour fast, to confession when we have sinned seriously.

Then: he will show you a large room upstairs, furnished and ready. Make preparations for us there (Mark 14:15). The room was ready, but the disciples still had to prepare the meal. The psalm says: you prepare a table before me (Psalm 23:5). God prepares; we prepare. How do we prepare our hearts? With a short prayer before Mass, by arriving early, by an act of contrition, by keeping the Eucharistic fast, by a moment of silent thanks after Communion.

So the disciples set out and went to the city, and found everything as he had told them (Mark 14:16). If we prepare, we will find everything as he promised: the Lord himself, truly present, waiting for us. Let us prepare our churches beautifully, our homes for the procession, and above all our hearts for every Mass. Amen.

opts.a: From the altar to the street
intro: The Lord we receive at the altar is the same Lord we must recognise in the poor. Corpus Christi joins adoration and charity.

points.apply: Spend half an hour in adoration this week.

sub: The mediator of a new covenant.
points.apply: After Communion, ask the Lord to change one thing in your heart.

points.h: The same Lord in the poor
sub: Open your hand to the needy.
points.apply: Do one concrete act of charity this week as the fruit of your Communion.

concl: The Eucharist makes us dwell in Christ and Christ in us.
Whoever adores him at the altar must serve him in the poor.
opts.resolve: This week I will spend time in adoration and serve Christ in one poor person.
homily: Dear friends, today we carry the Blessed Sacrament through our streets. The procession is a picture of the whole Christian life: we begin at the altar and we go out to the street. Let us reflect on that journey.

It begins with communion. Jesus said: those who eat my flesh and drink my blood abide in me, and I in them (John 6:56). To abide means to stay, to make a home. Jesus does not come to us as a visitor who leaves. He wants to make his home in us. The psalm says: O taste and see that the LORD is good (Psalm 34:8). In adoration before the Blessed Sacrament, we learn to stay with him as he stays with us.

The second reading calls Christ the mediator of a new covenant (Hebrews 9:15). Jeremiah had promised: I will put my law within them, and I will write it on their hearts (Jeremiah 31:33). The old covenant was written on stone; the new covenant is written on hearts, and the Eucharist is how God writes. Each Communion, received with faith, changes us a little: we become more patient, more pure, more generous.

And that change must show in the street. St Paul warned that those who eat and drink without discerning the body bring judgment on themselves. St John Chrysostom told his people: do you want to honour the body of Christ? Do not ignore him when he is naked; do not honour him here in church with silk and then neglect him outside, where he is cold and naked. Jesus said: just as you did it to one of the least of these who are members of my family, you did it to me (Matthew 25:40). Moses commanded: open your hand to the poor and needy neighbor in your land (Deuteronomy 15:11).

So let us adore him at the altar and serve him in the street. Spend time in adoration this week. Ask him after Communion to write his law on your heart. And let every Mass end in one act of charity for someone in need. Then the procession will not end today; it will continue every day of our lives. Amen.

Dear friends, Paul and his companions had good plans. They wanted to preach in Asia; the Holy Spirit said no. They tried Bithynia; the Spirit of Jesus did not allow them (Acts 16:7). Two closed doors. And then, at Troas, by the sea, a dream: a man of Macedonia saying, come over to Macedonia and help us (Acts 16:9).

We do not like closed doors. An exam failed, a job refused, a marriage proposal that did not work out, a transfer we did not want. But sometimes God closes a door to keep us for another. Paul did not sit down and sulk at Troas. He prayed, he listened, and when the call came he crossed the sea at once. Because of that crossing, the Gospel came to Europe.

Jesus is honest with us in the Gospel. Not every door will be opened by the world. If the world hates you, be aware that it hated me before it hated you (John 15:18). The servant is not greater than the master. Paul would be beaten in Philippi only days after he landed. Following the Spirit is not always comfortable. But it is always fruitful.

Today is also the first of May, and the Church shows us St Joseph the Worker. People in Nazareth looked down a little on Jesus: is not this the carpenter's son? But Joseph's hidden, honest work kept the Holy Family alive. Let us offer our work to God today, pray for every worker and for those who have no work, and begin this month of May close to our Mother Mary. Amen.
kids: Children, Paul wanted to go somewhere, but God said no. Then God showed him in a dream a man saying: come and help us! So Paul went, and many people came to know Jesus. Sometimes when we do not get what we want, God has a better plan. And today we remember St Joseph, the carpenter who worked hard for Jesus and Mary. Let us help at home today, like Jesus helped Joseph!

homily: Dear friends, today we celebrate two apostles about whom the Gospels say very little: Philip and James. They were not the famous ones like Peter or John. But through them, and through the Twelve, the faith has come down to us. St Paul says: I handed on to you what I in turn had received, that Christ died for our sins, was buried, was raised on the third day, and appeared to Cephas, to the Twelve, and then to James (1 Corinthians 15:3–7).

This is the oldest creed of the Church. It is not a beautiful story invented later. It is the testimony of people who saw the risen Lord with their own eyes, and James was one of them. When we say the Creed on Sunday, we are standing with Philip and James and repeating what they saw.

Look at Philip in the Gospel. He was a practical man. When Jesus asked how to feed five thousand people, Philip calculated: six months' wages would not be enough. And at the Last Supper he asks a very honest question: Lord, show us the Father, and we will be satisfied (John 14:8). Many people today ask the same: show me God, and I will believe.

Jesus answers with tenderness and a little sadness: have I been with you all this time, Philip, and you still do not know me? Whoever has seen me has seen the Father (John 14:9). Philip was looking past Jesus for God. But God was there, at the table, in the face of Jesus. If you want to know what God is like, look at Jesus: touching the leper, forgiving the sinful woman, washing feet, dying on the cross, rising again.

And Philip teaches us how to share this. When he found Jesus, he did not give his friend Nathanael a lecture. He said: come and see (John 1:46). That is still the best way. Bring a friend to Mass, to adoration, to a prayer meeting. Let them see Jesus.

St James, the leader of the Church in Jerusalem, reminds us that faith must be lived: be doers of the word, and not merely hearers (James 1:22). Tradition tells us he died praying for those who killed him. Today let us thank God for the apostles, pray for our bishops, their successors, and ask Philip and James to make us witnesses: people who say, come and see, and people whose lives show what they believe. Amen.
kids: Children, Philip asked Jesus: show us God! And Jesus said: when you see me, you see God the Father. So if you want to know what God is like, look at Jesus: he loves children, he helps the sick, he forgives.
Philip brought his friend to Jesus by saying: come and see! Who can you bring to Jesus? Maybe you can invite a friend to come to church or to say a prayer with you.

homily: Dear friends, picture the scene. Paul and Silas have been stripped and beaten with rods in Philippi. They are in the innermost cell, their feet locked in the stocks. It is dark, it is cold, every bone aches. And about midnight Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God, and the prisoners were listening to them (Acts 16:25).

The other prisoners were listening. People are always listening to how Christians suffer. When we complain, curse and despair, they hear. When we pray and praise God in the middle of pain, they hear that too. A Christian singing at midnight is one of the strongest sermons in the world.

Then the earthquake, the open doors, the jailer with his sword. And Paul's cry: do not harm yourself, for we are all here (Acts 16:28). The prisoners could have run away; they stayed, and their staying saved a life. The jailer asks: what must I do to be saved? Believe on the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved, you and your household (Acts 16:31). By morning there is a baptized family and a joyful meal.
